Which brings us to the hinge point of 1990, when a trio of MIT researchers published The Machine That Changed the World, which both named the Japanese system—“lean production”—and urged corporate America to learn from it. Just then, the Japanese economy crashed, easing the pressure on U.S. firms. In the years that followed, American manufacturers instead doubled down on outsourcing, offshoring, and financial engineering. This round of wounds was self-inflicted. Already infused with a stench of decay, manufacturing was written off as yesterday’s activity. At GE, which produced three of Boeing’s last four CEOs, manufacturing came to be seen as “grunt work,” as the former GE executive David Cote recently told Fortune’s Shawn Tully. Motorola—founded as Galvin Manufacturing and famed for its religious focus on quality—lost its lead in mobile-phone making after it leaned into software and services. Intel’s bunny-suited fab workers were the face of high-tech manufacturing prowess until the company ceded hardware leadership to Asian rivals. “Having once pioneered the development of this extraordinary technology,” the current Intel CEO, Pat Gelsinger, wrote recently, “we now find ourselves at the mercy of the most fragile global supply chain in the world.” Phil Condit, the talented engineer who had overseen design of the hugely successful 777, was atop Boeing when I visited the company in late 2000. He was no stranger to the shop floor. Traversing Boeing’s Everett plant in a golf cart, he pointed out the horizontal tail fin stretching above us. Hard to believe it was larger than the 737’s wing, he marveled. Waiting back in his office—still located on the bank of the Duwamish River but greatly swollen by the recent merger with McDonnell Douglas—was a different sort of glee. “Wow! Double wow!” his mother had emailed him, referring to Boeing’s closing stock price that day. And, it would soon emerge, he wanted to get some distance from what he described to the Puget Sound Business Journal as “how-do-you-design-an-airplane stuff.” The next year, he moved Boeing’s headquarters to Chicago, pulling the top brass away from the shop floor just as the company was embarking on a radically new approach to airplane assembly. Its newest plane, the 787 Dreamliner, would not be an in-house production. Instead Boeing would farm out the designing and building to a network of “partner” companies—each effectively its own mini-Boeing with its own supply chain to manage. “It used to be you’d have some Boeing people develop the blueprints, then march over and say, ‘Hey, would you build this for me?’” Richard Safran, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners and a former aerospace engineer, told me. “Now, instead, you’re asking them to design it, to integrate it, to do the R&D.” The allures of this “capital light” approach were many: Troublesome unions, costly machine shops, and development budgets would all become someone else’s problem. Key financial metrics would instantly improve as costs shifted to other firms’ balance sheets. With its emphasis on less, the approach bore a superficial resemblance to lean production. But where lean production pushed know-how back onto the shop floor, this pushed the shop floor and its know-how out the door altogether. Beyond that were the problems that a Boeing engineer, L. J. Hart-Smith, had foreseen in a prescient white paper that he presented at a 2001 Boeing technical symposium. With outsourcing came the possibility that parts wouldn’t fit together correctly on arrival. “In order to minimize these potential problems,” Hart-Smith warned, “it is necessary for the prime contractor to provide on-site quality, supplier-management, and sometimes technical support. If this is not done, the performance of the prime manufacturer can never exceed the capabilities of the least proficient of the suppliers.” Boeing didn’t listen. Wall Street dismissed Hart-Smith’s paper as a “rant,” and Boeing put each supplier in charge of its own quality control. When those controls failed, Boeing had to bear the cost of fixing flawed components. Most troubling was the dangerous feedback loop Hart-Smith foresaw. Accounting-wise, those fixes, which in reality are the costs of outsourcing, would instead appear as overhead—creating the impression that in-house work was expensive and furthering the rationale for offloading even more of the manufacturing process. In the short term, this all worked wonders on Boeing’s balance sheet: Its stock rose more than 600 percent from 2010 to 2019. Then the true folly of this approach made its inevitable appearance when two strikingly similar crashes caused by faulty software on Boeing planes killed a total of 346 people. Today, if you stand along the Seattle waterfront long enough, sooner or later you’ll catch sight of a train headed south carrying the distinctive shape of a Boeing 737. Though it’s colored a metallic green and missing its tail—clearly not the finished product—it’s the kind of thing you point to and say, Look kids, a Boeing plane’s on that train! Not so. The logomark on the side spells it out: Spirit AeroSystems of Wichita, Kansas, has built this fuselage, which isn’t coming from Boeing. It’s going to Boeing. A plane is a complex system in which the malfunction of one piece can produce catastrophic failure of the whole. Assembly must be tightly choreographed. But now—especially with Boeing continually trying to wring costs from its suppliers—there were many more chances for errors to creep in. And when FAA investigators finally toured the premises of Spirit AeroSystems—maker of the blown-out door as well as the fuselage it was supposed to fit in—they did not find a tight operation. They found one door seal being lubricated with Dawn liquid dish soap and cleaned with a wet cheesecloth, and another checked with a hotel-room key card. A dark age doesn’t descend all at once. The process of emerging from one also takes time. It must begin with a recognition that something has been lost. Boeing’s fall just might have provided that rush of clarity. You could be from the 12th century and still know that soap and cheesecloth aren’t for making flying machines. Boeing’s chief financial officer recently admitted that the company got “a little too far ahead of itself on the topic of outsourcing.” It is in talks to reacquire Spirit AeroSystems and is already making the composite wings of its next-gen plane, the 777X, in-house at a new, billion-dollar complex outside Seattle. “Aerospace Executives Finally Rediscover the Shop Floor,” Aviation Week declared on the cover of a recent issue. As for the rest of corporate America, one of the strongest signals may be coming from the company Boeing has striven so hard to emulate: GE. Under operations-minded boss Larry Culp, the company is finally—only 40 or so years late—pushing itself through a crash course in lean manufacturing. It is belatedly yielding to the reality that workers on the gemba are far better at figuring out more efficient ways of making things than remote bureaucrats with spreadsheet abstractions. In the crucial field of semiconductors, meanwhile, Intel has recognized that Moore’s Law (the doubling of computing power roughly every 18 months) flows not from above but from manufacturing advances it once dominated. It has undertaken a “death march,” in the words of CEO Pat Gelsinger, to regain its lost edge on the foundry floor. The CHIPS Act has put a powerful political wind at his back. Green and other incentives are powering a broader, truly seismic surge in spending on new U.S. factories, now going up at three times their normal rate. No other country is experiencing such a buildout. Add all the capacity you want. It won’t reverse the country’s long decline as a manufacturing superpower if corporate America keeps gurgling its sad, tired story about the impossibility of making things on these shores anymore. It’s a story that helped pour a whole lot of wealth into the executive pockets peddling it. But half a century of self-inflicted damage is enough. The doors have fallen off, and it’s plain for all to see: The story was barely bolted together.

item.title: Amazon plots a new 'Tetromino' warehouse where robots tackle work that's notoriously hard to automate
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.89
Amazon is developing a new generation of highly automated warehouses that use AI and robotics to process packages at the final stop before delivery. The initiative, internally called Project Tetromino, is intended to build "fully automated" delivery stations, according to an internal planning document from last month that Business Insider reviewed. Delivery stations are the final facility in the shipping process, receiving packaged items from fulfillment centers before sorting and staging them for drivers to deliver to customers. According to the document, Amazon planned to invest $103 million in an initial Tetromino pilot in 2028, followed by five sites in 2029 and 10 more in 2030. Each 2029 site could cost about $85 million, bringing the total Tetromino investment to more than $530 million by 2029, the document said. It also said Tetromino could process packages at roughly 2.5 times the rate of its existing delivery station design. An Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider that this is an "early-stage concept" and the specific financial figures and road map in the document are "inaccurate and don't reflect our current plans." "We're always exploring and testing new technologies across our operations to improve safety and the delivery experience for customers," the spokesperson said. "Like any early-stage concept, this is one of many initiatives we regularly evaluate, and plans evolve significantly as we learn." Tetromino offers a glimpse of how Amazon is trying to automate one of the most stubbornly manual parts of its logistics network. Industry analysts say tasks such as organizing and loading packages into vehicles at delivery stations remain difficult and expensive to automate. The project comes as Amazon accelerates a broader warehouse automation push. On its latest earnings call in July, the company said it expects to more than double its fleet of robotic arms in 2026. Business Insider previously reported that Amazon is also deploying software that automatically recommends where warehouse workers should be assigned as workloads change. Amazon's Tetris-like challenge One of Tetromino's key technologies could come from Boxbot, an AI and robotics supply chain startup, according to the planning document. Boxbot's system moves packages from conveyors onto trays for storage, then uses AI to retrieve and sequence them for delivery. Boxbot's website says the system can make the vehicle-loading process up to 10 times faster. Boxbot did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. The Tetromino name itself may be a nod to the game Tetris, reflecting the puzzle-like challenge of efficiently organizing packages for delivery vehicles. Amazon isn't alone in trying to automate these tasks. FedEx is expanding its use of AI-powered Dexterity robots that autonomously load packages into trailers, while UPS and DHL use robots for unloading. The Amazon spokesperson also pointed to delivery station pilots announced last year as part of a €700 million investment in European facilities, including machines that unload, sort, and scan packages. The push toward more automated facilities raises questions about what Amazon's warehouses will ultimately need humans to do. Amazon robotics chief Tye Brady previously told Business Insider that robots are intended to make frontline work safer and more efficient, not replace employees. Nevertheless, Amazon has internally projected that some warehouse robots will "flatten" its hiring curve over the next decade, Business Insider previously reported. The Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider the company's delivery-station initiatives are "designed to complement and empower our workforce and employees remain central to how we operate." item.title: The job market for entry-level workers in the UK hasn't been this tough in years
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.85
The UK job market is looking grim for people fresh out of university. According to the latest UK Job Market Report from job-matching platform Adzuna, the company's index — which aggregates online listings from more than 1,000 sources — counted an average of 8,383 live UK graduate vacancies in July. That's down 45.6% from July 2025 and the lowest level since Adzuna launched the monthly series in April 2016. The figure has collapsed from more than 55,000 at its mid-2017 peak. Adzuna's broader entry-level category was less stark but still weak, falling 8.1% year over year. Across the market, vacancies also declined, while competition for each opening increased. "July's numbers are a step backwards, not a blip," Andrew Hunter, Adzuna's cofounder, said in a press release on Monday. "We'd been watching things improve gradually for months, but that stopped in July. The graduate job market also keeps setting new lows, which tells us employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring at that level." Findings from Indeed also point to a decline in listings, albeit a less dramatic one. In a report published on the 3rd of August, Indeed said postings with "graduate" in the title were down about 7% year over year as of July 10, their lowest level for that point in the year since 2020. The squeeze reflects more than one problem. Employers are contending with a sluggish economy, higher costs, and uncertainty. AI is also reshaping the bottom rungs of the career ladder by taking on routine work once assigned to junior employees. A PwC analysis, released in June and based on more than 1 billion job ads globally, found that US entry-level roles exposed to AI were seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills than comparable roles were in 2019. Companies are responding in different ways. EY has turned an eight-week internship into a yearlong residency to build judgment and critical-thinking skills, while PwC's UK arm cut its graduate intake amid economic weakness, AI, and offshoring. There are bright spots for entry-level workers: IBM, LinkedIn, and other employers are expanding early-career engineering programs, betting that AI-native graduates can be an advantage.

item.title: America's robotics industry sees a familiar 'Made in China' problem
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.40
The brains may come from the US, but the body could very well be Made In China. At Physical Intelligence, a San Francisco-based startup, cofounder and researcher Sergey Levine is building the models, or brains, designed to provide intelligence for a range of robots — be they warehouse robots or humanoid machines. Physical Intelligence is one of many startups in Silicon Valley working on robotics software. In an episode of The Peterman Pod published Monday, Levine said the US robotics industry has its own advantages against competition abroad, but the one area that could significantly advance America's progress is building the hardware supply chain. "Availability of reliable low-cost hardware is a big deal. And right now, hardware used for robotics research — a lot of that does come from China," Levine said. "It's good. It's relatively inexpensive. It's of high quality and meets the standards that people generally need. But it'd be awfully nice to be able to source all of that domestically as well. I don't think there's anything impossible about that." Building an AI capable of making robots smart enough to handle a wide range of tasks is only part of the industry's challenge. In the US in particular, robotics leaders have said sourcing the physical components for robots — the motors, chassis, batteries, sensors, and other materials — will be a major bottleneck for scaling, and that companies often rely on China to fill the gaps. "The United States is no longer competitive in manufacturing, and we're falling further behind every day. Any company that builds hardware can tell you that if you source from China instead of making it here, it's generally 5 to 10 times cheaper," Evan Beard, CEO of Standard Bots, said during a congressional hearing in April. A June analysis from McKinsey found that China holds a "significant share of capacity" for robotics parts, including 90% of permanent-magnet processing. China's progress, according to the report, is due in part to its electric vehicle ecosystem, which shares some of the components needed in robots. US robotics executives and policymakers say China's rapid progress in robotics and AI — combined with a strong manufacturing base — could hamper America's ability to effectively compete in what they view as a critical emerging industry. The concern is heightened as Washington sees China as a strategic adversary. In July, the Federal Communications Commission effectively blocked new foreign-made humanoids and other advanced robots from entering the US market, citing national security concerns. While US manufacturers welcomed the move, some researchers and startups told Business Insider's robotics reporter, Rya Jetha, that the ban locks out access to affordable hardware. Levine said in the podcast that "different industries that contribute to robotics need to individually be very healthy." "I think that it's important to sort of fully embrace that this is a holistic thing and not something where we can do just one piece of it and outsource everything else," he said. Have a tip? item.title: Netflix parts ways with a key ad exec in a leadership shake-up. Read the leaked memo from its ad chief.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.78
Netflix is shaking up its ads leadership. Jon Whitticom, a prominent Netflix exec who helped build the streamer's advertising business, is leaving the organization, according to a memo viewed by Business Insider. Advertising president Amy Reinhard shared the news with staff last week, saying she had "decided to part ways" with Whitticom. She added that ads product exec Marc Heneghan would lead the unit on an interim basis while a search is conducted for Whitticom's replacement. "At Netflix, we expect our leaders to build and maintain trust, share context generously, collaborate cross-functionally, and cultivate an environment where people can do their best work," she wrote. "Jon and I have discussed these needs directly over time, and my decision reflects this standard now and going forward." The ads business is one of the key levers Netflix is leaning on, along with live sports and creator content, as Wall Street worries about the streamer's US engagement growth slowing. The company said this year that in countries where it offers an ads tier, more than 60% of new subscribers choose its cheaper, ad-supported plan. Whitticom, Netflix's VP of ads product, started as an ad platform advisor in early 2023. His role was closely watched because of its potential to help Netflix decide how to level up its then-nascent advertising business. He previously was chief product officer at Comcast-owned ad startup FreeWheel. Under Whitticom, Netflix built out its ad tech and enabled advertisers to buy its ads through other companies like Google, The Trade Desk, and Magnite. The buildout has also had bumps along the way, with multiple leadership changes and competing internal visions over how to grow the business. "Speed got us from zero to one," Reinhard wrote in her memo. "Getting to what's next means knowing when to move fast and how to do it together." Netflix has said it expects to hit $3 billion in ad revenue this year, nearly doubling its 2025 haul. The company is also introducing new ad formats and expanded ways for advertisers to buy inventory, Reinhard said in an announcement concluding its Upfront sales process, where TV companies pitch big advertisers for extensive ad deals. Here's the full memo from Reinhard: Team, I wanted to let you know about a leadership change I'm making to better reflect the needs of the business and the growth ahead in Ads. After careful consideration, I've decided to part ways with Jon Whitticom, and today will be his last day. Jon helped build Ads Product from the ground up and led the launch of the Netflix Ads Suite last year, a major milestone for our business and Netflix. I'm grateful for all his contributions over the past two-plus years. At Netflix, we expect our leaders to build and maintain trust, share context generously, collaborate cross-functionally, and cultivate an environment where people can do their best work. Jon and I have discussed these needs directly over time, and my decision reflects this standard now and going forward. Speed got us from zero to one. Getting to what's next means knowing when to move fast and how to do it together. Marc Heneghan will lead Ads Product on an interim basis while I immediately begin an external search for a new leader. All of Jon's directs will now report to Marc. There's never a good moment for a change like this; I know it often carries risk and disruption. But I also know this team is resilient and our foundation is strong. What isn't changing are our priorities as a business, or my confidence in this team's ability to stay focused on the bigger picture and maintain our momentum on our near-term deliverables. I will host separate sessions with the Ads Product team and the Ads Platform teams to talk through our path forward and answer any questions. Those teams should look out for a calendar invite to join a session. Please join me in thanking Jon and wishing him the best in the future. Best, Amy

item.title: The most iconic breakfast restaurant in every state
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.71
Breakfast is often cited as the most important meal of the day, so why waste it on a bowl of cereal? Across the country, hole-in-the-wall diners, cozy cafés, and decades-old institutions have become known for signature breakfast dishes, famous customers, or simply for serving generations of loyal regulars. While there might be some debate about which spot is truly the most iconic, we identified famous breakfast restaurants in every state based on their longevity, reputation, famous dishes, and local history. From beignets at New Orleans' Café du Monde to classic Southern breakfasts at The Waysider in Tuscaloosa, these restaurants offer more than a good plate of eggs and pancakes — they offer a slice of local pride. Here are some of the most iconic breakfast restaurants in every state. ALABAMA: The Waysider Restaurant in Tuscaloosa The Waysider is a Tuscaloosa institution. In fact, it's the city's oldest operating restaurant. Legendary Alabama football coach Bear Bryant was a regular, and the restaurant is still filled with memorabilia for all devoted Roll Tide fans to enjoy. It's known for classic Southern breakfasts, including biscuits, grits, country ham, and gravy. ALASKA: Snow City Cafe in Anchorage Snow City Cafe has been a popular downtown Anchorage breakfast spot since its opening in 1998. During a 2015 visit to the state, President Barack Obama stopped by the cafe and ordered $18.25 worth of cinnamon rolls and muffins to go, the Anchorage Daily News reported. The menu includes Alaskan takes on breakfast classics, including eggs Benedict with salmon cakes. ARIZONA: Matt's Big Breakfast in Phoenix Matt's Big Breakfast opened in downtown Phoenix in 2004 in a small, 800-square-foot space. It quickly became known for its long lines. They've since expanded into a larger location due to demand. The restaurant focuses on simple breakfasts made with high-quality ingredients, including cage-free eggs, freshly squeezed orange juice, and real maple syrup. The restaurant later appeared on an episode of Guy Fieri's "Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives," cementing its status as a local legend. ARKANSAS: The Pancake Shop in Hot Springs The Pancake Shop has served breakfast in downtown Hot Springs since 1940, making it one of the city's longtime dining institutions. The restaurant is known for its made-from-scratch pancakes, fresh-squeezed orange juice, and homemade sausage, and its original 1940 menu still hangs inside for patrons to see. CALIFORNIA: Du-par's Restaurant & Bakery in Los Angeles Du-par's has been a local institution since James Dunn and Edward Parsons opened it at the Original Farmers Market in Los Angeles in 1938. The restaurant is best known for its buttermilk hotcakes, made with the same recipe the kitchen used in 1938. Along with its famous pancakes, the longtime diner is known for other classic American comfort foods, diner favorites, and housemade pies and pastries. COLORADO: Snooze, an A.M. Eatery in Denver Opened by brothers Adam and Jon Schlegel in Denver's Ballpark neighborhood in 2006, Snooze has become one of Denver's best-known brunch spots. It later expanded into a national chain and now operates about 70 locations across 10 states. It's particularly known for creative pancake flavors, eggs Benedict, and its pancake flight, which lets diners choose several pancake flavors. CONNECTICUT: Laurel Diner in Southbury Laurel Diner has been serving Southbury since 1949 and retains the feel of a traditional roadside diner. The small cash-only restaurant still has its counter stools and serves classic diner breakfasts, including its best-known dish, its house-made corned beef hash and home fries. DELAWARE: The Kozy Korner in Wilmington Kozy Korner traces its history to 1922, when John Vouras opened the original restaurant in Wilmington. Although its original building was demolished in 1984, the family-run restaurant continued in a new location with another crowd-pleasing menu. The restaurant has been repeatedly recognized by Delaware Today for serving the best breakfast in the state, according to its website. FLORIDA: Blue Heaven in Key West Blue Heaven, which is located in a venue with a history tied to Ernest Hemingway, opened in Key West's Bahama Village in 1992. The restaurant is known for its outdoor courtyard, roaming chickens, and live music, as well as its popular breakfast favorites, including eggs Benedict, shrimp and grits, and pancakes. GEORGIA: Home Grown in Atlanta Home Grown, which opened in Atlanta in 2010, has become one of the city's best-known breakfast spots, serving traditional Southern comfort food in a casual, retro-country diner setting. Featured in the Michelin Guide, the restaurant is especially famous for its Comfy Chicken Biscuit, which combines fried chicken, a large Southern biscuit, and sausage gravy. HAWAII: Eggs 'n Things in Honolulu Eggs 'n Things, which has been serving breakfast in Honolulu since 1974, has largely become known for its large breakfast plates, particularly pancakes topped with local fruit and generous amounts of whipped cream. The restaurant's popularity in the community and among tourists has led to additional locations in Guam, Hawaii, and Japan. IDAHO: Goldy's Breakfast Bistro in Boise Goldy's Breakfast Bistro has been a downtown Boise breakfast destination since 1999. The small restaurant is known for its eggs Benedict and large breakfast plates, including diner favorites such as chicken-fried steak. ILLINOIS: Lou Mitchell's in Chicago Lou Mitchell's has been serving Chicago since 1923, predating the establishment of nearby Route 66 by three years. Its location near the highway's historic starting point made the restaurant a longtime stop for travelers beginning the drive west, and it's also listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The restaurant is also known for handing out complimentary doughnut holes to customers waiting for a table — a tradition that dates back decades. INDIANA: Cafe Patachou in Indianapolis The first Cafe Patachou opened in Indianapolis in 1989, and the café has since built its reputation on made-to-order breakfasts and relationships with local farmers and producers. Bon Appétit later named it one of the country's best breakfast spots, according to the restaurant's website. IOWA: Waveland Cafe in Des Moines Waveland Cafe has been serving Des Moines since 1984 and is best known for its hash browns, which the restaurant calls the "best hashbrowns in the galaxy." Its customers over the years have included politicians, journalists, and celebrities, including Iowa local Jason Momoa, who called the establishment his favorite breakfast spot. The restaurant even named its signature breakfast, the "Da Momoa," after the actor. It includes a full order of hash browns, a full order of biscuits and gravy, two sunny-side-up eggs, and a side of bacon. KANSAS: Doo-Dah Diner in Wichita Doo-Dah Diner opened in Wichita in 2012 and built a following with its oversize takes on classic breakfast plates and complimentary sticky monkey bread. Other menu favorites include banana-bread French toast and the Brutus, which combines chicken-fried steak, hash browns, sausage gravy, onions, and eggs. KENTUCKY: Wagner's Pharmacy in Louisville Open since 1922, Wagner's Pharmacy has been located across from Churchill Downs and has spent much of that time feeding horse trainers, jockeys, owners, and racing fans who gather there from near and far. Its walls are covered in horse-racing memorabilia, and the restaurant has appeared in movies including "Secretariat," making it a local institution, particularly during Derby season. LOUISIANA: Café du Monde in New Orleans Café du Monde has been serving customers in New Orleans' French Market since 1862. Its menu is famously limited, with its best-known order consisting of three fried beignets covered in powdered sugar and a cup of chicory coffee or café au lait. The combination has become one of the foods most closely associated with New Orleans, making the café not just a breakfast spot but also a tourist destination. MAINE: Palace Diner in Biddeford Palace Diner may be small, but it is entirely worth the cramped quarters. The restaurant, housed in a former train dining car, has been in operation since 1927. Visitors flock to the unique restaurant for a classic diner breakfast, fried chicken sandwich, and other diner specialties. MARYLAND: Miss Shirley's Cafe in Baltimore Miss Shirley's Cafe has been putting a Maryland spin on Southern breakfast since it opened in Baltimore in 2005. Named after founder Eddie Dopkin's friend Shirley McDowell, the restaurant is known for dishes like shrimp and grits, chicken and waffles, and several takes on eggs Benedict. In a state famous for seafood, the menu also finds plenty of ways to bring local flavors into brunch. MASSACHUSETTS: Miss Florence Diner in Florence Miss Florence Diner doesn't have to try overly hard or stock up on kitschy decor to look like an old-fashioned diner. Operating from a preserved Worcester Lunch Car Company dining car, the vintage diner still has many of its original features and was even added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1999. More than 80 years after its founding, it's still serving pancakes, eggs, bacon, and other classic New England diner breakfasts. MICHIGAN: Golden Harvest in Lansing This small Lansing restaurant is covered in colorful signs, stickers, and artwork inside and out, making it hard to miss when driving through town. In addition to its quirky decor, this restaurant is equally well known for its over-the-top breakfasts, from creative pancakes and French toast to massive omelets. It's also known for long waits, limited seating, and a daily menu written on whiteboards that changes frequently. MINNESOTA: Al's Breakfast in Minneapolis Al's Breakfast in the city's Dinkytown neighborhood has been a Minneapolis institution since 1950, and customers regularly line up behind the restaurant's limited number of stools waiting for their turn to eat. The tiny restaurant has also received one of the industry's biggest honors — a James Beard America's Classics award — and has also been featured on "Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives." MISSISSIPPI: Big Bad Breakfast in Oxford Big Bad Breakfast has expanded across the South, but it got its start in Oxford in 2008. The restaurant comes from James Beard Award-winning chef John Currence, who built the menu around Southern breakfast staples like biscuits, grits, eggs, and house-cured meats. Its success in Oxford eventually turned Big Bad Breakfast into a regional chain with locations across several states. MISSOURI: Billy Gail's Restaurant in Branson Billy Gail's is the kind of breakfast place where ordering pancakes can become a photo opportunity. The Branson-area restaurant is famous for its enormous omelets and pancakes, which stretch well beyond the edges of the plate, along with oversize portions of biscuits and gravy, French toast, and other diner favorites. The large portions and cozy diner setting have made it a popular breakfast stop for visitors and locals alike. MONTANA: The Western Cafe in Bozeman The Western Cafe has been part of downtown Bozeman since it opened in the 1940s and is now run by three generations of the same Montana family. Its menu is about as Montana as breakfast gets, with dishes like chicken-fried steak and eggs, biscuits and gravy, and its famous "Bobcat" French toast, a nod to the nearby Montana State University. NEBRASKA: Tina's Cafe in Lincoln You might want to bring someone along if you're looking to split a cinnamon roll at Tina's Cafe. This small Lincoln restaurant is known for scratch-made cinnamon rolls that are roughly the size of a dinner plate and dripping with icing, along with hand-shredded hash browns and other classic breakfasts. NEVADA: The Peppermill Restaurant and Fireside Lounge in Las Vegas The Peppermill has been serving the Las Vegas Strip since 1972, and its neon-lit, over-the-top interior still pays homage to that era. The restaurant is known for large breakfast portions and its adjoining Fireside Lounge, complete with a sunken fire pit. The restaurant has also appeared in iconic movies and TV shows, including "Casino," and in 2024, the James Beard Foundation named the Peppermill an America's Classics award winner. NEW HAMPSHIRE: Polly's Pancake Parlor in Sugar Hill Polly's Pancake Parlor has been serving pancakes in New Hampshire's White Mountains since 1938, when Polly and Wilfred Dexter began making them to promote their homemade maple products. Back then, you could order all-you-can-eat pancakes, waffles, and French toast for 50 cents. The restaurant won a James Beard America's Classics award in 2006. NEW JERSEY: Tops Diner in East Newark NEW MEXICO: Frontier in Albuquerque Frontier has been a favorite among University of New Mexico students and Albuquerque locals since it opened in 1971. It's best known for Southwestern breakfast staples like burritos, homemade tortillas, and its famous Frontier Sweet Roll, a large cinnamon roll. NEW YORK: Clinton St. Baking Company in New York City Clinton St. Baking Company has been open on the Lower East Side of Manhattan since 2001 and has become known for its fluffy pancakes with specialty toppings like maple butter or wild Maine blueberries. Prepare to wait a while to grab breakfast here — wait times can stretch up to two hours at peak weekend brunch times. NORTH CAROLINA: Big Ed's City Market Restaurant in Raleigh Big Ed's was opened in 1958 by Wake County native "Big Ed" Watkins, who used recipes from his family's farm to inspire the first menu. The City Market location opened in 1989 and has become one of the most popular breakfast destinations in Raleigh, specializing in old-fashioned North Carolina country breakfasts with plenty of biscuits, eggs, country ham, and grits. NORTH DAKOTA: The Shack on Broadway in Fargo The Shack on Broadway isn't anything fancy, but its all-day breakfast has kept locals coming back again and again. Famous for its buttermilk pancakes, omelets, hash browns, and other classic diner breakfast staples, this breakfast spot's straightforward menu has made it a longtime favorite in Fargo. OHIO: Sugar n' Spice in Cincinnati Sugar n' Spice has served the Cincinnati community since 1941, and very little has changed at the diner since then. Known for its thin pancakes and fluffy, oversize omelets, this longtime favorite breakfast spot also sends each guest home with something less edible, but just as memorable: tiny rubber ducks. OKLAHOMA: Cafe Kacao in Oklahoma City Cafe Kacao, which opened in 2006, stands out among Oklahoma City institutions for its focus on Guatemalan and Latin American flavors. Featured on Yelp's list of the 100 best restaurants in the country and named best breakfast in Oklahoma by the Travel Channel, one bite of this family-owned restaurant's breakfast will show you why it's so acclaimed. OREGON: Otis Cafe in Lincoln City Otis Cafe was originally housed in an iconic historic building before a 2019 fire forced it to relocate to a new location in the Taft district. This family-run restaurant is known for serving scratch-made breakfast all day and for a few German breakfast classics, including German-style potatoes and marionberry pie. PENNSYLVANIA: Shady Maple Smorgasbord in East Earl Shady Maple is one of the most famous breakfast buffets in the country, but even that reputation doesn't quite capture its scale. Opened in 1985, Shady Maple has grown into a 161,000-square-foot restaurant that can seat nearly 1,200 people at one time. Its breakfast offerings include an enormous spread of eggs, pancakes, meats, baked goods, and Pennsylvania Dutch specialties — all served in what has been described as the largest buffet in the country. RHODE ISLAND: Modern Diner in Pawtucket While Rhode Island may be better known for its seafood, this classic Ocean State diner also reflects the small state's culinary history. Housed inside a 1940 Sterling Streamliner, Modern Diner was the first diner in the country to be accepted onto the National Register of Historic Places — it was listed in 1978. It is a Pawtucket landmark, famous for its classic breakfast plates and distinctive decor. SOUTH CAROLINA: Millers All Day in Charleston Millers All Day may not be the most historic restaurant on this list, but it's just as iconic. Opened in 2018 and helmed by chef Nathan Thurston and farmer and miller Greg Johnsman, the menu features a modern spin on classic Southern breakfast favorites like biscuit sandwiches and shrimp and grits. SOUTH DAKOTA: Phillips Avenue Diner in Sioux Falls Phillips Avenue Diner is known throughout the state for its retro feel and massive breakfast plates, including pancakes, omelets, and other classic American breakfast items. The restaurant operated as the Market Diner inside a silver Airstream trailer until 1996, when it moved to downtown Sioux Falls and became known as the Phillips Avenue Diner in a new brick-and-mortar location. TENNESSEE: The Loveless Cafe in Nashville The Loveless Cafe opened in 1951, when Lon and Annie Loveless began serving homemade fried chicken and biscuits to travelers from their home along Highway 100. Their food was so popular that the Lovelesses turned their house into a full-blown restaurant and added a 14-room motel to expand their business. More than 70 years later, Annie's famous biscuits are still a signature item on the menu, and the Nashville landmark welcomes more than half a million visitors a year, according to the restaurant's website. TEXAS: The Breakfast Klub in Houston Opened in 2001, The Breakfast Klub has become one of Houston's most iconic institutions, thanks to its famous "Katfish" and grits and wings and waffles. The Black-owned restaurant has garnered national recognition from outlets including "Good Morning America," USA Today, Esquire, and Forbes. UTAH: Ruth's Diner in Emigration Canyon Ruth's Diner allows guests to dine in a former trolley car that operated in the early 1900s, but has since been moved and restored. The restaurant focuses on brunch foods, serving cinnamon roll French toast, huevos rancheros, and deep-fried mac and cheese. When "Diners, Drive-Ins, and Dives" host Guy Fieri visited the restaurant, he said he couldn't get enough of the fluffy biscuits. VERMONT: Maple Sugar & Vermont Spice in Mendon Perhaps nothing is more signature Vermont than pancakes with maple syrup. Maple Sugar & Vermont Spice is located right where the action is, on the grounds of a historic Mendon maple farm, where visitors can watch sap being boiled into syrup. In addition to pancakes, guests can try the famous syrup with other breakfast staples, or purchase maple candy and other products to take home. VIRGINIA: Pocahontas Pancake in Virginia Beach Pocahontas Pancake and Waffle House has been serving up breakfast in the Virginia Beach oceanfront area since 1974, but rose to national fame in 2002 when the Food Network's "Best Of" series named it the best pancake house in Virginia Beach. Its most popular menu item is, unsurprisingly, its pancakes drenched in butter and maple syrup, but it also serves other breakfast staples like Belgian waffles, French toast, eggs, and omelets. WASHINGTON: Maltby Cafe in Snohomish Built in 1937, Maltby Cafe has served breakfasts for decades from the basement of a former schoolhouse gym. The restaurant is known locally for its massive portions and oversize cinnamon rolls, which have become one of the café's signature dishes. WEST VIRGINIA: Omelet Shoppe in Beckley If there's one item this Beckley diner is famous for, it's omelets. The restaurant serves breakfast around the clock, seven days a week, making it a favorite for locals and travelers looking for eggs, pancakes, biscuits and gravy, and, of course, omelets at any hour. WISCONSIN: Franks Diner in Kenosha Franks Diner has been serving the city of Kenosha since 1926 in an original Jerry O'Mahony lunch car, where it still stands today. Wisconsin's oldest continuously operating diner, this local favorite is best known for its Garbage Plate: a hefty breakfast of eggs, hash browns, meat, cheese, and vegetables that has become the diner's signature dish. WYOMING: Nora's Fish Creek Inn in Wilson Nora's Fish Creek Inn has been a Jackson Hole breakfast staple since Nora and Marvin Tygum opened it in 1982. Housed inside a rustic 1930s-era log cabin, the restaurant is famous for its large portions of breakfast favorites like huevos rancheros and pancakes, as well as fresh pan-fried Idaho trout.

item.title: Leaked Microsoft pay data shows how much hundreds of employees report making in AI, cloud, and other teams
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.69
Microsoft employees are once again comparing notes on pay, and this year's numbers offer a rare look inside how the tech giant is rewarding its workforce in the age of AI. An internal spreadsheet viewed by Business Insider, with nearly 600 employee submissions, details base salaries, raises, cash bonuses, and stock awards across the company as workers learn what they'll earn for the year. The employee-reported data show how Microsoft is rewarding talent across its sprawling organization at a time when retaining its most skilled people, especially in AI and cloud, is a key strategic priority. The data also provides an unusual snapshot of Microsoft's compensation strategy at a pivotal moment for the company. As the company pours billions into AI infrastructure, it is also competing with Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and a growing crop of well-funded startups for the engineers and researchers who can determine whether those investments pay off. Compensation, particularly stock awards that can dwarf annual raises and bonuses, is one of the clearest tools Microsoft has for recruiting and retaining those workers. Microsoft declined to comment. Microsoft employees typically share this information voluntarily and anonymously to promote pay transparency, but that means the data isn't official or comprehensive. The company had 223,000 employees on June 30, so a spreadsheet with nearly 600 submissions provides a very small snapshot. The company also recently cut thousands of employees in a fresh round of layoffs in July. Employees with higher pay or seniority may contribute less to such spreadsheets, so the pay ranges may skew lower than might be representative of the total workforce. Business Insider removed entries that seemed anomalous. item.title: Microsoft employees reveal how much cash they're burning on AI
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.53
Microsoft employees aren't just comparing salaries this year, they're comparing how much AI they use. An internal spreadsheet viewed by Business Insider shows hundreds of employees voluntarily reporting not only their raises, bonuses, and stock awards, but also the dollar value of the AI tools they used over the past month. Microsoft is offering employees an internal tool to track their AI usage and spending. The figures offer a rare glimpse into how AI is being used inside Microsoft as the company races rivals, including Meta, Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic, to build AI products. As the company spends hundreds of billions of dollars on AI infrastructure and pushes employees to weave AI into their daily work, the spreadsheet shows how usage varies dramatically across teams, from just a few dollars a month to tens of thousands. It also suggests that, at least for now, heavier AI use isn't translating into bigger raises, bonuses, or promotions. Microsoft isn't alone in trying to understand how employees use AI. Across Big Tech, companies are increasingly tracking AI consumption as they spend billions building models and infrastructure. New to this year's spreadsheet was a column asking employees to self-report their "AI $ Usage Per Month" using the internal tool, which shows the dollar amount of their AI usage over the last 28 days. A Microsoft spokesperson said the AI usage tracking tool is still in early testing. The document had nearly 600 entries from US employees when Business Insider analyzed the data, showing how much the employees say they received this year in base pay, raises, cash bonuses, and stock awards. About 350 of them had reported their AI usage at the time. Of those reported, the median AI usage amount was about $300 over 28 days. The highest reported figure was $28,000 from an employee in the Microsoft Customer and Partner Solutions organization. Business Insider's analysis excluded levels and teams with few entries. The data is self-reported and may contain errors. Self-reported AI usage among Microsoft employees | Org | No. of entries | Median AI usage, last 28 days | Range | | Azure | 33 | $241 | $1 to $7,500 | | Cloud + AI | 107 | $325 | $1 to $15,000 | | CoreAI | 14 | $975 | $40 to $16,000 | | Experiences and Devices | 69 | $250 | $1 to $3,391 | | Microsoft AI | 15 | $490 | $45 to $10,000 | | Microsoft Customer and Partner Solutions | 25 | $134 | $1 to $28,000 | | Security | 12 | $526 | $58 to $10,000 | Microsoft employees typically share this information voluntarily and anonymously to promote pay transparency, but that means the data isn't official or comprehensive. The company had 223,000 employees on June 30, so a spreadsheet with only around 350 figures on AI usage provides a very small snapshot. Business Insider found no meaningful correlation in the spreadsheet between reported AI usage and rewards. Higher AI usage did not appear to be associated with higher bonus ratings, merit increases, or a greater likelihood of promotion. Have a tip? item.title: These are the 6 most annoying air traveler habits according to Americans, from wearing pajamas to reclining your seats
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.82
From seat-reclining disputes to disagreements over when it's OK to switch seats, many Americans say airline etiquette has gotten worse over the past five years, according to a new survey from the travel website The Points Guy (TPG). Among the respondents' biggest pet peeves were people listening to audio without headphones, reclining their seats too far back, and taking off their shoes in the cabin. TPG commissioned the survey through YouGov, a global public-opinion and data company. It polled more than 2,500 US adults and found that 42% say flying etiquette is worsening, with 52% blaming other passengers rather than the airlines themselves. The culture shift has sparked debate among passengers and flight attendants in recent years. Current and former flight attendants have previously told Business Insider that disregarding seat belt signs and attending to your personal hygiene are big no-nos, while a parent flying with their baby in economy class doesn't bother them. US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy has also weighed in. In November, he cautioned passengers against wearing pajamas and slippers to the airport, and advised them to control their frustration during travel: "I would encourage people to dress a little better, which encourages us to maybe behave a little better," he said in a press conference. Some airlines are also pointing out etiquette expectations. German airline Lufthansa unveiled a giveaway-only apparel collection on Wednesday that playfully nods to the rule that the 'Middle seat gets the armrests,' as displayed on its sweatshirts. Other slogans include 'Live, love, exit by row,' and 'Recline responsibly." In a June post to Threads, Southwest Airlines said passengers "won't get off the plane faster by standing up .001 seconds after the seatbelt sign turns off." Just 12% of survey respondents, about 300 people, said they don't get annoyed by passenger behavior. Here are the etiquette behaviors that are top of mind for most Americans. Cabin noise is the biggest pet peeve among respondents. Loud conversations and listening to music or videos without headphones were respondents' biggest annoyances, with 27% choosing them as the most frustrating inflight behaviors. "You are one of hundreds in an enclosed metal tube, and no one else wants to hear what you're watching or listening to," flight attendant Micayla Keeley previously told Business Insider. Forty percent said airlines should ban phone or video calls during flights — something that could become more relevant as high-speed WiFi from Starlink becomes more widely available. Another 33% said such a ban isn't necessary. You should ask before reclining your seat. Fifty-one percent of respondents said it's acceptable in-flight etiquette to recline your economy seat only if you check behind you first. 21% of passengers said it's acceptable at any time after takeoff. Meanwhile, 10% of respondents said seats should never recline. There have been viral moments of laptops and drinks on a tray table getting smashed because the person in front reclined. Some believe subtly introducing that they are reclining by slowly doing so is enough communication between both parties. "You paid for your plane seat, so you should get to recline," frequent flyer Sophie-Claire Hoeller told Business Insider. "And this is a big caveat — you should recline respectfully." The middle seat doesn't automatically get both armrests. Who gets the middle seat armrests was among the most divisive questions in the survey. While 31% of respondents said everyone should share the armrests equally, 11% said the passenger in the middle seat should get both armrests. Twenty-six percent of respondents were unsure what the etiquette should be. Passengers largely agreed that there is no need to agree with their row mates on whether to close the window shade, with 51% of those surveyed said the window-seat passenger should control it. Twenty-eight of the respondents, however, said everyone in the row should work it out together. Asking to swap seats has mixed opinions. Forty-four percent of passengers believe asking to swap seats is not rude, while 34% believe it is. Twenty-two percent of those surveyed, however, were unsure of the proper etiquette. In a viral 2023 TikTok with over 2.4 million views, one user detailed her experience helping another flyer turn down a seat-swap request. Many commenters said seat-swap requests are fine when the person offers an equivalent seat, like a window for another window, rather than asking someone to give up a window seat for a middle seat. Most people say pajamas should not be worn to fly. Thirty-eight percent said the most appropriate attire when flying is whatever is comfortable, while 34% said that casual athletic or loungewear, such as leggings, sweatpants, and T-shirts, is acceptable. Together, 72% chose one of those two comfort-focused options. Just 1% of respondents said pajamas are appropriate, and another 1% said they're OK with revealing clothing. Most US airlines already have rules against clothing that is considered too revealing or contains offensive or vulgar language. Eight percent of those polled said the most annoying behavior on planes is someone going barefoot. Most people agree deplaning should be row-by-row. Sixty-five percent of respondents said leaving row-to-row from front to back is the most proper way to exit an airplane. Ten percent said it's OK to move ahead when there is an opening, while 9% of respondents believed it's appropriate to cut ahead if the passenger is trying to make a tight connection. "The most polite way to deboard a plane is to let the people in the front go first," etiquette coach Mariah Grumet told Business Insider in July, saying the exception is if a passenger has a close connection, and that those individuals should ask airline staff for assistance.

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg bought a castle in Ireland to add to his real estate collection. Here's a look at the rest of his portfolio.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.67
Mark Zuckerberg has amassed a real estate portfolio that has easily exceeded $100 million, but, until recently, he kept it within the confines of the US. A spokesperson for Zuckerberg confirmed to Business Insider that he and his wife, Priscilla Chan, purchased a 200-year-old castle in Waterford County, Ireland. "Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters," Zuckerberg's spokesperson, Brian Baker, said in an email statement to Business Insider. The purchase price is unknown; however, The Irish Times, which first reported on the sale, estimates Zuckerberg paid between 20 and 30 million euros — or between $23 million and $35 million. A drop in the bucket for the Meta CEO, who has an estimated net worth of $192.4 billion, according to Forbes. The castle is just the latest addition to Zuckerberg's portfolio, which includes a doomsday bunker in Hawaii and a waterfront mansion in Miami. See what other Zuckerberg properties are in his portfolio. Zuckerberg owns a residential compound in Palo Alto. It's no surprise that a tech titan has more than one property in Silicon Valley. The Meta CEO owns five homes in the Crescent Park neighborhood of Palo Alto. He gave viewers a rare peek inside one of them in 2016; the house is even tricked out with a "custom-made artificially intelligent assistant," according to CNBC. The home is only a 10-minute drive from the Meta HQ in Menlo Park. He bought the first Crescent Park property in May 2011 for $7 million. Architectural Digest described it as a "'no frills abode" that chooses function over extravagance. Zuckerberg then spent over $43 million on the four homes surrounding his original residence in Crescent Park, The Wall Street Journal reported. He sold his San Francisco townhouse in 2022 for a reported $31 million. The four-bedroom, four-bathroom home is located near San Francisco's Dolores Park. He and his wife, Priscilla Chan, reportedly spent $10 million to purchase the townhouse in 2010. At the time of the sale in 2022, it was the largest residential real estate deal in the city. He bought two adjacent estates on the shore of Lake Tahoe around 2019. Lake Tahoe is a popular vacation destination for wealthy Californians in both summer and winter, and Zuckerberg and his family are no exception. The tax records of the two properties — known as Carousel Estate and Brushwood Estate — display the same address as tax records of other properties linked to Zuckerberg, according to documents viewed by BI. Zuckerberg reportedly paid $59 million for both properties. At 5,322 square feet, the Brushwood Estate features six bedrooms, five baths, and two half baths, according to SF Gate. Inside are high-beamed ceilings and picture windows; outside are lush trees, a private dock, and a hot tub. There's also a 2,293-square-foot guesthouse. The Meta exec owns over 1,200 acres of land in Hawaii. It's unclear exactly how many acres of land Zuckerberg currently owns on Kauai, but he began buying up a region of the island back in 2014. Business Insider tracked down at least 1,200 acres between 17 parcels of land that have the same tax address as other properties mentioned above, but are owned by LLCs including Kahu'aina Holdings LLC and Pila'a International LLC. The 1,200 acres include about 750 acres he reportedly paid $100 million in 2014 for. That encompasses a more than 350-acre span of land on Pila'a Beach. His plans for Koolau Ranch seem to be in preparation for the worst case scenario. Another part of Zuckerberg's Hawaii holdings is the nearly 600 acres of land on Kauai's North Shore that reportedly cost him around $53 million in 2021. On one of his Hawaiian parcels, Zuckerberg is reportedly building a huge compound that's said to include a 5,000-square-foot underground bunker with an escape hatch. It's been dubbed Koolau Ranch, and Wired reported that buying the land and creating the compound cost the executive an estimated $270 million. In March 2025, he purchased a 15,000-square-foot mansion in Washington, DC. As Silicon Valley continues to infiltrate Washington, DC, Zuckerberg established a residence in the US capital, Politico said. The home that's reportedly his new pad is situated in Massachusetts Avenue Heights, not far from the Naval Observatory and the Washington National Cathedral, according to Builder magazine. Zuckerberg kept the purchase private, Politico said. The mansion in question was sold for $23 million in cash. It was designed by local firm Robert Gurney Architect and sits on about one acre of property. Business Insider was unable to independently confirm that Zuckerberg purchased the property. Zuckerberg is also moving down the street from Jeff Bezos after reportedly buying property in Miami. Mark Zuckerberg is reportedly adding a second East Coast property to his portfolio after buying a home in Miami, according to The Wall Street Journal. Zuckerberg is said to be purchasing a waterfront mansion on Indian Creek, an exclusive island in South Florida that's home to Jeff Bezos, Carl Icahn, and Jared Kushner. It's unclear how much this off-market deal was worth, but an empty lot next door to Bezos sold for $105 million in 2025. Zuckerberg went international and bought a 200-year-old castle in Ireland. In his first reported international buy, Zuckerberg purchased a three-story Gothic castle on 440 acres. The castle, named Strancally Castle in Waterford County, Ireland, is about 140 miles south of Meta's international headquarters in Dublin. It was built between 1825 and 1835. Zuckerberg bought the castle from the cofounder of the London-based private investment firm RAB Capital for an undisclosed amount. The Irish Times estimates the castle sold for between $23 million and $35 million. Hillary Hoffower contributed to an earlier version of this story. Correction: February 26, 2026 — An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the previous owners of Zuckerberg's Miami home.

item.title: The AI race is moving fast. What does that mean for employees' summer vacation?
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.35
Sun's out, laptops out. Summer is the season of endless out-of-office messages, as workers cash in on their paid time off. But is the same true for those locked in the AI race? Miles Brundage, OpenAI's former head of policy research, theorized on X that some AI labs may be more keen on vacay time than others. While it's difficult to know how Anthropic or OpenAI actually compare on PTO usage, Brundage's post sparked a debate about vacation days in the white-hot AI race. For AI employees chasing the singularity or a white-hot IPO, do you really want a Euro summer? The OpenAI vs Anthropic vacation debate In Brundage's comments, OpenAI and Anthropic staffers debated their own vacation time. One Anthropic staffer showed off his trip to the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. An OpenAI employee said that it was "a sign that I should take some vacation." Leo Gao wrote that, as "someone who has always had a tendency to let my work consume my entire life," he's felt at home at OpenAI. Others took it as an opportunity to take jabs. OpenAI's Jason Liu asked Anthropic's Thariq Shihipar whether he agreed. "Aren't you always on vacation," Shihipar responded. OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. Commenters also chimed in on vacation culture at other AI labs, such as Meta and Google DeepMind. "Having just transferred from academia I'm still trying to figure out what this 'vacation' thing is," wrote Alex Imas, Google DeepMind's director of AGI economics. Angel investor Kevin Wimer pointed to a lab with a notoriously hardcore reputation: "Now do SpaceXAI. I don't think they sleep." Brundage, the former OpenAI staffer, said the main point he was trying to make by posting about PTO within the AI community was that "rest is important!" Are you 'hardcore' if you take PTO? Most tech workers do have access to vacation days. Taking it is another question. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, 95% of information workers have access to paid vacation. A 2025 Alliant survey of tech industry benefits found that tech companies offered an average of 19.8 days of PTO. Still, the AI race is getting faster and fiercer. To stay competitive, some tech companies are instilling hardcore work cultures. Some software engineers are 996ing — working 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week — and abstaining from vices like alcohol. Under such work pressure, taking a trip may be last on the list. Or the engineers may not personally want to travel, for fear of falling behind. AI bros told Business Insider that keeping track can be overwhelming. One described it as "drinking from a water hose, and the hose just keeps getting bigger." What does OpenAI CEO Sam Altman think of time off? He said in 2018 that he was a "bad example of work-life balance." "I do try to take vacation," he said at WIRED25. "But the rest of the time I just work."

item.title: My entire family moved to the same small town in Indiana. I was finally able to buy a home, and it's great for my kids.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.13
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with McKenna Shamburg, 25, who moved from Utah to Indiana to be closer to her family to help raise her children. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I've lived in eight states now. I was born and raised mostly in South Carolina. I left when I was 12 years old to go to Louisville, Kentucky, for two years. Then we moved to Austin for a year, and then we moved back to South Carolina when I was 15. That's where I met my husband in high school. Then we moved to Norfolk, Virginia, and then to Hot Springs, North Carolina. Then I graduated from high school, joined the military, and went to Knoxville, Tennessee, for college at the University of Tennessee. Then my husband and I moved to Washington Terrace, Utah, which is about 45 minutes north of Salt Lake City. I was only applying to jobs in Utah because of the nature. I'm an outdoorsy person, and I was super excited about the mountains. Utah wasn't for us We lived in Utah for a little under two years. We really tried to have a community in Utah, and it just didn't work out. I like to think I'm a friendly person. I like to wave at people when I'm walking or running. It's a small thing, and I don't get butt-hurt about if people wave back or not, but nobody would in Utah. People weren't as friendly there as they are out East or in the Midwest. So when we had twins in July 2025, it was just really hard. Also, there's a big drought in Utah, and it's pretty bad. A lot of the water Utah gets is from snowfall, and it barely snowed. The month we left, the city had enacted water conservation rules where they were fining people for using too much water. With twins, I do one million loads of laundry all the time — and that's not including baths and all that jazz. So it was a good thing we were getting out of there. In this phase of life, being that far from family and friends wasn't great for us. Also, financially, buying a house in Utah is just a lot more expensive. And with the water situation, I wouldn't really want to invest in a property — even if we had funds to do so — if there's no water. We missed living near family, so we came up with a unique solution One of the biggest reasons we wanted to move was that we had twins, and in Utah, we didn't have any family nearby. When everybody says it's hard to do it on your own, and it takes a village, they aren't lying. I was locked in my house in Utah. Even though I would get outside and we'd go to the park, it was just us. I was lonely. My family and I have always been close. We just haven't been nearby. My brother was living in South Dakota, and he, similarly, wanted to be closer to family — or at least to the East. My parents wanted to open a pizza place, Vinyl Pies, and that's what brought us all together. We all decided to move to Vincennes, Indiana, at the same time to collaborate on the pizza place. Now, we're all in Indiana as of two months ago. Buying a home was definitely the goal for us, but it seemed unattainable in Utah. We moved to Indiana in April 2026 and closed on our home for $273,000. The house we have here would probably go for three times as much in Utah, which is kind of crazy. And we want more kids, so trying to fit them in a smaller house than what we have here in Indiana would be a pain. Getting the house was a bit of a roller coaster because we were still living in Utah and we didn't have the time or the money to fly out. The twins were maybe six or seven months old at the time, and it would have been a mess to try to bring them. My parents had to come look at it for us. Our real estate agent also did video tours. Our real estate agent sent an incentive program to us. I also heard about it from other folks — people in Vincennes were eager to share it. The city gave us $5,000 — half of it upfront, and then half of it after a year — to move there. So we've received half so far. One of the big perks — aside from them giving you a bundle of money, which you can always take as a young couple buying a home — is that they also gave us a year membership to the YMCA, which has been amazing because I can go work out and they watch the kids. I can't explain how much of a blessing that is. As a current stay-at-home mom, my sanity rides on getting out of the house. Even though there are certainly no mountains here, the parks they have are actually really nice. And they do a lot of events here in town — almost every weekend, even though it's a small Midwestern town. I think they do a really good job keeping everybody occupied, especially kids. Having family nearby to help raise my kids is invaluable It was bittersweet leaving Utah, but I was excited to have support again. It was a pretty rough nine months there with just me, the husband, and the kids. Being close to family has been so amazing. My brother hadn't met our kids until they were nine months old. Not because he didn't want to, but because we were so far away. And now he sees them almost every other day. My brother has two kids, too, and another on the way. So I've not been close to my niece or nephew at all, but now I see them almost every other day, too. I love the mountains, and I was pretty sad to leave Utah for that reason — Indiana is literally one of the flattest states. But coming here, people have been so nice. There's a sense of pride here, in a good way.

item.title: The Greatest Speeches of All Time, and What Biden Said
item.description:
Source: Caitlin Flanagan | The Atlantic Score: 2.03
If you want to reach the kids, you’ve got to go where the kids are. Where are they right now? With their devices, of course. And what are they doing on those devices? Listening to podcasts, of course. This, presumably, was the reason behind the release of a corker: NATO Through Time, in which a grandfatherly former NATO official and three young and extremely well-informed co-hosts plunge into the past. What’s next, Yalta: The Musical? It would probably be a more successful venture, because Yalta was once; NATO is forever. From age to age, a new generation of supporters must be rallied, and that is becoming the 13th labor of Hercules. If the thudding disappointment of Unfrosted taught us anything, it’s that young people hate Boomer nostalgia. And NATO is the rotary phone of geopolitical alliances. I grew up a long time ago, when the world was every bit as complicated and dangerous as it is today. But, if only as a reassuring fiction, the American president was often referred to as “the leader of the free world.” America was the most powerful country in history, and it was sworn to protect—and was protected by, should the terrible day come—an alliance of other free nations. NATO was principally a firebreak against the Soviet Union and remains one against Russia. But Barack Obama felt that a foreign policy in which Russia was our chief enemy was a little old-fashioned. Too From Russia With Love. Too Rocky IV and Rambo III. In a presidential debate in 2012, he mocked Mitt Romney for saying that Russia was the biggest threat to America: “The 1980s are now calling to ask for their foreign policy back because, you know, the Cold War’s been over for 20 years.” Then the Cold War rose from the dead and Russia invaded Crimea, and two years ago began its bloodthirsty attack on Ukraine. Two people who don’t like NATO are Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump (who once told his foreign-policy adviser, “I don’t give a shit about NATO”). This ought to ring a distant alarm bell. Managing the very special relationship between these two powerful men seems to be Trump’s version of NATO: cheaper, more direct, perhaps one day turning into an alliance of its own. Around the world, autocracy is rising; spend any time at all reading about the evidence, and your hair catches on fire. Russia, China, North Korea—they have all been strengthening their ties to one another; all of them have a dim view of America and of democracy. Toward self-preservation, allow me to offer my own extremely brief assessment of NATO through time, in the form of three speeches by American presidents. No one really knows what John F. Kennedy actually said in his famous 1961 inaugural address, because he was so goddamn sexy and so goddamn confident that the beautiful words and soaring phrases float through your receptive brain but can find no purchase. But by looping the video for a week, this is what I’ve got: Kennedy believed that the Second World War—which had ended just 15 years earlier—was a turning point in American history. The war had revealed the extent of America’s commitment to freedom and its special role as the defender of nations where tyrants ruled. The speech recognized that the dropping of atomic bombs in Japan had forever changed the equation of human progress: “The world is very different now. For man holds in his mortal hands the power to abolish all forms of human poverty and all forms of human life.” America had nuclear weapons, but so did its greatest enemy. Embedded within the beautiful speech was the rationale for a lot of very questionable foreign policy. But the speech was also a flex and a warning: “To those old allies whose cultural and spiritual origins we share, we pledge the loyalty of faithful friends. United, there is little we cannot do in a host of cooperative ventures. Divided, there is little we can do—for we dare not meet a powerful challenge at odds and split asunder.” In his beautiful words, he was talking about the rotary phone—NATO. And the desperate need to keep the peace: “To those nations who would make themselves our adversary, we offer not a pledge but a request: that both sides begin anew the quest for peace, before the dark powers of destruction unleashed by science engulf all humanity in planned or accidental self-destruction. We dare not tempt them with weakness. For only when our arms are sufficient beyond doubt can we be certain beyond doubt that they will never be employed.” Ronald Reagan presided over the Soviet Union’s demise. He also popularized that oxymoronic piece of realpolitik “Trust but verify.” In 1984, he gave a speech marking the 40th anniversary of the invasion of Normandy. Peggy Noonan wrote it, and it took its place among the greatest American political speeches of all time. No one could sell a speech like Reagan, and this one opened like a novel, or better yet, a screenplay: ESTABLISHING SHOT: “We stand on a lonely, windswept point on the northern shore of France.” DISSOLVE: “The air is soft, but 40 years ago at this moment, the air was dense with smoke and the cries of men, and the air was filled with the crack of rifle fire and the roar of cannon.” The genius of the speech was that, while it described dramatic action that took place in the context of extremely complicated political history, it left that history as assumed fact and centered on the individual and collective actions of very young American men, some of them boys, who had more or less been dumped out of landing craft into waist-high waves, and were immediately under German machine-gun fire. Some survivors of that pitiless day sat in the front rows of the audience, and Reagan addressed them directly: “You all knew that some things are worth dying for. One’s country is worth dying for, and democracy is worth dying for, because it’s the most deeply honorable form of government ever devised by man.” I doubt if any of the terrified young men bleeding and dying on that beach thought of themselves as morally bound to defend democracy. But Reagan followed an established tradition of recognizing the highest aspirations of American troops in combat and of finding within the individual acts of one soldier the aims and honor of a just war. In one of the speech’s most arresting passages, Reagan tied the horrors of combat back to the suffering of parents and families. “The Americans who fought here that morning knew word of the invasion was spreading through the darkness back home. They thought—or felt in their hearts, though they couldn’t know in fact—that in Georgia they were filling the churches at 4 a.m., in Kansas they were kneeling on their porches and praying, and in Philadelphia they were ringing the Liberty Bell.” I don’t think any other politician of the past 50 years could have sold that line about the Liberty Bell, but when Reagan said it, you were pierced by it. Young Americans then had comparatively little experience with the Second World War as an exercise of American greatness. They’d been ground down by Vietnam, and by all the music and movies about it, and by the homeless vets who sat in wheelchairs panhandling and drinking. Vietnam had brought shame to America—but the Second World War was different. This speech gave them a chance to reconsider America in a new light, as the hero of a global catastrophe. This was before Tom Brokaw’s The Greatest Generation and Steven Spielberg’s Saving Private Ryan, and Spielberg and Tom Hanks’s Band of Brothers. In fact, those lionizing, mythmaking inventions probably would not have existed without Reagan’s speech. The tone was Shakespearean, Prince Hal into Henry V: “These are the boys of Pointe du Hoc. These are the men who took the cliffs. These are the champions who helped free a continent. These are the heroes who helped end a war.” But the real heart of the speech was here, in the emphasis on the ways that the Allied powers had worked together to achieve this joint victory: “All of these men were part of a roll call of honor with names that spoke of a pride as bright as the colors they bore: the Royal Winnipeg Rifles, Poland’s 24th Lancers, the Royal Scots Fusiliers, the Screaming Eagles, the Yeomen of England’s armored divisions, the forces of Free France, the Coast Guard’s ‘Matchbox Fleet,’ and you, the American Rangers.” And then he said this, possibly the point of the whole thing—his endorsement of the idea that the “strength of America’s allies is vital to the United States”: “We were with you then; we are with you now. Your hopes are our hopes, and your destiny is our destiny.” When I read that Joe Biden was giving his own speech in Normandy this month, I think I actually said, “O almighty God, forbid it.” I knew it would feature our ever-diminishing president delivering a warmed-over version of Reagan’s great speech. It was that. But, in its unspectacular way, it was also a speech that drew the sharpest possible contrast between Biden and Donald Trump, and what Trump imagines is his ability to cajole and bully our enemies, to find common cause with them and to stage dramas in which he emerges as a global ambassador of peace through strength. During his administration, Trump threatened North Korea with nuclear attack (sweet Jesus!). But he softened after Kim Jong Un “wrote me beautiful letters.” The kind of foreign policy that involves, say, sending aid to Ukraine to beat back Russian soldiers seems far less interesting to him. Biden said this: “When we talk about American democracy, we often talk about the ideals of life, liberty, pursuit of happiness. What we don’t talk about is how hard it is.” He said the “most natural instinct is to walk away, to be selfish, to force our will upon others, to seize power.” “American democracy asks the hardest of things: to believe that we’re part of something bigger than ourselves.” You would think that freedom is the force that flows naturally, but it’s not. Freedom generally has to be fought for and always must be vigilantly—and sometimes militarily—guarded. There’s no point listing Joe Biden’s manifold shortcomings here. They’re in front of our eyes, and they’re not all “cheap fakes.” But Biden believes in NATO and in supporting our allies. Maybe that seems quaint, and rotary-phone-as-hell, but these are very good things. Trump is flashier: a convicted felon, an insult comic, the last man on Earth to run on a platform of “Trust me,” and yet it’s working on a huge number of Americans. If you vote for Biden, you’ll have to ask yourself a question: Is he still fit for office, or is he too frail, too ancient-seeming to make another term anything but a mockery of the country? And if you vote for Trump, you’ll have to ask yourself this one: Do you feel lucky?

item.title: Asia Pacific set to lose title as the world's largest travel region
item.description:
Source: CNN Travel Score: 5.16
Editor’s Note: Sign up for Unlocking the World, CNN Travel’s weekly newsletter. Get news about destinations opening, inspiration for future adventures, plus the latest in aviation, food and drink, where to stay and other travel developments. Asia Pacific is home to some of the world’s most beloved travel destinations, from the natural beauty of Bali to the urban buzz of Singapore. These dreamy vacation hotspots – teamed with the region’s business power – secured Asia Pacific the title of world’s largest travel region for much of the past decade.
