"The format is seen as being entertaining and informative," he said. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is one of three states set to vote in a new regional parliament next month. Polls suggest the CDU is seriously struggling in the state, which has never exactly been a happy hunting ground for it. Most surveys put the center-right party somewhere in the region of 10% support, compared to 13.3% in 2021. The AfD appears set to become the most popular party in the state, overtaking the Social Democrats (SPD) and claiming first place but falling well short of the majority it would need to govern. As major German parties maintain a policy of non-cooperation with the AfD — known as the "firewall" — the far-right party is unlikely to form government in the state. The vote takes place on September 20. Fuel prices continue climbing, ADAC says costs unjustified The prices at fuel pumps in Germany are still climbing according to the latest averages collated by the ADAC motoring club. The price of E10 gasoline or petrol reached a national average of just over €2.16 per liter on Wednesday. That equates to $9.54 per US gallon. It's a slight increase, just under 4 cents per liter on the previous Wednesday. Diesel, meanwhile, climbed more sharply in the past week, rising by just over 5 cents per liter. It reached an average price of just over €2.25 per liter, or $9.95 per US gallon. Regional variations are fairly stark at present, as the problems transporting fuel on the Rhine River amid its low levels create delivery difficulties in western states like North Rhine-Westphalia and Hessen. The ADAC, however, said it believed that neither the shipping issues in the Strait of Hormuz nor the summer drought could explain the prices. "In the view of the ADAC, the fuel prices in Germany remain on a level that is too high," the organization, which often criticizes petrol pricing practices, said. "While the historically low water levels on the Rhine and the transport difficulties that causes and the slight increase in oil prices explain a part of the fuel cost rises, they are not sufficient to fully explain the current price levels. Filling up is still too expensive." Eurowings looks to restart Dubai flights after months German airline Eurowings plans to restart flights to Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, after a hiatus of almost six months as a result of the US war with Iran that has impacted the wider Persian Gulf region. The airline made the announcement on Wednesday, albeit only for a probable restart on October 25, by which point almost eight months will have elapsed. The routes from Berlin, Stuttgart and Cologne/Bonn to Dubai were all suspecnded soon after the joint US-Israeli attack on Iran at the end of February. Iran has targeted sites in Gulf countries over the course of the war, including in the UAE, saying it is in retaliation to the US and Israeli bombardment. The Lufthansa subsidiary, typically seen as a budget alternative, also announced that from December 1, new premium business seats would be available on Dubai flights. For the first time, except on long-distance routes, the airline will use a more spacious layout with just four seats per row for these seats. Eurowings said it was extending this concept to all eight of its A320neo planes, meaning that the new seats will also be available on flights to London, Mallorca and Malaga. NRW's interior minister visits Monschau amid Belgian border wildfire The interior minister of Germany's western state of North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), Herbert Reul, has visited the border town of Monschau, which remains on alert amid the wildfire a short distance away in Belgium's High Fens nature reserve. Some 30 residents in the most at-risk parts of the town are still under evacuation orders. Local officials in Belgium like the Liege regional governor however reported "positive developments" fighting the 3,000-hectare blaze on Wednesday amid sporadic light rains and cooler temperatures. Reul, meanwhile, warned against rumors and speculation about the cause of the fire during his visit to Monschau. He was speaking as unsubstantiated allegations of wild campers triggering the vast fire circulated. "There's no point to it," Reul said when asked about speculating on the cause. He said it would require thorough investigation, and then prosecution if applicable. If investigations did not yield fruit, he said, the most important lesson was for people not to behave irresponsibly in the woods, not to drop cigarette butts or cook using hot coals. The majority of forest fires are ultimately man-made, with very few naturally occurring sources of heat (other than lightning strikes) sufficient to spark fires amid foliage. Dry ground, high temperatures and winds help the fires to spread once they have begun. Merz condemns 'unacceptable' remarks by Israeli security minister — spokesman Chancellor Friedrich Merz has described as "inhumane" remarks made by far-right Israeli Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir advocating the targeted killing of Palestinians in Gaza, a government spokesman said on Wednesday. "The chancellor strongly condemns the inhumane appeals made by Minister Ben-Gvir, which violate international law," spokesman Sebastian Hille said. "They are unacceptable." Ben-Gvir made the remarks during a podcast with Rom Braslavski, a former hostage held in Gaza after the October 7, 2023 attacks on Israel by Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups. "I think that targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza, removing 30, 40 people every night," he said in the podcast, which was broadcast on Saturday. Ben-Gvir added that he meant not only militant Palestinians who were an immediate threat but other people in the Gaza Strip who he said did not deserve to live. On Tuesday, Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil also sharply criticized what he called the "dehumanizing" remarks by Ben-Gvir and said sanctions on him at the European level should now be considered "very seriously." Ever more foreign qualifications recognized in Germany — Destatis Germany is accepting the qualifications of a growing number of foreign professionals, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported on Wednesday. It said authorities had approved 86,600 applications last year, almost 10% more than in 2024. That rise is, however, smaller than in 2024 and 2023, which saw the number of approvals increase by 21% and 25% respectively. As in previous years, most of those accepted in 2025 came from Turkey (9,800), accounting for 11% of overall approvals. Around 8,300 recognitions from Ukraine were also reported. Most of the recognized qualifications were in medical professions, as was also the case in 2024. Nursing professionals had 32,000 applications approved, followed by doctors (13,900). There were also 4,600 acceptances for engineers, meaning that those three professions together made up more than half (58%) of recognitions. A number of sectors in Germany are relying ever more on foreign professionals as the birth rate falls and the population ages. Investigation bureau gives details on near-accident in Munich Germany's Federal Bureau of Aircraft Accident Investigation (BFU) has said the causes of a near-accident at the weekend involving a Vietnam Airlines aircraft were still unclear but presented details on the incident. In a statement issued late on Tuesday, the BFU said the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner started its takeoff at Munich Airport at 1:57 pm (1157 GMT) on Saturday and was late getting into the air. It said the tail touched the ground just before lift-off and that tire marks had been found at the end of the runway that were probably from the aircraft. The plane eventually turned around, landing back at Munich Airport at 3:58 p.m. The agency said its experts were currently analyzing the plane's flight recorders and that authorities in Vietnam and the US were also participating in the investigation. "The investigation does not serve to establish blame, liability or claims," the authority said, but rather was intended to help prevent any such accidents and incidents in future. Experts have said that the 270 passengers and crew on board the plane narrowly escaped disaster. The aircraft had great difficulty taking off despite the pilot's efforts to pull the nose up. When it landed two hours later, smoke was visible from the undercarriage and tires had burst. Passengers and crew were uninjured. Tenants should be able to install heat protection more easily — justice minister Laws on rented accommodation could potentially be changed to allow tenants more freedom in adapting their apartments to cope with heat ways, Federal Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig has said. "Conventional legal policy can also make a contribution to heat protection," she told the daily Rheinische Post in an interview published on Wednesday morning. "I am thinking about tenancy laws in particular," she said. "I can imagine, for example, that we make it easier for tenants to equip their apartments with air conditioning or sun shades." At present, tenants have no legal right to install built-in air conditioning devices or external shades but need permission from their rental owner. Hubig also spoke out in favor of the proposal made by her Social Democratic Party to enshrine climate protection in the German constitution, or Basic Law, as a joint obligation of both the federal government and state administrations. Currently, the primary responsibility for heat protections lies with the states and municipalities. "This would make it easier for the government to give states and municipalities sustained support in heat-protection measures," she said. Germany, like much of Europe, has experienced successive heat waves this summer with temperatures repeatedly approaching 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit). This has reignited public debate over the use of air conditioners, which remain rare in the country. Runaway sheep goes through bus wash A German sheep has probably had the experience of its life after it boarded an empty bus that was then driven through a bus wash. The sheep had escaped from its home in the western town of Lüdinghausen and gone aboard the bus at the local bus depot, police said on Tuesday. According to the transport company RVM, the sheep entered the bus as it was about to be cleaned in the depot's wash hall, causing officers to be called to the scene. The police then escorted the vehicle as it went through the wash to prevent the sheep escaping, as the bus was already in such a position that it could not back out of the facility. The owner then collected the animal after what must have been a confusing ride for it. RVM said the sheep was one of several that had run across the depot grounds during the incident a few days ago. Defense startup CEO living under ground due to Russian plots — reports The head of a German defense startup that is supplying attack drones to Ukraine as it defends itself against invading Russian troops has been in hiding for months after warnings that he was at risk of his life from Russian agents, reports said on Tuesday. Donaustahl CEO Stefan Thumann told private broadcaster RTL and magazine Stern in a joint interview that he had received warnings from German officials in late 2025 that Russian intelligence was plotting against his life. "I'm fighting a duel with the Russian military intelligence service for my life," he said. "Constantly changing locations, 24-hour personal security, my private life has ceased to exist," he added. Thumann said he now slept next to his computer and started working as soon as he woke up to distract himself from his personal situation. In March, prosecutors said they had arrested two so-called disposable agents who were alleged to have spied on Thumann to prepare an assassination attempt. Disposable agents is the name given to people with little training who are hired by military intelligence services for small pay to carry out missions. But RTL cited a German lawmaker who said there were still plans targeting him that were well advanced and involved using a nerve agent. In 2024, the United States thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of German defense giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, according to a CNN report. Welcome to our coverage DW's newsroom in Bonn wishes all its readers guten Tag! Today, we will be looking at proposals by the Social Democrat justice minister to change the law to make it easier for tenants to install heat protective measures as heat waves increase in frequency and severity. And as Russia continues with its strategy of hybrid warfare against the West, reports say that the CEO of a German defense startup is living in constant fear of his life amid warnings of a Russian plot against him. On a lighter note, we also have the story of a runaway sheep that boarded an empty bus and got to experience the thrill of the vehicle going through the wash facility. Read on for details on these stories and more.

item.title: Bauhaus Manifesto: Broad alliance promoting artistic freedom
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.45
The "Bauhaus Manifesto 2026," published on August 20, was initiated by Germany's Minister of State for Culture, Wolfram Weimer. "Together, we're making it clear that we want to strengthen the Bauhaus and its principles while defending them against any form of anti-democratic attack," the independent politician told the German press agency DPA. A statement accompanying the manifesto said it was intended as a cultural and sociopolitical commitment to the principles that have made the Bauhaus art school, which operated from 1919 to 1933, a global cultural icon. Those principles include freedom of artistic thought, openness to new ideas, the connection between different disciplines, and the belief that cultural innovation can make an important contribution to a democratic society. Something to be proud of At the publication of the manifesto, Weimer said, "The Bauhaus demonstrates the innovative power that emerges when art, craftsmanship, design and technology converge. It stands for creativity and exchange, courage and openness to new ideas." He said those values remain an important source of inspiration: "We can be proud of that." The signatories include the German Cultural Council, the German Commission for UNESCO, the German Bishops' Conference, the Evangelical Church in Germany, the Association of German Cities, the German Museums Association, the Academy of Arts, the German Confederation of Skilled Crafts and the German Lost Art Foundation. The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar in 1919 by architect Walter Gropius and other artists as a school of art and design. It later moved to Dessau and eventually to Berlin. When he founded the school, Gropius outlined its goals in his own "Bauhaus Manifesto." In 1933, the prestigious institution was forced to close permanently under pressure from the Nazis. The Bauhaus and its sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 1996. The Bauhaus' international influence is not based solely on its modern design language and avant-garde approach, the new manifesto says. It also stems from its ethos, which remains a model today: the courage to pursue bold ideas, a belief in freedom of artistic thought and the conviction that only an open society can foster cultural renewal. The signatories also set out to defend the Bauhaus movement itself against populist criticism: "Bauhaus institutions should be strengthened; their creative freedom and social openness recognized as exemplary and they should be defended against any anti-democratic attacks," they say. A 'misguided aberration of modernity'? The Alternative for Germany (AFD) party, which has described the Bauhaus as a "misguided aberration of modernity," is not named in the manifesto. But the document can be seen as a response to the far-right party's cultural agenda. The AfD could emerge as the largest bloc in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament after the September 6 election. The party says it wants to promote a "patriotic cultural policy," primarily supporting art that "contributes to the development of German identity." The AfD also plans to replace Saxony-Anhalt's current image campaign, #moderndenken (think modern), with #deutschdenken (think German). In its current election manifesto, the party says the Bauhaus has always sought to avoid any hint of "national roots." The signatories of the "Bauhaus Manifesto 2026" take the opposite view. "We need the sociopolitical impetus of the Bauhaus pioneers precisely at a time when political fringe groups are gaining strength and advocating regression rather than progress," they state. They also point to the Bauhaus' persecution under the Nazis. "The example of the Bauhaus and the hostility it faced from the Nazi regime reminds us that the culture of remembrance is not a nostalgic look back, but a prerequisite for democratic self-understanding." The manifesto states that cultural institutions that preserve memory and provide spaces for constructive debate should therefore be supported. The autonomy of artists and cultural institutions, it says, is a fundamental prerequisite for a vibrant democracy. The Bauhaus is built on the idea of bringing together creative ideas, bold experimentation, high-quality craftsmanship and technological innovation, the manifesto says. It also represents openness and renewal, exchange and networking. "This openness is a great strength of German culture and enriches Germany," its supporters say. "We reject nationalism that is hostile to culture." This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter: 50 years on stage
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.35
The list of international composers who have written for star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter is a long one. It features names like Krzysztof Penderecki and Sofia Gubaidulina, along with Andre Previn and Jörg Widmann. In recent years, women like Iranian-Dutch composer Aftab Darvishi and South Korean composer Unsuk Chin have also written works for Mutter. On the occasion of the violinist's 50th stage anniversary, she's now recorded over 30 works either dedicated to her or commissioned by her — all part of her "ASM Forte Forward" project on the Alpha Classics label. The first album in the series, "East Meets West," reflects not just the artist's musical passions but also her social engagement. The opening "Likoo for Solo Violin," composed by Aftab Darvishi for Mutter in 2024, leaves a powerful impression. "Likoo" is a lament about loss, written at a time when especially women in Iran were fighting repression by the regime. Giving women a voice "I wanted to create a musical tribute to the people in Iran and to those fighting for freedom, coexistence, empathy and equality, in the hope that these atrocities would never be repeated," Mutter told DW. "War is raging on our wonderful planet even as I'm playing, but I won't give up hope for love and empathy." Mutter's performance of it is deeply moving — one can almost hear the women's cries in the violin, fading into silence. With the situation in Iran deteriorating, Mutter says it's especially important to her to keep "Likoo" in her repertoire. "I have great admiration for Persian culture and for the female composers who still live in Iran — such as Golfam Khayam, who managed to send me her score by email during a pause in the shelling. I still hear from her from time to time," Mutter says. "These female composers in Iran fascinate me, and the piece 'Likoo' in particular. That's why — also sadly because of the current situation — it's very important to me to perform 'Likoo' at the anniversary concert." The concert is being held on August 25 at the Lucerne Festival. Her 1976 stage debut in Lucerne On August 23, 1976, a 13-year-old Anne-Sophie Mutter took the stage at a young artists' concert in Lucerne. It was there that conductor Herbert von Karajan first encountered the young talent. A year later, he hired her for a concert with the Berlin Philharmonic at the Salzburg Easter Festival. So began Mutter's long collaboration with Karajan and his Berlin orchestra. Another figure who shaped her musical life on stage in the 1980s was Swiss conductor and patron Paul Sacher. "He was a major influence on my interest in contemporary music," Mutter says. She cherishes the undogmatic learning experience she gained from Sacher and her other mentors. Sacher always afforded her the freedom to decide how she would approach an assignment. He passed a motto on to her: "What I can't do, I can learn. What I can't learn today, I can learn later." The Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation A four-time Grammy winner and recipient of Japan's Praemium Imperiale, she's now supporting highly gifted young musicians through the Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation. She encourages her scholarship recipients to embrace social engagement alongside contemporary music. She's herself a supporter of humanitarian organizations such as Save the Children and Doctors Without Borders, and from 2021 to 2025 served as German Cancer Aid's chairwoman. It's difficult for young musicians to build an audience and make money with contemporary music, Mutter says. "All the same, I want to keep them grounded and show them it's not just about getting rich and famous; they have a role to play in society — in social environments. Playing at a nursing home, for example, or teaching, supporting charitable organizations with benefit concerts." A platform for composers As well, Mutter uses the work she commissions — including from former and current scholarship recipients — to help advance their careers. "I want to give these pieces a platform, along with a recorded presence. Without that, these wonderful works couldn't be heard all over the world." The next album in the "ASM Forte Forward" series being released for the anniversary is "American Tunes #1." It includes works by Andre Previn, whom Mutter was married to for four years, as well as US composer Sebastian Currier, who has written several pieces for Mutter. "It gives me particular pleasure that many works by colleagues from my foundation, as well as by former and current scholarship recipients, have actually been recorded," Mutter says. "I have managed to put many of my young musicians at the center of this new 'Forte Forward' series, and that makes me very happy." Albums of memories To further mark her onstage milestone, Mutter has planned several projects with her longtime label, Deutsche Grammophon. Among them is the release of seven location-centered albums featuring selected works — pieces that, as in the case of the city of Lucerne, were premiered there or hold special significance in Mutter's musical life. So far, "My Berlin," "My London" and, in connection with the anniversary concert in Lucerne, "My Lucerne" have been released digitally. The seven planned albums will follow the artist around the globe, from Berlin, London and Lucerne to Tokyo and New York. Anne-Sophie Mutter's constant companion is her Stradivarius violin. "The violin is the coolest instrument in the universe. For 50 years I've tried again and again to show that," she says. The instrument is her voice, too, she adds: "I find it fascinating how music becomes so expressive precisely where language ends, and how in this cosmos of creativity we can connect, discover ourselves, give ourselves over to expression, and truly experience life." This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Could Russia's growing fuel crisis help end the Ukraine war?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.19
Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries have triggered a new fuel crisis in Russia. Reuters news agency reports that at least 30 regions are now affected. Unlike the previous wave of shortages, which began in late May and lasted until mid-July, the current crisis is particularly affecting Moscow and the surrounding area, as is apparent from posts on social media. The gas station chains Gazprom Neft and Tatneft have already restricted the sale of fuel in the capital. "You can't say there isn't any fuel. But it's obvious there's a crisis," says Oleg Grigorenko, editor-in-chief of the Russian independent media portal 7x7, which Russia has branded a "foreign agent." "It's not just a personal problem if you leave the city and don't know whether you can get back again, for example. It's also an economic problem," Grigorenko reports that in several regions taxi drivers, courier services and the construction industry are already losing business, as many of their supply chains are fuel dependent. "The logistics of private construction companies is heavily reliant on gasoline," Grigorenko explains. People are also having to queue for hours at gas stations in the southern Russian region of Krasnodar, according to local media. The authorities are blaming this on a supposed increase in demand during the holiday period. But many locals are saying that this summer season is a disaster. Real estate agent Igor Zakharchenko, from Sochi on the Black Sea coast, wrote on Instagram: "With its quiet atmosphere and leisurely pace of life, Sochi today is reminiscent of the time before the Olympic Games, when there were still not many cars on the roads and the city had far fewer holidaymakers and inhabitants. But the thing is: There's no gas in Sochi." A two-fold fuel crisis: Poor quality and shortages Speaking on the Russian broadcaster RTVI, Igor Ananskikh, first deputy chairman of the energy committee in the Russian parliament, said he expected the gas supply situation to normalize within two to three weeks. Economist Nikolai Korzhenevsky says this is unlikely. He left Russia in protest at Moscow's war against Ukraine and now lives abroad. In an interview with DW, he highlighted the worsening quality of fuel in Russia. Acquaintances had sent him photos of their cars displaying error messages that indicate engine damage caused by impurities in the fuel. "The car won't start and has to go to the garage. The same people are telling me garages have waitlists of several months, even in Moscow," Korzhenevsky says. "And then you have to wait again for months for replacement parts. Obviously, some vehicles can't handle the gasoline that's being put in their tanks." He sees the ongoing problems in the oil and gas industry as harbingers of a much larger and lasting crisis. Russia's oil exports have fallen more sharply during the war than ever before, Bloomberg news has reported. Oil production has also dropped. "In 2019, Russia produced 11.5 million barrels per day," says Korzhenevsky. "Today it's less than 9 million. If this trend continues, and the problems with oil refining get worse, production may fall to 8 million barrels. That would create the conditions for a complete economic and systemic crisis." He doesn't see any quick solution to these problems. In fact he sees Russia going down a similar route to Venezuela, an economy with national income in chronic decline. Could India and China ease Russia's fuel shortages? The Russian authorities propose to remedy the fuel shortages with imports from India, China or other countries. But Vyacheslav Shiryaev, a Russian business journalist who also now lives abroad, says this is not viable. Given Russia's current isolation, it's impossible to ensure a daily supply of 200,000 tons of fuel, which is the approximate amount of gasoline and diesel Russia needs every day, he told DW. Shiryaev, who publicly opposed the war in Ukraine, is also on the Russian authorities' list of so-called "foreign agents." Another Russian economist on that list is Igor Lipsits. He told DW that the damaged refineries cannot quickly be restored and will be vulnerable to further air attacks. This, he says, is why the authorities are already restricting fuel consumption. Municipal services vehicles — medical and rescue workers, police, firefighters — are allowed to jump the line and fill up and so are security personnel and the authorities. "This is happening in front of people who've waited for hours and it's causing a lot of resentment," says Lipsits, a Kremlin critic who left his teaching post at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow because of increasing political pressure. He too now lives in exile in Europe. To Lipsits, the current developments in Russia are strongly reminiscent of the collapse of the Soviet Union. "There were special supply systems for the elite, their own shops and warehouses where they could buy everything they wanted without much difficulty, without waiting in line, and at relatively low prices. That made Russians very angry," he recounts. "When Boris Yeltsin announced that he was going to abolish these closed distribution centers, the people enthusiastically supported him. We are now in a similar situation." Lipsits says a closed system for fuel distribution is evolving in Russia that will make it a luxury to be able to drive a car. A threat to Putin's Ukraine war plans? The economist Shiryaev believes Ukrainian attacks on Russian targets that serve both a military and a civilian purpose could cripple the Russian economy and hasten the end of the war. He believes it would end in just a few weeks if the West supported Ukraine in doubling or tripling the intensity of its attacks. "Ukraine could bring about disorganization and chaos in the Russian interior, resulting in a total loss of control," Shiryaev says. He also thinks the fuel shortage could have a decisive role in undermining the stability of Vladimir Putin's regime. "If there's no diesel, Russia's 6,000-kilometer railway network comes to a halt," he says. "It could also cripple hundreds of factories and businesses. Without diesel, tens of thousands of trucks would be unable to run, food wouldn't get to the stores, and farmers wouldn't be able to harvest their crops." Shiryaev says all this could result in curtailing Putin's plans to continue the war. "If Ukraine destroys the whole oil refining infrastructure, Putin will find that, when he gives an order, it isn't implemented," the economist predicts. Everything will grind to a halt for lack of fuel. This article was originally published in Russian.

item.title: German army helps Poland protect itself against Russia
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.16
Poland started to construct a defensive barrier along its border with Russia and Belarus in 2024. The East Shield defense system will eventually be around 800 kilometers long, and is intended to protect this country on NATO's eastern flank against attack from the east. When the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, inspected the first completed section in November 2024, he declared that the project was meant to "deter and discourage a potential aggressor" and was "truly an investment in peace." The Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 was a profound shock to Poland's sense of security. The Tusk government has increased defense spending in 2026 to 200 billion zlotys (around 46 billion euros, or 54 billion dollars) ― almost 5% of Poland's GDP. This means that, in relative terms, Poland has the highest defense spending of all the members of NATO. The government has also bought the most advanced weapons available, particularly from the US, and is proceeding with the construction of the East Shield, a complex defense system along its eastern border. A shield against Russia Since June, around 40 German sappers, or combat engineers, have been helping to establish the defenses. The German army's combat engineer unit is specially trained in blocking the movement of enemy troops. The sappers are currently deployed near Budry in Masuria, close to the border with Russia. The fence marking the border is visible from where they are working, partially obscured by a row of trees on the Polish side. The German soldiers are installing anti-tank obstacles to impede battle tanks in the event of an attack. A yellow backhoe loader lifts the spiky concrete blocks, known as Czech hedgehogs, off a truck and places them on the muddy ground. This installation, around 200 meters back from the border, consists of three rows of these concrete blocks. A deep ditch and another line of hedgehogs run along the border itself. A Polish officer explains that mines can quickly be laid in the zone between the two lines of Czech hedgehogs. "The German sappers have done an excellent job," the Polish general Stanislaw Czosnek said when he inspected the works on Thursday. He added that he was "very impressed" by his German colleagues' performance. In the six weeks since their deployment, the German engineers have laid more than a kilometer of blocks. "We stand ready to fight for democracy and freedom," stressed the German general Tito Gante, who accompanied Czosnek on the inspection. He praised the comradely atmosphere between the German and the Polish soldiers. The Bundeswehr has declared its support for the East Shield an official mission: "We want to maintain peace with a credible deterrent," Gante said. The German contingent will stay until October, but the sappers will soon be deployed at other sections of the East Shield. The work near Budry is due to be completed over the coming week. Politically symbolic "Above all, the participation of German sappers has politically symbolic significance," Lukasz Jasinski, an analyst at the Polish Institute for International Affairs, told DW. "Poland wants to convince Germany and other partners that Poland's eastern border is also the external border of the EU and NATO. Our Western partners should treat this border a bit like their own." Poland and Germany were quick to establish military cooperation after the end of the Cold War. Later, when Poland joined NATO in 1999, this created the necessary political and institutional conditions for close collaboration. Since then, NATO's Multinational Corps Northeast, in which Poland and Germany both have leading roles, has been headquartered in the Polish city of Szczecin. In 2003, Germany sold the MiG-29 fighter jets it inherited from the former East German Air Force to Poland for the symbolic price of one euro each. Joint military exercises and exchange programs for both officers and soldiers are now standard practice. When Russia attacked Ukraine in February 2022, there were initial tensions between Germany and Poland on account of the cautious response from Berlin. Overall, though, the attack has further strengthened cooperation between the two. The Bundeswehr has supported Polish air defense by supplying several units of the Patriot air defense system, with their German crews. German fighter jets are helping to protect Polish air space, most recently as part of the NATO mission Enhanced Air Policing North (eAPN) in Malbork. Questions of military cooperation were also prioritized in the closing statement that followed German-Polish intergovernmental consultations on December 1, 2025. The process culminated in the signing of the German-Polish defense agreement on June 17, 2026. On August 15 this year, three German planes, two Eurofighters and an A400M transport aircraft, participated in the celebration of Polish Armed Forces Day. The head of the German air force, Holger Neumann, was one of the guests of honor. Some American GIs marched in the military parade ― but no German soldiers. Kaczynski: No German soldiers in Poland However, not all the political forces in Poland are happy about this new Polish-German brotherhood-in-arms. Memories of the trauma of World War II are still very much alive in Polish society and are regularly instrumentalized by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) to stir up anti-German feeling. Back in 2014, PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski said he didn't want any German soldiers in Poland. "It will be at least seven generations before that is acceptable," he said. In the fall of 2022, when the German government offered to relocate two German Patriot batteries to Poland after an incident involving a Ukrainian rocket gone astray, the PiS government blocked the move. "Germany's previous behavior gives us no reason to believe that it will decide to fire on the Russian rockets," Kaczynski declared. Just last March, Poland's president Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by the PiS, vetoed legislation that would have allowed Poland to access almost 44 billion euros (55 billion dollars) in EU defense loans because German armaments companies could also have benefited. Poland sees the US as the most important guarantor of its security, and is trying to establish a special relationship with Washington. Around 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in various places around the country. Warsaw is keen to establish a permanent military base on its territory: Until now, a significant number of the US soldiers are in Poland on rotation. This article was originally published in German.

item.title: How to add Bluetooth to a TV that doesn't have it
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.99
How to add Bluetooth to a TV that doesn't have it Look, we're all tired of hearing your shows echo through the house. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. With the right audio upgrades and a streaming device that unlocks the world of on-demand content, most televisions can last a very long time. Of course, there are certain upgrades that are harder to ignore — wireless connectivity being one of them. Bluetooth has become mainstream in most televisions now, with many infrared remote controls relying on the technology too. If you've purchased your TV in the past decade, there's a good chance it comes with Bluetooth support. Head to the settings menu and look for connectivity options that mention Bluetooth, wireless devices or accessories. If you do own a television without support for Bluetooth, you're not necessarily out of luck. Pretty much all popular streaming devices, like the Apple TV, Roku or Fire TV Stick, feature Bluetooth as a standard feature. If you own a pair of wireless headphones or a keyboard, you can connect them directly to the streaming device. At $30, the Roku Streaming Stick HD is one of the most affordable ways to not just add Bluetooth support to your TV but also breathe some new life into it with a modern OS. The only big downside of going the streaming device route is that your Bluetooth accessories will only work when your TV is set to that particular input source. If you switch back to any other device that's also connected to your TV, the sound will once again play from the TV's speakers. If you're looking for a more universal solution, picking up a dedicated Bluetooth transmitter is the better option. How does a Bluetooth transmitter work? Bluetooth transmitters do exactly what you'd expect — they carry over the audio from a device that doesn't have native Bluetooth support to a pair of wireless headphones or earbuds. The setup process is relatively straightforward. You plug the Bluetooth transmitter into your TV's audio output, put both the transmitter and your headphones into pairing mode, and wait for them to connect. Your TV then feeds its audio signal into the transmitter, which converts it into a Bluetooth signal that your headphones receive. Depending on your TV model, you can find Bluetooth transmitters that accept audio through the optical port, a 3.5mm headphone jack or RCA outputs. You'll also need to plug the adapter into a power source — an available USB port on your TV usually does the job. You can find these adapters at various price points online, with decent options at around $25. Look for transmitters that come with newer codecs like aptX Low Latency, which can help reduce the delay between what's happening on screen and what you hear through your headphones.

item.title: What's the difference between Dolby Digital 5.1 and Dolby Digital Plus?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.99
What's the difference between Dolby Digital 5.1 and Dolby Digital Plus? These naming conventions are getting out of hand. The names make the difference sound simple: Dolby Digital 5.1 is regular surround sound, while Dolby Digital Plus must be the better version. The actual difference isn't quite that simple. Dolby Digital is the older format and tops out at 5.1 channels, while Dolby Digital Plus can carry 5.1 or 7.1 surround sound and can also deliver Dolby Atmos. That makes DD+ more capable, but the "Plus" doesn't guarantee more channels or better sound every time. Dolby Digital tops out at 5.1 surround sound First, it helps to decode the number. A channel is essentially a separate audio feed assigned to a particular speaker position. In a 5.1 surround sound system, the five main channels cover the front left, center, front right, left surround and right surround positions. The ".1" refers to a separate low-frequency effects channel, usually handled by a subwoofer for things like explosions and other deep bass. Dolby Digital, which you may also see labeled AC-3, can carry anything from mono sound up to that full 5.1 configuration. It became closely associated with DVDs, digital television and earlier generations of home-theater equipment. Like Dolby Digital Plus, it uses lossy compression, which reduces file size by discarding some audio information. Dolby Digital Plus can carry 7.1 and Dolby Atmos Dolby Digital Plus, also called E-AC-3, still uses lossy compression but supports up to 7.1 channels. A 7.1 soundtrack adds two more surround channels beyond the conventional 5.1 layout, typically giving the system more separation around and behind the listener. The important word is can: DD+ also supports ordinary 5.1 audio, so seeing the newer format doesn't automatically mean more channels are being used. In other words, a Dolby Digital Plus logo isn't an instruction to go shopping for two more speakers. The newer format becomes particularly useful for streaming. Dolby designed Digital Plus for streaming, on-demand and downloaded content, and services such as Netflix use it for multichannel audio. Its combination of surround-sound support and compression makes it well suited to delivering that audio over the internet. Dolby Digital Plus can also carry Dolby Atmos. Atmos goes beyond assigning every sound to a fixed speaker channel by including information about where sounds should be positioned around the listener, allowing compatible equipment to adapt the soundtrack to the speaker setup. That doesn't make Dolby Atmos and Dolby Digital Plus the same thing. Streaming services can use Dolby Digital Plus to deliver Atmos, while Blu-ray discs can instead pair Atmos with Dolby TrueHD, a separate lossless format that preserves the audio data rather than discarding some of it during compression. Should you use Dolby Digital or Dolby Digital Plus? If your TV, streamer and audio equipment all support Dolby Digital Plus, DD+ is generally the better setting to leave enabled. It can carry a regular 5.1 soundtrack just fine while leaving room for 7.1 or Dolby Atmos when the source offers them. You don't need to choose standard Dolby Digital simply because you have a 5.1 speaker system. Older equipment is where Dolby Digital is still the safer choice. DD+ content can be converted into standard Dolby Digital so older systems can play it, but an older Dolby Digital decoder can't read the newer DD+ bitstream directly. For that to work, a compatible device such as your TV, streaming box or Blu-ray player needs to convert the DD+ audio to standard Dolby Digital before sending it to the older equipment. So if your equipment supports both, leave Dolby Digital Plus enabled. Switch to Dolby Digital when compatibility with older hardware requires it.

item.title: Hot vs cold: What's the ideal temperature for solar panel efficiency?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.90
Hot vs cold: What's the ideal temperature for solar panel efficiency? There is a correct answer, but ambient temperature is just one of several variables. Sunlight is a solar panel's best friend. But heat, not so much. The most common number you will see is 77 degrees Fahrenheit. That is 25 degrees Celsius, which is the temperature of the cell when manufacturers rate panels under standard test conditions, alongside irradiance of 1,000 watts per square meter. It's a good indicator, but it's not a magic outdoor temperature at which your roof achieves peak output. So yeah, cold wins, technically. The efficiency of solar cells is typically higher at lower temperatures because the voltage decreases more than the current increases with temperature. The problem is that efficiency and total electricity production are not the same. A cold panel might generate more power from the same amount of sunlight, but a hot summer day might generate more power because there might be more sunlight. Why solar panels lose efficiency as they get hotter The first wrinkle is that the temperature on your weather app isn't necessarily the temperature of the panel. A module in direct sunlight can be much hotter than the ambient air temperature, and Sandia National Laboratories, a US Department of Energy lab, models module temperature based on ambient temperature, solar irradiance, wind speed and mounting configuration. As soon as the cells get hotter than their rated reference temperature, output begins to drop according to the panel's temperature coefficient. There isn't one universal 0.5 percent penalty. REC Group, a leading solar panel manufacturer, has a maximum-power temperature coefficient of -0.24 percent per degree Celsius for its current Alpha Pure-RX, while solar manufacturer Qcells lists -0.29 percent per degree Celsius for its residential Q.TRON BLK M-G2+ series. If you live in a place that's really hot, that's something to consider. Nor is 77 degrees Fahrenheit "too hot" in the sense that the panel is in danger. The Q.TRON model has a continuous operating range of up to 158 degrees Fahrenheit, according to Qcells. REC lists a T98 module operating temperature of 176 degrees Fahrenheit for the Alpha Pure-RX. The Department of Energy says extreme heat can still damage cells and other module materials and shorten their operating lifetimes. The best weather for efficiency isn't always the best for production This is where the simple hot vs cold answer gets complicated. While a bright, cold day can be great for solar efficiency, clouds, snow, roof orientation, sun angle and daylight hours may be more important to the amount of electricity your system can generate. So the best time is not necessarily 10AM to 4PM. Output generally rises as more direct sunlight reaches the panels, then falls later in the day, but an east-facing array will be different from a west-facing array. Although panels can run hotter in the summer, the longer days and often stronger solar resources can result in more total electricity being produced. That's also why some homeowners size a solar system above their typical electricity needs. The 20 percent rule for solar panels is based on giving a solar system some breathing room when conditions aren't ideal. The National Laboratory of the Rockies' PVWatts calculator (the lab's free online estimator) allows you to input location and system information to estimate monthly and annual production, which gives you a more specific answer than "summer" or "midday." NLR does not specify a single best month or time of day, and it cautions that PVWatts cannot account for all site-specific variations or differentiate between higher- and lower-performing PV technologies. Its expected production range is based on 30 years of actual weather data.

item.title: How to cancel your ChatGPT subscription (and why you might want to)
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.53
How to cancel your ChatGPT subscription (and why you might want to) If you want to cancel your subscription, you'll need to go through the same payment system you used to sign up. Canceling a ChatGPT subscription only takes a few clicks. But if your goal is to quit ChatGPT entirely, stopping the recurring charge may be only one part of it. You might also want to delete your account, keep new chats out of model training or simply stop paying for features you no longer use. Canceling the subscription handles only the billing, so the right next step depends on what you actually want to stop. Reasons to reconsider a paid ChatGPT plan A paid plan makes the most sense when you regularly run into the Free tier's limits or rely on tools reserved for higher tiers. If that's no longer true, paying every month gets harder to justify. One option is ChatGPT Go, a lower-cost paid tier that OpenAI now offers in every country where ChatGPT is supported. Spending less doesn't necessarily require giving up a paid plan altogether. AI subscriptions have another unusual wrinkle: the product can change while you are paying for it. OpenAI retired GPT-4o from ChatGPT on February 13, 2026, after previously restoring it when some Plus and Pro users said they preferred its conversational style. For someone who subscribed partly for access to a particular model, that's a reminder that a paid AI service can change substantially from one month to the next. Features and price aren't the only reasons someone might reconsider a paid ChatGPT plan. After OpenAI's February 2026 agreement with the US Department of Defense to deploy its models on the department's classified network, Sensor Tower data reported by TechCrunch showed US ChatGPT app uninstalls jumping 295 percent day over day. OpenAI later amended the agreement to explicitly prohibit domestic surveillance of US persons and said its services would not be used by Defense Department intelligence agencies such as the NSA without a new agreement. The Sensor Tower figure measures app uninstalls, though, not paid subscription cancellations. How to cancel your ChatGPT subscription For a personal subscription purchased on chatgpt.com, log in, select your profile icon, open Settings, choose Billing and select Cancel under Cancel plan. OpenAI recommends canceling at least 24 hours before the next billing date to avoid another charge. If you subscribed through Apple, open the iPhone Settings app, tap your name, tap Subscriptions, select ChatGPT and tap Cancel Subscription. On Android, open Google Play, make sure you're signed in with the Google account used for the purchase, then go to Subscriptions > ChatGPT and tap Cancel subscription. Uninstalling the app does not cancel an App Store or Google Play subscription. If you can't find the cancel option, first check where you originally subscribed. Web, Apple and Google subscriptions are managed separately, and OpenAI warns that it's possible to end up with more than one active subscription across those platforms. If you have lost access to the ChatGPT account or its email address, OpenAI support can also cancel the subscription after locating the account using the email address, the last four digits of the payment card and the date of the most recent payment. What canceling a ChatGPT subscription does and doesn't change Canceling the subscription stops future renewals, but it doesn't delete your OpenAI account or erase existing chats. Standard chats remain saved to your account until you delete them, so canceling a paid plan is not the same thing as removing your data. Whether your chats are used for model training is controlled separately. Under Settings > Data Controls, turning off Improve the model for everyone prevents new conversations from being used to improve OpenAI's models while leaving those conversations in your history. Temporary Chats are another option for individual conversations: they don't appear in history or get used to improve the models, and OpenAI says it may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Deleting your OpenAI account is separate from canceling the subscription. Account deletion is permanent, prevents access to OpenAI services and triggers deletion of account data within 30 days, apart from limited information OpenAI may retain where required or permitted by law. If Apple or Google is billing you, cancel the subscription through the relevant app store before deleting the account. What happens after you cancel ChatGPT Canceling doesn't remove paid features immediately. OpenAI says the cancellation becomes effective the day after the next billing date, so you can keep using the paid plan through the current billing period. Canceling also doesn't automatically result in a refund. If you subscribed through chatgpt.com or Google Play, you can request one through OpenAI's Help Center. App Store refunds must be requested directly from Apple. For chatgpt.com and Google Play purchases, accidental purchases are generally eligible for a refund if you contact OpenAI within 14 days of the charge. Customers in the EU, UKand Turkey are also eligible for a prorated refund if they cancel within 14 days of purchase. Once the paid period ends, your account remains available along with any chats you haven't deleted. Canceling the subscription stops the recurring payment without requiring you to decide whether to keep using ChatGPT.

item.title: How to use Samsung's new My FanCam feature to make yourself the main character in your videos
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.52
How to use Samsung's new My FanCam feature to make yourself the main character in your videos My FanCam works after you record, turning a wider group video into a tighter tracking shot around one person. Samsung's My FanCam is built for videos where several people are moving through the frame. Instead of trying to keep one person centered while you're recording, you can capture the wider scene and choose your subject afterward. Galaxy AI then reframes the existing footage around that person in an aspect ratio you select. Samsung introduced the feature on the Galaxy Z Fold8 lineup. Because My FanCam works on a video you've already recorded, there's nothing special you need to turn on before shooting. How to use My FanCam in Samsung Gallery My FanCam lives in Samsung's Gallery editing tools. On a supported device, start with a video that contains the person you want Galaxy AI to follow. Open Gallery and select the video you want to edit. Then, tap the Galaxy AI icon and select My FanCam. Wait for Galaxy AI to identify the people in the video and select the person you want to follow. Next, choose an aspect ratio for the new clip. Finally, tap Follow to create the reframed video. The aspect-ratio choice is useful if you already know where the finished clip is going. A vertical crop makes more sense for platforms built around portrait video, while a wider frame may work better if you want to keep more of the original scene visible. My FanCam handles the tracking either way, so you can make that decision after you've recorded the footage. Shoot a wider frame if you plan to use My FanCam My FanCam differs from Samsung's Auto framing feature in one important way. Auto framing adjusts the composition while you're recording, while My FanCam does its work afterward. That gives you more freedom to capture the whole scene first, but it also means the feature can only reframe footage that made it into the original recording. Imagine recording a school performance, a soccer game or a group dance. Rather than constantly moving the phone to keep one person centered, you can keep more of the scene visible and decide who you want to focus on when you edit the clip later. It helps to think of My FanCam as moving a smaller frame around inside the video you already recorded. If you're filming several people, keeping the shot reasonably wide gives Galaxy AI more room to reposition that crop as your chosen person moves from one side of the scene to the other. If you start with a very tight shot, there's simply less surrounding image available for My FanCam to use. The same limitation applies when your subject moves outside the original frame. My FanCam reframes what the camera captured, but it can't recover parts of a scene that were never recorded. Samsung also says the feature won't work when it can't find a subject to track, and it doesn't guarantee tracking accuracy. So for something unpredictable, such as a sports game or a group performance, keeping the person you care about comfortably within the wider shot gives the feature a better starting point. Which Samsung phones support My FanCam? Samsung currently demonstrates My FanCam on the Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra. Both phones launched with One UI 9, which is where Samsung lists My FanCam among its new Galaxy AI features. One UI 9 isn't limited to those two phones. Samsung first rolled it out to the Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Flip8, with more Galaxy devices set to follow. My FanCam is a little less straightforward, though, since Samsung says individual AI features can vary by device, language and region. So even if your phone gets One UI 9, My FanCam may not come along with it.

item.title: How does converting a video to 4K actually work?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.50
How does converting a video to 4K actually work? Upscaling software is getting better all the time, but there are still some caveats to be aware of. The shift from analogue film to digital video happened quickly. Before you knew it, tape-based video recorders had been replaced with digital video cameras and, later still, smartphones. 4K is now the gold standard for video creation, with 1080p left as its lower-quality sibling. Despite widespread 4K adoption, there's still plenty of video being created in 1080p. And that's not to mention content made in the past, from home videos to old movies, available in standard definition or even lower. That can lead you to thinking about converting video to 4K, giving it a boost to make it look as sharp on a modern 4K OLED display as something you'd shoot today. Converting a video to 4K is possible, but it's a process with a lot of steps and points to consider first. Converting a video to 4K means creating millions of new pixels When we talk about 4K and 1080p, or ultra-high and high definition, we're talking about the amount of pixels contained within each video frame. For ultra-high definition video content, which is what most people usually mean by 4K, that means a resolution of 3,840 x 2,160 pixels, versus 1,920 x 1,080 pixels for 1080p high definition video. Standard definition video, meanwhile, sits at either 480 or 576 vertical lines depending on your region; width can vary depending on how the content was originally filmed. You can also find cinematic 4K resolutions, so-called 'true 4K' or DCI 4K, with a resolution of 4,096 x 2,160. You can upscale any output file to 4K — 4K is just the frame size. To move from 1080p to 4K, you're going to need three additional pixels on-screen for every original pixel that was recorded, so four times overall. Managing that without losing any quality is the issue. That is almost impossible and simply changing the resolution won't reveal a hidden version with extra clarity or sharpness, either. Traditional upscaling software uses interpolation to manage this, scaling up each frame and figuring out what it should look like. How accurate upscaling software can be is the main question. It has to estimate what the pixels should look like, but it can't recover the real detail if it wasn't recorded in the first place. Often, this means that sizing up will make the footage look softer. The "guess-timation" used to add extra pixels often makes it look smooth as a result. Sharpening can help around the edges, but it's a Goldilocks dilemma: too much, or not enough, can ruin it. The same is true for noise reduction, which can make the final footage look unnatural. Professional 4K restorations often return to high-quality original source files If you're a professional looking to convert a video to 4K, you're going to want to work from the best source data available to you: the original source files. The better that source data is, the better quality a job you'll be able to achieve. The HD restoration of Star Trek: The Next Generation proves how tricky this can be if you want to get the process right. That upgrade, commissioned by CBS in 2011, used the show's original 35mm film negatives, which were described as having a quality equivalent to a 20 megapixel resolution, to remaster all seven seasons of the show from their original broadcast quality to 1080p for Blu-ray release. 25,000 reels of original film stock were used, with visual effects and CGI upgrades to help the process. It took over three years to complete and reportedly cost the studio over $12 million, according to one of its producers. Ironically enough, the analog film to digital video conversion here makes this type of job easier. If you're working with an older digital master file with a set resolution, you're stuck with a fixed number of pixels to work from. The original negatives used in the Star Trek upgrade capture far more detail that wouldn't have made it into the original television broadcasts. Unfortunately, when the best source files are already low resolution, you're not able to work from the real data. All of the missing pixels that are created are guesses. The best result is that this will look pretty convincing, but it won't be 100 percent true to form. Home upscaling uses interpolation or AI to fill in the gaps Unlike CBS, you're unlikely to have $12 million to convert your videos to 4K. Home users converting video to 4K will instead have to choose between traditional interpolation or newer AI-based tools. Both methods will create the additional pixels needed to fill out an enlarged 4K frame, but not in the same way. 4K upscalers using interpolation rely on good, old-fashioned math. It takes a pixel from a single frame and looks at the color and brightness of the pixels around it. From there, it'll try to calculate how the pixels surrounding it will look. At a basic level, it might achieve this by sheer duplication, but more advanced algorithms will focus on trying to preserve edges and avoid jagged lines. The end result is pretty predictable, but one problem is softness. Interpolation can't magically recreate genuine detail or textures, making it seem slightly fake. Your TV might be able to do this automatically too, with varying degrees of success. Luckily, AI upscaling looks to solve that problem. These models are trained on examples of low and high-resolution images that allow it to identify how common features should look on your screen. Instead of estimating each pixel, the AI is predicting what a sharper image will look like. The result can be sharper and more convincing but, like interpolation, it won't be an exact match for the real world. AI upscalers can also introduce unusual artifacts that interpolation doesn't. AI models are constantly improving, however, so the quality and consistency you'll see today might seem antiquated in just a few years' time. If you're working with older video, you may also need to think about interlacing, where video frames were split into two halves by odd and even horizontal lines, with each line refreshing each time the screen refreshes. Modern displays don't use interlacing, but older broadcasts meant for CRT-like screens would. Converting these kinds of videos will require you to de-interlace before upscaling, although how well you'll be able to upscale a 480i NTSC video to 4K in a way that maintains a watchable video quality is questionable. Upscaling tools often feature plenty of configuration to help you get the result you want, whether it's using AI or interpolation. If a single pass through doesn't get you the result you're looking for, you can tweak the settings to have another go (as long as you've got the disk space). Upscaling a 1080p video to 4K doesn't automatically improve it You can't just whack a 1080p video into an upscaler and expect a perfect 4K video at the end. You can achieve it in the technical sense, by increasing the size of the video frame, but getting the video to scale up without losing quality is difficult. It may take several attempts to get the result to match up to your expectations. It's easier to achieve if you've got good source material to work from, and the smaller the leap in resolution, the better. Upscaling from 1440p to 4K, for instance, won't require as many 'fake' pixels as 1080p to 4K, or worse, 480p to 4K. 4K upscaling software can only guess what the missing pieces, those extra pixels, should look like. AI is making the process easier, and potentially better, but a like-for-like match isn't guaranteed. Resolution isn't the only factor at play here, though. To save on disk space, video files can be compressed with a lower bitrate, meaning the amount of data saved for each second of video is lower. Upscaling to 4K won't undo that, and you can't just lose common compression artifacts like blocks or banding if you're working from a low bitrate file. It all comes down to the source, and if that's good enough, upscaling becomes a whole lot easier to handle.

item.title: What is a VESA mount and how to know what type your TV has
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.40
What is a VESA mount and how to know what type your TV has The VESA dimensions tell you where the mounting holes line up, but you still need to check the mount's weight limit and hardware. Thankfully, VESA 400 × 400 isn't another TV resolution you need to learn. VESA stands for Video Electronics Standards Association, and in TV-mount shopping, a VESA size or VESA pattern describes the spacing between the mounting holes on the back of a TV or display. A VESA mount isn't one particular style of bracket; it simply supports one or more of those standardized patterns. What does a VESA size such as 200 × 200 mean? Look at the back of a typical mountable TV and you'll find threaded mounting holes, usually arranged in a square or rectangle. The VESA pattern describes the distance between those holes, measured in millimeters. The first number is the horizontal distance and the second is the vertical distance. So a TV with a 400 × 200 pattern has mounting holes spaced 400mm apart from left to right and 200mm apart from top to bottom. A 200 × 200 pattern measures 200mm in both directions. The VESA numbers don't describe the TV's resolution or screen dimensions. Larger TVs often use larger mounting patterns, but screen size alone doesn't tell you which pattern a particular model uses. Checking your exact TV model is more reliable than guessing from its screen size. You also don't need a mount limited to that exact VESA size. Many mounts support multiple VESA patterns, so you don't need a bracket labeled only for your exact size. Your TV's pattern just needs to appear on the mount's list of supported patterns. How to find your TV's VESA pattern The easiest method doesn't require a ruler at all. Look up the exact TV model in its manual or on the manufacturer's support page and find the wall-mount or VESA specifications. Manufacturers commonly list the mounting-hole pattern in millimeters. If you can't find the specification, you can measure the mounting holes yourself. Measure from the center of one mounting hole to the center of the corresponding hole horizontally, then do the same vertically. Write the result as horizontal × vertical, in millimeters. For example, if the mounting holes are 400mm apart horizontally and 200mm apart vertically, the TV has a 400 × 200 VESA pattern. Measure in millimeters so you can compare the result directly with the mount's specifications. A matching VESA pattern isn't enough A matching VESA pattern tells you the bracket can line up with the TV's mounting holes. It doesn't tell you whether the mount can safely hold the TV, so the next specification to check is its weight limit. Compare the mount's maximum load with the weight of your TV. A bracket can support the correct VESA pattern and still be unsuitable for a TV that's too heavy. You should also check the hardware required by your TV. VESA compatibility also says nothing about how the bracket should attach to the wall. Once you've confirmed the pattern and weight rating, use the TV manufacturer's instructions to check the required mounting screws and follow the mount manufacturer's instructions for attaching the bracket to the wall.

item.title: Why are more movies not shot in IMAX?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.23
Why are more movies not shot in IMAX? Shooting an IMAX movie is an expensive endeavor that most filmmakers avoid, at least for now. IMAX movies are dramatic experiences: big, bold, bright, with a sense of scale that's much bigger than the average cinema screen. It's a demanding process for filmmakers to create IMAX movies, requiring specialist equipment and a big budget. Only a select few, like Christopher Nolan, have fully embraced the standard, with Nolan's latest movie, The Odyssey, being one of the few to be filmed entirely on IMAX film. IMAX films deliver the goods — but if the format is so impressive, why aren't more movies being shot in IMAX? IMAX film has always been difficult to shoot IMAX isn't a new development, but it wasn't designed with Hollywood cinema in mind. The first IMAX film, Tiger Child, was a Japanese short film released in 1970, with a later film, North of Superior, used in 1971 to more widely showcase the format. Its early years were dominated by documentaries, educational films and more short films to showcase IMAX's huge screen size and high-resolution detail. It's not a platform that has ever seen a huge amount of adoption. Shooting an IMAX film has always required bigger and more cumbersome equipment. Modern IMAX film cameras are still larger and heavier than their traditional counterparts, and are louder to operate, adding extra difficulty on a film set where clean audio is a necessity. Their size and general bulkiness make them an impractical option for a lot of scenes. You're not taking an IMAX camera with you if you're filming on a small set, or if you need to film fast-paced action scenes, for example. IMAX film itself is big and bulky, too. The 65-70mm size is much larger than traditional 35mm film, which gives it its impressive quality, but the camera physically can't hold as much. That means regular film changes, a problem faced by Tom Holland on The Odyssey film set, who mistook the regular three-minute stoppages for film changes as a critique on his performance. Given the filming schedule for a Hollywood movie, extra stoppages like this simply add to the cost. So, to film in IMAX, you'll need specialist cameras that are bulky and harder to film with, require expensive film, and can lead to a longer film schedule. Even newer IMAX cameras, like the quieter 65mm IMAX Keighley camera used in The Odyssey, are still bulky to operate, weighing almost 400 pounds. Most movie theaters can't show true IMAX screens in the original 15/70 format, so the true experience is reserved to a much smaller set of cinema screens. Some digital cameras are now IMAX-certified, but these don't deliver the same quality as traditional 15/70 IMAX film. As a result, most filmmakers have chosen to use IMAX selectively. The Dark Knight, another Christopher Nolan movie, was the first major Hollywood film to use IMAX for some of its scenes, reserving it for parts of the film that he believed its impressive detail would have the biggest impact. Nolan, however, is a rarity. Most producers aren't willing to accept the trade-offs and additional costs, while others more typically go down the IMAX-certified digital route instead. Digital cinema made shooting movies easier and cheaper If we count Nolan as one of IMAX's biggest cheerleaders, his decision to partially film The Dark Knight using IMAX cameras in 2008 is an interesting contrast to how filmmaking was shifting in this period away from traditional film. Hollywood wasn't going for bigger IMAX films, but instead moving to digital production. It's not hard to see why. Traditional filmmaking requires physical film, larger cameras, longer takes and more extensive post-production to edit and cut down. You eliminate almost all of these stress points with digital film cameras: quieter, smaller, easier to handle. If you compare and contrast to IMAX, which we've already mentioned as being even bigger and louder than traditional 35mm film cameras, then IMAX already felt antiquated in 2008, let alone in 2026 for most directors. Digital film production became the obvious and practical choice for Hollywood very quickly. Slumdog Millionaire, released a year after Nolan's Dark Knight in 2009, won the Oscar for Best Cinematography in the same year, the first digitally-shot movie to do so. The industry hasn't looked back. That left IMAX as an experimental and niche option for most filmmakers. Nolan, a traditionalist who uses physical 65mm IMAX film cameras, is an enthusiast for the format that few else are, believing that IMAX film offers the highest quality of any film format available today. "Filmed for IMAX" movies are the alternative. Tom Cruise is one of the most recognizable names making movies like this, with Mission Impossible: The Final Reckoning filmed using Sony IMAX-certified digital cameras. They're designed to capture a bigger image area to fill IMAX's expanded 1.90:1 size, with quality good enough to create movies that can still take advantage of IMAX cinema screens. Unlike Nolan's movies, however, The Final Reckoning isn't true IMAX. It can't scale to the full IMAX screen, with an aspect ratio smaller in size. Other movies, like Ant-Man and the Wasp, only manage to hit 1.90:1 for a portion of each film: at least 45 minutes is the aim for it to be given the 'Filmed for IMAX' tag. You also have 'Experience in IMAX' movies which are remastered from their original widescreen format to fill the bigger size but lacking the same IMAX quality. IMAX is too niche and difficult to justify for most productions A movie, filmed truly for IMAX cinema screens, is visually impressive, but out of reach for most filmmakers. You can consider all of the impracticalities, but cost trumps them all. IMAX is a very expensive format to film on. It requires specialist cameras, film and operators trained to use it. Filming with it takes longer, and post-production longer still. Once it's filmed, it can only be experienced in its true format in just 41 movie theatres worldwide. For studios, you're paying more to produce a movie that only a fraction of your likely audience is going to be able to see at its very best. Digital cameras have narrowed the gap somewhat. IMAX-certified cameras, like the Sony Venice cameras used on Mission Impossible: The Final Reckoning, let filmmakers create movies that can take full advantage of an IMAX cinema screen, but "Filmed for IMAX" isn't the same as shooting on IMAX film. Digital cameras have closed the distance, but the film used in traditional IMAX filmmaking still captures far more detail. IMAX is the premium filmmaking format. Big showstoppers like The Odyssey are rare and expensive to film, and rare because they're expensive to film. Most blockbuster filmmakers will choose normal digital filmmaking instead, getting their movies out into more theaters with still-very-good cinema quality so that more people are able to enjoy them.

item.title: The new Shokz OpenFit Air 2 earbuds are nearly 20 percent lighter than the previous generation
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 4.94
The new Shokz OpenFit Air 2 earbuds are nearly 20 percent lighter than the previous generation They feature an open-ear design that reduces pressure and heat buildup. Shokz just introduced the OpenFit Air 2 earbuds, a refresh of the original model. These earbuds are around 17 percent lighter than the previous version, clocking in at 7.2g per unit. That's around the same weight as a handful of paperclips. This is an open-ear design, which delivers a couple of benefits. First of all, there's no ear canal pressure, as the earbuds don't create a seal of any kind. The design also gives users quicker access to their surroundings, making them a decent choice for exercising outside in a busy city. As a matter of fact, the standard Shokz OpenAir 2 earbuds easily made our list of the best headphones for running. The only potential downside to this form factor is that they connect via an ear-hook. The ergonomic design ensures long-term comfort, with a caveat. These ear-hooks could get in the way of glasses and certain hats. Take a look at photos and decide for yourself. Otherwise, the company promises "richer bass" and "fuller sound." The earbuds use the company's proprietary Bassphere audio driver and its OpenBass 2.0 algorithm. There's an angled speaker that directs audio toward the ear for a "more natural listening experience" and an app with access to four preset EQ modes and two custom EQ profiles. The OpenFit Air 2 earbuds last eight hours per charge, with up to 36 hours of use when considering the included charging case. They also offer a 10-minute quick charge that gives three hours of playback. This model integrates with Bluetooth 6.1 and allows for multipoint connections. They will be available to purchase on August 27 for $130. Shokz also just introduced the OpenRun Air 2 earbuds, which feature a design that wraps around the back of the head. These are also lighter than the previous iteration, with an overall form factor that prioritizes stability and minimizes bounce. After all, these are for runners. They use a bone conduction driver and also connect to the company's app for EQ adjustments. The battery lasts ten hours on a single charge, with a five-minute quick charge for two hours of playback. The OpenRun Air 2 earbuds are also available on August 27 and, lo and behold, also cost $130.

item.title: The only GameCube that could play CDs and DVDs is rarely found below $1,000 today
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 4.67
The only GameCube that could play CDs and DVDs is rarely found below $1,000 today This is one strange console. One reason GameCube games hold their value so well today is that, compared to other Nintendo consoles, it wasn't exactly a hot seller. Why was that? Well, it's partly because the PS2 had what the GameCube didn't: a built-in DVD player. Out of that market pressure was born the Panasonic Q. While this oddball GameCube/DVD player hybrid barely got off the ground, its scarcity has led to a second life as a niche collector's item. The Japan-only Panasonic SL-GC 10, widely known as the Panasonic Q, arrived in December 2001, three months after the Nintendo GameCube debuted in Japan. Looking less like a Nintendo console and more like a home-theater appliance, the Q had a reflective front panel, a backlit LCD and ports with a blue glow. If you want quintessential 2001 consumer electronics design, look no further. The oddball pairing of Panasonic branding with Nintendo gaming stemmed from an existing relationship between the two companies. It turns out Panasonic's then-parent company, Matsushita (which is essentially Panasonic today), helped design the GameCube's optical miniDVD format. It seems likely Nintendo saw the gaping DVD hole in its console strategy and decided to roll the dice. A GameCube for the DVD era The Panasonic Q was a bizarre mashup. Its motorized disc tray accepted GameCube discs, DVDs and audio CDs. The company took the home theater part seriously. The Q had a Cinema mode for picture processing, along with audio features like Dolby Digital, DTS (Digital Theater Systems) for surround sound, Dialogue Enhancer and Bass Plus.
