item.title: “The Strategy of Terrorism”
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.30
A quarter century before 9/11, an upsurge in global terrorism prompted the historian David Fromkin to examine its purpose and method. Terrorism was a strategy of the weak, Fromkin wrote in these pages, but modern technology had enabled it “to enter the political arena on a new scale.” And its surprising success seemed to be due, in large part, “to a miscomprehension of the strategy by its opponents.” Those who are the targets of terrorism—and who are prepared to defend themselves by doing whatever is necessary in order to beat it—start with a major advantage. The advantage is that success or failure depends upon them alone. Terrorism wins only if you respond to it in the way that the terrorists want you to; which means that its fate is in your hands and not in theirs. If you choose not to respond at all, or else to respond in a way different from that which they desire, they will fail to achieve their objectives. The important point is that the choice is yours. That is the ultimate weakness of terrorism as a strategy. It means that, though terrorism cannot always be prevented, it can always be defeated. You can always refuse to do what they want you to do. Whether to pay the price of defeating terrorism is increasingly going to be a major question in our time. The answer is relatively easy in most kidnapping and ransom situations: experience has shown that blackmailers and extortionists usually are encouraged to try it again if you give in to their demands the first time. So, if you can do so, you should accept the consequences, however terrible, of standing firm in order to avoid an infinite sequence of painful events. But the price of doing so is constantly rising, as technology increases the range and magnitude of horrible possibilities. Terrorist outrages, when they occur, are bound to become more deadly. Increasingly, we will be under pressure to abridge our laws and liberties in order to suppress the terrorists. It is a pressure that should be resisted.

item.title: The Abandoned Order
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.16
Five years ago, the Chinese housing market crashed, leaving thousands of apartment buildings unfinished across the country. A generation of Chinese citizens who had bet all their savings on indefinite expansion suddenly found themselves homeless. Over time, however, some intrepid people moved into the ruins of these edifices, setting up tents on the concrete floors, using bed sheets as walls, cooking on makeshift stoves. The Chinese call these abandoned structures lanwei lou, a phrase that literally means “rotten-tail buildings,” signifying a project gone awry, a plan in suspension. The inhabitants of rotten-tail buildings repurpose the old and improvise to find a way of surviving an economic storm. The state of the Chinese housing market is a good metaphor for the U.S.-led rules-based international order. After decades of expansion, it, too, is being abandoned. Never fully accepted by China and Russia and resented by newly assertive middle powers, its main financial backers—the American people—have lost interest in underwriting its further development. And as in the case of China’s failed housing projects, no alternative provider is stepping in to take over. A rotten-tail world is emerging, one in which states will have to adapt cunningly, improvise new uses for elements of the old order that remain valuable, and adjust swiftly to the dramatic decay of others. But too many leaders still act as if the old order can somehow be salvaged or even perfected. The UN General Assembly still meets every year, despite being increasingly sidelined from diplomatic efforts. The World Trade Organization carries on adjudicating trade disputes, despite a surge in protectionism. UN climate change conferences convene to chart an increasingly hopeless path to net-zero emissions. International working groups still meet to discuss grand plans for a two-state solution, even as the Middle East burns. The United States’ allies, in particular, simply do not understand yet that Washington has withdrawn its support from the old order and from them. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has mocked those Europeans who suggest learning to defend themselves without U.S. help, telling them to “keep on dreaming.” NATO’s July 2026 summit offered one of the most surreal examples of cognitive dissonance: European leaders frenetically pledged tributes to U.S. President Donald Trump in the form of arbitrary defense spending increases—unrelated to their own defense analysts’ assessments—in the hope that he would not withdraw from the alliance. The United Kingdom continues to entrench its security dependence on the United States by buying U.S. fighter jets, and Denmark is approving major arms purchases from Washington even as Trump threatens to forcibly annex its constituent territory, Greenland. Australia is plowing ahead with investments in AUKUS, its trilateral security partnership with the United Kingdom and the United States, subsidizing the U.S. industrial base even as American commitments falter. Leaders who fail to confront their new reality are failing their countries. It is time to acknowledge that the old order really has disappeared—and to plot a new approach to geopolitics. This moment does not constitute a short interregnum between a U.S.-led order and a Chinese-led one. For some time, the world will be without any order at all—swept by fragmentation, contagion, and strangulation or the temptation to weaponize a wide variety of geographic, economic, and technological chokepoints. Rather than constructing a grand strategy, states will need to develop far more flexible and artisanal responses. REALITY CHECK U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger once asserted that world order rests on two pillars: a reasonably stable balance of power and a set of commonly agreed-on rules about what states may or may not do. Today, both pillars are crumbling, and it is unlikely that they can be fortified or rebuilt any time soon. The United States remains the world’s preeminent military, economic, and technological power. But it is increasingly clear that Washington no longer has the ability to prevent conflicts or ensure the free flow of commerce worldwide; it could not even open the Strait of Hormuz after a militarily hobbled Iran shuttered the waterway. Even at the height of U.S. power, adversaries in Afghanistan and Iraq were able to exploit asymmetric advantages to challenge it. But swift technological change, especially the proliferation of cheap missiles and drones, is rapidly undermining the U.S. military’s command of the seas and skies and the relative peace that went with it. Even before Trump, the alliance system that helped the United States enforce the rules was weakening; China, Russia, and rising powers that didn’t make the rules were pushing against them. Then, Trump launched a rebellion from within against the U.S.-led order, bullying American allies, ditching the World Health Organization, scrapping the U.S. Agency for International Development, and imposing widespread punitive tariffs. His will to dismantle the order the United States built has been extraordinary. But even after his presidency ends, in 2029, it is highly unlikely that the United States will resume its old role. Americans had already lost interest in being the world’s primary provider of public goods, its police officer, and its free-trade champion. And no other power has the ambition to take up the mantle. In dozens of private conversations I have had over the past year with leaders worldwide, the only thing they agree on is that they do not know what will come next. They are struggling to use history or theory to find their bearings. The briefings they get from their intelligence agencies and diplomatic services no longer give them any certainty. Ahead of every NATO summit, I receive text messages from European leaders asking me what I think might happen. One Gulf leader recently admitted to me that he simply had no idea what arrangement would settle the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz. The national security adviser of a U.S. ally in the Indo-Pacific said his government no longer knew whether the United States would defend his country in a crisis. The central feature of these conversations is uncertainty, a sense that the world defies conventions and understanding. Episodes of rule breaking always characterized the rules-based order, but they took place within an overall framework that still held. This is the distinction: in a disordered world, actors violate rules they still recognize. In a world defined by what might be called “un-order,” they act without reference to any common framework at all. A WORLD IN PIECES The uncertainty that pervades this orderless age is driven by three forces upending the international system: fragmentation, contagion, and strangulation. Trump’s predatory approach to partners is fragmenting the West as a political community. Alliances are splintering, and not just Western ones; consider the disarray in the Gulf Cooperation Council. Trade restrictions are breaking up world markets, but not into tidy blocs. Global problems no longer attract global solutions but rather a patchwork of short-term fixes. The deepest fragmentation is epistemic. A digitally connected world is not simply dividing over interpretations; its inhabitants no longer agree on facts, erasing the sense of shared reality that underpins diplomacy itself. Consider the war that the United States and Israel launched against Iran in February. The parties to the conflict have been unable even to agree on whether a cease-fire exists, what leverage they have, or who won or lost. The aspiration to establish a single global order is giving way to a reality in which many organizing systems coexist and compete. Some frameworks are organized around regions. Others, including the Pax Silica (a new initiative to secure tech supply chains), the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, and AUKUS, seek to govern arenas such as technology, trade, and security. Gone is the idea that the United Nations or even the United States could oversee comprehensive peace deals that successfully address territorial claims, postwar justice, and reconstruction. Instead of such deals, limited cease-fires and truces—negotiated not by diplomats but by a motley crew of intermediaries such as the American real estate mogul Steve Witkoff, the Russian banker Kirill Dmitriev, and Asim Munir, Pakistan’s top general—aim to freeze conflicts rather than resolve them. In a world of unreliable allies, countries will hedge. The Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty could cease to function as a meaningful constraint, and Germany, Iran, Poland, Saudi Arabia, and South Korea could move to acquire nuclear weapons within two decades. Also gone is the notion that consistent rules ought to govern the global economy. Economic nationalism and protectionism are on the rise; the EU’s introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, Trump’s tariffs, and China’s export controls are all accelerating the breakup of the global economy. Identical barrels of oil now trade at vastly different prices depending on where they are sold, through which payment system, to which buyer, and under which sanctions regime. In early April, for instance, Brent futures traded at around $113 per barrel while physical cargoes of the stuff sold for as much as $144. Oil futures and spot prices usually diverge, but only by a few dollars; such a spread is extremely unusual. The London and New York gold markets are also experiencing bouts of sharp price divergence. This kind of fragmentation will only become more pervasive. The dollar’s dominance will erode more rapidly, with its share of global foreign exchange reserves perhaps falling below 50 percent as bilateral currency arrangements proliferate and the pricing of commodities diversifies. U.S. borrowing costs will rise, and global transaction costs will balloon as incompatible systems multiply. OUT OF CONTROL Another big challenge is contagion. International law and norms formerly put limits on states’ actions. Great powers might not always have adhered to the rules, but they were imposed on smaller powers and set expectations for how business would be conducted. But in this era of disinhibition, crises no longer stay in their original domain, and actors no longer feel constrained by norms governing proper conduct—indeed, many of the world’s most powerful actors no longer even seem aware that they are breaking rules. In this environment, disputes are also less likely to remain compartmentalized. France and Germany strongly opposed the war the United States launched against the Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein in 2003, but that did not prevent them from continuing to share intelligence with and trade with the United States, nor did it stop them from cooperating with Washington on other NATO matters. When Trump threatened tariffs against European allies who opposed his claim to Greenland, by contrast, he demonstrated that even among allies, economic and security relations are no longer separate. During the recent Iran war, when several European countries expressed reservations about the conflict, Trump threatened to halt trade with them and withdraw troops stationed in their countries. Too many leaders still act as if the old order can somehow be salvaged. And after Israel and the United States attacked Iran, the Islamic Republic and its proxies launched strikes on U.S. partners Bahrain, Oman, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, and even Europe, by assaulting Cyprus. Rather than seeking to hinder the U.S. war effort directly, Iran seemed intent on disrupting global markets as much as possible. Frustrated by Pakistan’s closeness to Iran, the United Arab Emirates, for its part, also retaliated across domains by forcing an early repayment of a $3.5 billion debt and deporting thousands of Pakistani workers. This same disinhibition increasingly governs how war itself is waged. The taboos against assassination, targeting civilians, and embarking on wars of territorial conquest are vanishing. According to reporting in The New York Times, Israel planned to assassinate the Iranian foreign minister and speaker of parliament while the two were conducting negotiations with the United States. Throughout its war in Gaza, Israel attacked people and facilities that were previously not considered legitimate targets: journalists, hospitals, cultural sites, religious institutions, and civilian infrastructure; Israel claimed that Hamas used such targets as covers. Russia regularly targets civilian infrastructure in its war in Ukraine, and both countries are killing each other’s citizens in third countries in targeted assassinations. This kind of uncontrolled escalation will almost certainly lead to more wars. Countries beyond the United States may be tempted to blackmail their allies, and the threat of nuclear attacks could become normalized. Most worrying is the prospect of a proliferation of small wars for territory. There is no shortage of possible catalysts. China could target Taiwan outright; Venezuela could decide to use force in pursuit of its claim on Essequibo, the resource-rich western half of neighboring Guyana; Ethiopia might try to wrest access to Eritrea’s Red Sea ports; and Russia might decide to seize the Estonian border town of Narva. THE BIG SQUEEZE In a marriage that has gone wrong, the ties that bound a couple together in good times—the house, the children, the dog—become the weapons they use to hurt each other in bad times. Likewise, in today’s geopolitics, states are increasingly turning the systems that once connected them—energy routes, semiconductor supply chains, financial infrastructure, shipping lanes—into weapons. A country’s control over chokepoints is becoming a key marker of its power, just like its GDP and the size of its military. Western countries have been particularly active in identifying and weaponizing chokepoints, above all through their control of the global financial system and essential technologies. The first Trump administration restricted Chinese companies’ access to high-level microchips. The Biden administration stepped up this technological throttling by imposing wider export controls, taking advantage of the fact that U.S. and allied firms dominate the production of chip manufacturing equipment and the software required to make advanced chips. In 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a coalition of European and North American countries took the remarkable step of weaponizing the dollar to punish a G-20 country when they cut Russian banks out of the SWIFT payments system and froze $300 billion of Russian central bank reserves. China, learning from this, is rapidly expanding its own authority over chokepoints. In 2010, Beijing briefly experimented with cutting off rare-earth exports to Japan amid a territorial dispute, but it had not yet established the bureaucracy to target such controls precisely. Since then, it has built its own export control system explicitly modeled on Washington’s and extended the resource chokepoints it commands from raw materials to processing. In late 2025, China adopted its own version of the U.S. foreign direct product rule, asserting a right to decide whether companies can access magnets anywhere in the world if they contain even trace amounts of Chinese materials or were made using Chinese technology. In effect, Beijing turned against Washington the same extraterritorial tactic Washington had invented to control chips. Smaller countries and nonstate actors are increasingly exploiting chokepoints, as well. According to German prosecutors, a Ukrainian team destroyed the Nord Stream pipelines to break Europe’s dependence on Russian gas. Even before Iran shuttered the Strait of Hormuz, bringing 20 percent of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipping to a near halt, the Houthi militia in Yemen was using cheap drones and missiles to block transit through the Red Sea. Such exploitation of chokepoints will soon be universalized. The consequences could be extraordinary, because the potential bottlenecks are innumerable: they exist not only in physical waterways but also in the supply chains for weapons as well as food, health care, and basic technology—all the essentials people need for everyday life. The United States might prevent Europeans from using its AI models or even block their access to Microsoft’s products. China could further restrict the rare earths used in U.S. and European weapons systems and high-end technologies or leverage its control over the global electric vehicle, solar, and wind industries. And because it makes the vast majority of active pharmaceutical ingredients, Beijing could even constrain the production of vital medicines. The food supply would be particularly easy to throttle: over 55 percent of globally traded maize, wheat, rice, and soybeans pass through at least one maritime chokepoint, and energy disruptions can become food-price crises within weeks. Blocking one chokepoint diverts traffic to others, congesting alternatives. The Hormuz closure forced oil shipments around the Cape of Good Hope. A simultaneous closure of the Suez Canal and the Strait of Malacca would have no viable solution. Both Iran and the United States have suggested they intend to extract tolls from ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, and other states might be tempted to start charging for access to international waterways. The closure of any single chokepoint might be manageable. But numerous lockdowns would not be. GET REAL Two broad ways of dealing with this new world are emerging: the method of the architect and the approach of the artisan. Architects develop blueprints for order and try to mold the world to their designs, developing universal norms and anchoring security in multilateral institutions. Artisans, on the other hand, don’t assume they have the power or resources to build grand structures from scratch. Instead, they use improvisation and flexibility to cope with a world that doesn’t lend itself to sweeping plans. In many ways, China already behaves like an artisan state. It advances its interests by repurposing existing institutions, such as when it used the International Telecommunication Union to build surveillance-friendly controls into global Internet standards, and by creating new institutions, such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and BRICS+, the geopolitical bloc that marshals Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, and four other new members. These institutions are flexible in their membership and purpose and not intended to set global rules. Other middle powers such as Brazil, India, Iran, and Turkey are creating and joining a plethora of similar groupings, balancing and hedging between the great powers. In many other middle powers in Europe, the Indo-Pacific, and North America, by contrast, grief over the rules-based order is bringing out an architectural instinct. Although they admit uncertainty, leaders in those places fail to grasp the changes they are facing, and their strategies too often propose maintaining the form of the old order without its substance—the legitimacy and enforcement capacity conferred on it by the United States. They are still scrambling to shore up the rules-based global trading system by attempting to build a carbon copy of the World Trade Organization’s deadlocked appeals mechanism and continuing to lodge complaints against U.S. tariffs at the WTO, the equivalent of shouting into the void. Too many governments are still trying to curb conflicts using the UN or international courts. Ireland, for example, joined Spain in backing South Africa’s genocide claim against Israel at the International Court of Justice, a much-ballyhooed effort that has had virtually no effect on Israeli policy. Australia’s foreign minister has spoken of a “new era of amplified middle power diplomacy” that would seek to shore up formal multilateral commitments and enforce international law. The key difference between these projects and the more artisanal ones being embraced by China and others is that their purpose remains primarily legalistic, focused on achieving change by adhering to increasingly obsolete frameworks. The old rules-based order was never, in fact, just about rules. It proffered rules backed by a specific power willing to bear disproportionate costs to maintain them. The United States and its European allies were the architects of the postwar and post–Cold War orders, but they no longer have the resources to maintain them. And middle powers cannot simply pool their resources and replicate the past. No coalition can keep the WTO relevant, ensure the dollar’s dominance, or open the Strait of Hormuz. Politicians talk like architects because they believe it inspires confidence. In reality, such talk undermines confidence. The United States’ former allies must instead think and act like artisans. Many of these countries are better equipped for this strategy shift than they realize. Their histories are peppered with examples of innovation and flexibility. Whereas architects seek stability, artisans prepare for chaos and change. Architects might try to reform the UN Security Council or restore the WTO’s appellate body. They would be wasting their time. Artisans follow the course diplomacy is already taking. China is an observer on the Arctic Council. The EU should likewise apply to join BRICS+, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, or the Association of Southeast Asian Nations as an observer. On trade, an artisanal approach would mean investing in new infrastructure nodes built around corridors and ports, such as the Lobito Corridor, a logistics route connecting mineral-rich central Africa to the Atlantic. These promise greater rewards than sweeping trade deals such as those the EU has sought with India or the South American economic bloc Mercosur, which can take decades to negotiate. And instead of competing to nominate their diplomats as UN special envoys, Australia, Norway, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and similar states should seek to contribute to the more unconventional conflict mediation efforts now being spearheaded by countries such as Pakistan and Qatar. Whereas architects believe there can be a single rule book for everyone, artisans accept that multiple sets of guidelines will coexist. Groupings such as the EU should increasingly turn their efforts toward creating rules-based orders in their own neighborhoods rather than striving for an unattainable global order. Sweeping multilateral regulatory approaches, such as the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation, are losing their efficacy as other major markets, including China, cease copying the EU playbook. So are global frameworks to solve problems such as climate change. The competition to dominate renewable technologies has probably done more to combat rising emissions than all the Conference of the Parties meetings combined. Europeans and members of the G-6+ should make every effort to understand how Brazilians, Indians, Indonesians, Russians, and South Africans are viewing this moment. If they want to hedge more efficiently, they must better understand their fellow hedgers. Whereas architects see globalization as a means to transform others, artisans worry about the vulnerabilities that interconnectedness creates. Europe and its allies have more means to develop self-reliance and work out arrangements with other powers than they give themselves credit for. To protect itself from Chinese blackmail, Europe could leverage its Airbus sales by withholding software updates for China’s Airbus fleet, which would ground more than half the country’s commercial planes. To retaliate against U.S. tariffs, it could cut off market access for American social media companies. To deter China from threatening its sovereignty, Taiwan could restrict its critical semiconductor industry. A country’s control over chokepoints is becoming a key marker of its power. Such strategies may be more defensive in focus, but if countries want to thrive, they need to boost their security, industrial competitiveness, clean energy leadership, and global influence. A core part of doing so is pursuing technological sovereignty. Instead of accepting dependence on American technology or betting the bank on building autonomous tech stacks, they need to use the leverage they already have to minimize the risk of aggressive actions against them and expand their natural advantages. In 2023, the United Kingdom’s National Health Service awarded the U.S. technology company Palantir a major contract to provide its new data platform; this year, a new British police AI program expressed interest in working with the firm. Instead, it should use the power of its purse to incentivize domestic providers, using open-source tech, to develop specialized tools and mandate open standards and portable data formats as a condition of public contracts, so no single vendor’s platform becomes a permanent chokepoint. Perhaps most important, while architects think about security from the outside in, artisans realize a country must be defended from the inside out. European and Indo-Pacific states must salvage what they can from the old security architecture—by, for instance, drawing on NATO’s command structures for military operations—and become far less reliant on the United States as an eternal security provider for their regions. And they must not simply try to replicate the United States’ capital-intensive military methods. They must develop more frugal ways of war that are relevant to their individual situations. Ukraine and Iran have both demonstrated how to adapt cheaper technologies for both offensive and defensive purposes, neutralizing their opponents’ advantage in vastly more expensive high-tech systems. Many countries will benefit from similar hedgehog strategies that draw on the technological revolution favoring defense, insulating their territories against contagion. For European countries, this means building military capacity, fighting tooth and nail to prevent Russia and the United States from making deals over their heads, and taking a more detached approach to conflicts in more distant parts of the world. Japan and South Korea must similarly invest in self-defense and work to stop China and the United States from cutting them out of choices that shape their future. Even if the United States is no longer willing to police the world, it has its own important role to play in these efforts, encouraging partners to adapt rather than vassalizing them—even if that means fewer orders for U.S. defense firms. Well before Trump’s second term, changes in the global power structure had hollowed out the old order. And the forces of disruption are likely to accelerate. The next decades will be defined by explosive changes and waves of crises, not a reversion to the old order or the creation of a new one. Like the resourceful denizens of China’s rotten-tail buildings, the most successful leaders will be the ones who take their fate into their own hands instead of waiting for a new set of rules to rescue them. item.title: America’s Fatal Attraction to War
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.99
Donald Trump campaigned for a second U.S. presidential term on a promise to end wars, not start them. And for the first year after his return, there were indications that he might make a real break with the status quo that has led Washington to overextend itself. He pushed the United States’ European allies to spend more on defense, promoted peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, and pursued a cautious détente with China that has dialed down tensions over Taiwan. Eighteen months later, however, the United States is bogged down in a new war in the Middle East. Although the U.S. military has enjoyed tactical successes, Washington has not achieved any kind of meaningful strategic victory; in certain respects, Iran exerts more power now than it did in February. Nonetheless, Trump has shied away from making diplomatic compromises. Just like his nemesis, U.S. President Barack Obama, Trump promised Americans that he would extract the country from pointless “forever wars” in the Middle East and then proved unable to do so. But the fact that the United States again became mired in a Middle East conflict is even more surprising today, because over the past two decades, the American public as well as many U.S. leaders have firmly concluded that such wars are mistakes. At heart, structures and incentives pull Washington back, repeatedly, to avoidable quagmires. For starters, military action is easy for U.S. presidents to initiate. Since 1991, U.S. leaders have gotten in the habit of deploying force to secure even the most minor U.S. interests. The short-term costs and risks of using force against a smaller, distant state or nonstate actor often appear small—most Americans can go about their day-to-day lives without even realizing their country is at war—and Congress has largely become willing to cede its constitutional oversight. But getting out of these kinds of conflicts is far harder. Washington is accustomed to setting maximalist goals for even marginal wars, and U.S. leaders balk at halting an intervention without meeting promised objectives. Particularly if the ongoing costs of a conflict are relatively diffuse, there are few incentives for presidents to face accusations of weakness. Yet the costs of these interventions are not small. They are merely hidden. Repeated wars add to a growing national debt, overstretch the U.S. military, and generate opportunity costs, drawing spending away from needed military investments and domestic priorities. Simply desiring to change the United States’ habit of waging war has not been enough to change it. If U.S. foreign-policy makers want to break the cycle, they need to think of ways to make using force a harder and less attractive option. PERVERSE INCENTIVES The Trump administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy broke with precedent. Most national security strategies populate laundry lists of so-called vital U.S. interests through an interagency process that ensures that no issue goes unmentioned. Last year’s document, by contrast, admitted that the United States has a set of discrete, circumscribed interests that policymakers “must evaluate, sort, and prioritize.” It argued that “not every country, region, issue, or cause—however worthy—can be the focus of American strategy.” And it went on to emphasize the importance of the Western Hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific while concluding that “the days in which the Middle East dominated American foreign policy in both long-term planning and day-to-day execution are thankfully over.” For much of the first year of his second term, Trump loosely adhered to this stated approach. The White House did use military force abroad, engaging in campaigns to strike Iranian nuclear sites and boats in the Caribbean that were allegedly involved in drug trafficking. But Trump also aggressively pushed allies in Europe and Asia to share the burden of defending their regions and moved to facilitate peace talks in both Gaza and Ukraine. The June 2025 U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, the so-called 12-day war, was at least brief and its objective specific. Similarly, the January seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro by U.S. Special Forces did not attempt full regime change. Instead, the White House struck a deal with Maduro’s vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, to take over. But the successes in Venezuela and during the 12-day war strengthened the neoconservative wing of the Republican Party and made it easier to argue for subsequent interventions. A mere month after the Venezuela operation, U.S. forces launched Operation Epic Fury, targeting Iranian military infrastructure and killing senior regime leaders; the administration’s early rhetoric openly promised regime change in Tehran. Six months on, the damage to Iran’s military capabilities has been significant. But the United States has expended much of its stockpile of precision munitions and suffered substantial damage to its regional bases. The Islamic Republic remains in power and has expanded its ability to threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Structural conditions keep pulling the United States back into marginal conflicts. In part, the Trump administration’s abandonment of the principles in his own National Security Strategy reflected a split in Republican policy circles. Younger, “America first” conservatives are skeptical of regime-change wars and of Washington’s duty to aid Israel above other allies. But traditionalists who still subscribe to a George W. Bush–era vision of the United States as a purveyor of democratization worldwide continue to wield influence. The Iran war has been widely portrayed as evidence that hawks (such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the now deceased Senator Lindsey Graham) won an internal battle within the administration against restrainers such as Vice President JD Vance. But the Iran war cannot be blamed entirely on the influence of individual personalities. Broader structural conditions keep pulling the United States back into marginal conflicts. First is the sheer ease with which U.S. presidents can turn to force. The U.S. Constitution grants the power to declare war only to Congress. But legislators have not done so since World War II, partly because subsequent wars were smaller and partly to avoid the political risk of registering votes for unpopular conflicts. Congress has not issued an “authorization to use military force” since 2002. The United States maintains a large active-duty military, with a network of bases spread across the globe and assets that it can deploy worldwide in a relatively short period. And as its commander in chief, the president decides when and how to deploy it. With no real checks on the president’s ability to do so as he sees fits, it is all too easy to start a war. The U.S. media and the United States’ broad networks of allies make it even easier. Cable TV commentators lean hawkish, as do many of the United States’ major newspapers. Outlets such as Fox News, CNN, and The Wall Street Journal are often enthusiastic about the start of a new conflict and the accompanying dramatic visuals but criticize any U.S. pullback. Regional allies, meanwhile, often have an incentive to encourage U.S. involvement in their conflicts and the political connections to drag Washington in. The fact that the United States often has bases in or near these countries exacerbates the dynamic. In March, for instance, Rubio argued that because an impending Israeli attack would expose U.S. service members already stationed in the Middle East to retaliation, Washington had to join the country in its strikes. WHEN WAR IS A GAME Persistent myths about past conflicts add to the problem, particularly the notion that the U.S. military failed not because it should not have started a war or because its goals were unattainable, but because it did not pursue the right tactics or commit enough resources. In the mid-2010s, for example, Republicans blamed President Barack Obama’s withdrawal of troops from Iraq for the subsequent rise of the Islamic State (also known as ISIS), not the 2003 invasion of Iraq itself. In the opening days of the recent Iran conflict, Vance told reporters that he remains skeptical of foreign military entanglements, but he trusts Trump to “get the job done” because he is “smarter” than past presidents. The same forward bases and alliances that incentivize U.S. presidents to start wars make getting out of them harder. The United States’ triumph in the Cold War also helped shape a strategic culture in Washington that presumes setting expansive goals such as nation building and regime change is both possible and desirable. Yet even overwhelming military victories are not easy to convert into enduring social and political transformations. U.S. leaders too often refuse to accept partial success, making the perfect the enemy of the good. Debates about sending aid to Ukraine after Russia’s 2022 invasion are a prime example. Many members of Washington’s foreign-policy establishment argue that even though U.S. military and economic aid helped Ukraine repel Russia’s initial onslaught and create a stalemate, there can never be a negotiated solution. (In fact, although Russia may be a reluctant interlocutor at best, the peace process has been handicapped by poor management and lack of expertise on the American side.) For most Americans, the only visible price tag on the Iran conflict is inflation. The run-up to Operation Epic Fury suffered from similar black-and-white thinking. The administration had, in fact, been able to leverage the economic pressure and the threat of military force into serious negotiations with Iran on containing its nuclear ambitions. Shortly before the war started, Iran had offered to halt domestic enrichment, remove its existing enriched uranium, and allow for the return of International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors. But the administration was unsatisfied with such a compromise, choosing to gamble on absolute victory. Perhaps the most important structural factor encouraging presidents to repeatedly engage in unnecessary wars is that U.S. citizens remain unusually insulated from these interventions’ consequences. So far, blowback from the Iran war has fallen primarily on the Gulf states. The establishment of an all-volunteer force in the United States means that the direct cost of war is felt by a much smaller and self-contained segment of the U.S. population; those who choose to enlist are increasingly the relatives of veterans themselves rather than a broad cross-section of the U.S. public. Technological advancement means that fewer soldiers are needed to wage long-distance wars. The casualties incurred in Iraq and Afghanistan—roughly 7,000 U.S. military deaths—are low compared with wars such as Korea or Vietnam. U.S. service members and their families undoubtedly feel dread and anxiety, but for most Americans, the only visible price tag on the now protracted Iran conflict is creeping inflation driven by disruption in energy markets. This cost is real: the United States’ 2026 GDP growth is expected to be smaller than 2025 estimates, and the war has made it more difficult for many Americans to afford daily staples. A cost-of-living increase is the main reason Trump is trying to negotiate a resolution. Yet it remains remarkable that the United States launched a war against a country of 93 million, killed its leadership, bombed military and civilian infrastructure, and contributed to the throttling of the world’s key energy-shipping waterway, and the sharpest impact for the average American was a two-point rise in inflation, to 4.8 percent in May. (It has since fallen back to 3.5 percent.) Americans’ very insulation from the wars Washington wages, and the diffuse nature of those wars’ costs, serves to defuse political opposition. According to a July Washington Post–IPSOS poll, the Iran war is now as unpopular among Americans as the Vietnam war was in its sixth year, but Americans are unlikely to be marching in the streets about it anytime soon. TIP OF THE ICEBERG The fact that U.S. wars’ costs remain hidden might lead some to conclude that even a war as ill conceived as Operation Epic Fury is not a big deal. After all, the economic and human toll, for ordinary Americans, of the previous 20 years of war in the Middle East were also relatively moderate. The numbers of Americans killed and wounded in Afghanistan and Iraq were far smaller than in earlier U.S. wars; in Vietnam, more than seven times as many people died as in both those conflicts combined. The economic costs were diffuse and passed off to future generations as additions to the national debt. But this conclusion is a mistake. The United States’ wars in the Middle East—both past and present—carry long-term strategic costs that have already damaged the country’s position in the world and its ability to compete against other great powers. History is clear: great powers that overextend themselves in minor conflicts often end up unable to handle core strategic interests. Most visibly, the United States is running critically short on munitions. Despite discussion about dialing up production, the Pentagon cannot easily replace these systems soon, setting up a tradeoff: every interceptor used to defend a U.S. base or ally against Iranian rockets is one that cannot be used elsewhere. Effective deterrence requires both credibility and military capability. If U.S. troops in East Asia, the Baltics, or elsewhere do not have sufficient munitions, they cannot deter China, Russia, or anyone else. The broader opportunity costs of the United States’ Middle Eastern follies are even more insidious. The troops deployed for Middle East campaigns cannot be sent to other regions, the money spent on these wars cannot be invested in new capabilities or cutting-edge technology, and the cost of rebuilding bases in the Gulf limits the United States’ ability to harden its basing infrastructure in the Indo-Pacific. Regime-change wars even require a different force structure—far more land forces than naval, for instance. If Washington’s primary goal is protecting the hemisphere or stopping a Chinese assault in the South China Sea, for example, the consistent demand for regime-change wars undermines those goals by preventing the Pentagon from restructuring its forces or planning for other contingencies. The United States is running critically short on munitions. These opportunity costs cannot be solved simply by raising the defense budget. Even if the Trump administration’s proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget could be made politically palatable, that level of military spending—almost five percent of U.S. GDP, higher than it has been in decades—will draw investment away from other priorities and act as a long-term drag on U.S. innovation and economic growth. Military Keynesianism sounds good in theory but is rarely an effective way to boost the economy. It produces fewer jobs per dollar outlaid than other forms of government spending and does not drive broad innovation as effectively as other kinds of economic activity. The notion that the United States ever enforced a truly liberal rules-based order worldwide was always overblown. But it is true that the U.S. military has been a global guarantor of shipping and the free flow of energy for decades. The fact that the United States, in its recent conflict with Iran, directly destabilized international energy markets undermines the country’s claim to be a fair arbiter of the global commons. Polls now suggest that only about a third of people around the world view the United States as contributing significantly to global peace and stability. Meanwhile, the administration burned diplomatic capital on this conflict, reducing its influence and capacity to shape outcomes elsewhere, such as Ukraine, where the administration’s peace efforts have been largely abandoned since the start of the Iran war. All these costs are diffuse and deferred. But in 20 years, as a result of its choice to pursue these wars, the United States may well have a less effective military force, less global influence, and even a weaker economy. Indeed, the Iran war has shown that the Trump administration’s own original argument was correct: in a competitive world, the United States needs to prioritize the allocation of its scarce resources to meet the most pressing strategic challenges. That Trump, like his predecessors, proved unable to resist the use of force only strengthens the case for reform. BITE THE BULLET The United States’ militarism now is constricting its future choices. There is no consensus in Washington about whether the United States should defend Taiwan in the case of a Chinese attack; many thousands of pages of debate on the issue have been published. Yet the expenditure of munitions in the Middle East is increasingly making the question moot. If the United States cannot come to Taiwan’s aid, then it’s no longer a choice. Over time, restrictions created by excessive military adventurism will increasingly shape policy choices elsewhere, too. It will require radical change to break the incentive structure that leads the United States too easily into far-flung military conflicts, not just electing leaders who promise to end forever wars. Closing some forward bases, for example, would diminish the United States’ ability to conduct interventions. Congress should also reestablish more authority over the United States’ wars, first by exerting more power over military spending. The Pentagon is already struggling to cover the Iran war from its existing accounts; Congress could refuse to add contingency funding for this or future conflicts. Congressional committees have grilled Trump appointees on the Iran war but have achieved little but soundbites. Congress could expand this oversight by hitting the administration where it hurts: refusing to authorize discretionary spending on the war. Negative publicity can sometimes be useful, and legislators could easily do more to publicize the abysmal conditions to which the Iran war has subjected U.S. service members. In the future, legislators could refuse to confirm to executive branch positions appointees who have been involved in the decision to start marginal wars. Despite so many past failures, Washington’s foreign policy debates are frequently still dominated by aging officials who made disastrous choices. It would be difficult, but future policymakers might also seek to break up the cozy relationship between the Pentagon and U.S. defense contractors. The defense acquisition ecosystem is bloated and lacking in accountability. Yet the defense industry’s disbursement of billions of dollars to lobby Congress and influence policy debates helps drive the United States’ mindless militarism. A ban on legislators trading stocks in defense companies would help, as would anticorruption legislation that closes or restricts the revolving door between senior military posts and defense contracting sinecures. Just as U.S. officials encouraged the consolidation of defense contracting after the end of the Cold War, they could now encourage diversification of the industry away from influential corporate behemoths. The American public long ago turned against military adventurism and regime-change wars, particularly in the Middle East. Yet a full 20 years after Obama was elected on a promise to break free of Bush’s legacy, policymakers keep getting sucked into the region by an incentive structure that makes the use of force attractive and minimizes its short-term costs. However harmless these forever wars might feel to average Americans, they are burning through the country’s military resources and thus eroding Washington’s might. Eventually, the United States will find itself constrained—no longer able to fight everything, everywhere, all at once. The question is whether it wants to proactively decide where it uses its resources, or whether it wants its hands tied by a parade of forever conflicts. item.title: The End of Thailand’s Long Stalemate?
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.99
For more than 25 years, Thailand’s conservative establishment and opposition forces have been locked in a struggle for the soul of the country. Royalists want palace institutions insulated from public criticism, a military licensed to intervene in times of political crisis, deferential political parties and politicians, and free rein to clamp down on political actors who fail to toe the line. The opposition calls for a constitutional monarchy, a military that stays in the barracks, a competitive party system responsive to the people’s wishes, and predictable checks and balances that do not unduly punish elected politicians. More often than not, the royalists have had the upper hand. They have mobilized protest movements, staged military coups, and banned opposition parties to prevent troublesome politicians from instituting changes that could limit their power and privileges. Yet every attempt to strike a decisive blow against the opposition has failed. Conservatives have not translated legal or extralegal victories into lasting governments. Opposition movements, meanwhile, have consistently reinvented themselves. Thaksin Shinawatra, the larger-than-life former policeman and telecom billionaire, built up enormous power as prime minister in the early 2000s, incurring the disdain of royalists. And even after a military coup removed Thaksin from the premiership in 2006, his parties remained electoral juggernauts. A yet more alarming challenge emerged on the horizon after a 2014 coup ousted Thaksin’s sister, Yingluck Shinawatra, from government: youth-based mass protests calling for reform of the monarchy in 2020 and progressive political parties who appealed to these younger voters. A stalemate had prevailed over Thai politics, with neither side able to overpower the other fully. That changed in February 2026, when Bhumjaithai, a low-profile party previously known primarily for campaigning to legalize cannabis, swept into power in national elections. With the implicit backing of the monarchy and the conservative establishment, Bhumjaithai has seized control of the Thai state, giving rise to a new mode of politics capable of both suppressing progressive forces in favour of cozy collaboration among elites and winning a general election without overt manipulation. Far from an electoral anomaly, the rise of Bhumjaithai is the culmination of a long effort by conservatives to retake the levers of power. In fact, the formerly also-ran party’s February triumph was part of a methodical, behind-the-scenes campaign to commandeer the state’s nominally neutral apparatuses, including its Senate and Constitutional Court. The alliance between the monarchical network and Bhumjaithai is more a marriage of convenience than a shared ideological project, and it may not last indefinitely. But shallow as it may be, it has already succeeded in decisively strengthening the conservative position, disempowering the major rival parties that threaten elite control, and potentially remaking the Thai state for years to come. RAINBOW COALITIONS The origins of Thailand’s current political order date back to 1997, when a group of elite liberal royalists, claiming a mandate from civil society, introduced a landmark new charter. Often referred to as “the people’s constitution,” it was a reaction to a disastrous military coup in 1991 and its bloody aftermath, including the deadly suppression of unarmed protesters in May 1992. The reforms aimed to coup-proof the political system by introducing checks and balances to prevent elected politicians from abusing their power and facilitate a smooth royal succession. It established an electoral commission, a constitutional court, an anticorruption agency, and a human rights commission, as well as a fully elected, purportedly nonpartisan Senate. The project backfired. It failed to stabilize Thai politics—probably an unrealistic goal to begin with—and the new parliamentary system allowed for the election of Thaksin as prime minister in 2001. A charismatic figure with populist authoritarian tendencies, he successfully mobilized lower-income voters in the heavily populated north and northeast regions of Thailand, melding them into an unbeatable electoral bloc. He used his considerable personal wealth, his party’s parliamentary dominance, and his bureaucratic connections to create a startlingly successful political machine. Thaksin bought off the Senate and the independent agencies, defanging them as neutral bodies, and installed loyalists in crucial posts intended to check the prime minister’s power. The country’s traditional elites were deeply threatened by Thaksin’s ascendance. The so-called Yellow Shirt movement, which appropriated a royal color, sought to make Thailand ungovernable. Through mass street protests and the occupation of public spaces and buildings, it paralyzed opposition rule three times: in 2006, 2008, and in 2013–14. But for all its success in ousting opposition-led governments, the Yellow Shirt movement never solved a basic problem: conservatives could bring down an elected government, but they couldn’t win an election to replace it. Conservatives were unable to tolerate ambitious, independent-minded administrations. The 2006 and 2014 political crises initially followed a similar pattern. Street protests destabilized and delegitimized Shinawatra-led governments, and military coups then removed them. Each time, the establishment brought in the Royal Thai Army to reorganize politics, rewrite the constitution, and reconfigure the party system in its favor before holding fresh elections. But military force failed to bring about durable conservative rule. Coups were short-term fixes that gradually eroded the legitimacy of the establishment. The Thai public was willing to tolerate only short interludes of military rule, and coup makers had no choice but to promise the imminent restoration of democracy. Generals, however, were bad at politics. The public quickly tired of them, and voters soon welcomed back the same kinds of politicians that soldiers had kicked out. In the 2007 elections, the first called by the ruling junta after the 2006 coup, for instance, Thaksin’s party was voted back into power. The experience was imprinted on the minds of conservatives when they launched the 2014 coup; the new government postponed elections until 2019. The inability of conservatives to break the opposition once and for all persuaded the establishment to try to cut deals with Thaksin’s Pheu Thai Party instead. A strategy of conciliation permitted the opposition to front a government as long as party leaders concentrated on managing the economy and did not challenge the special status of the monarchy. Pheu Thai, conservatives believed, could always be co-opted or browbeaten into a politics of benefit sharing in which wealth and power were divided between a Pheu Thai figurehead and conservative power brokers. This was the deal behind Yingluck Shinawatra’s administration of 2011 to 2014, an arrangement that both conservatives and Thaksin supporters found unsatisfying and were reluctant to acknowledge. But government by veto was inherently unstable. Eventually, the conservatives were unable to tolerate ambitious, independent-minded Pheu Thai administrations and brought them crashing down, as they did in the 2014 military coup. Where they did not want to use force, they turned to lawfare to limit the opposition’s power. Starting in 2019, a series of more progressive “orange” opposition parties proved wildly popular, especially among younger voters. After the orange Move Forward Party won the largest number of seats in Thailand’s National Assembly in the 2023 elections, the military-appointed Senate blocked its leader, Pita Limjaroenrat, from assuming the premiership. The following year, Move Forward was summarily dissolved—the fifth major opposition party to meet this fate—and the Constitutional Court banned Pita from political office for ten years. By 2025, the establishment was running out of options to disempower the opposition. Challenged by both pro-Thaksin forces and progressive orange parties, its old methods—military coups, dodgy deals, party bans, the judicial removal of prime ministers—were wearing thin. Conservatives desperately needed an alliance with a reliably deferential party that could win elections. HOLLOW PARTY Enter Bhumjaithai, a previously medium-sized party based in the northeastern province of Buriram. The product of a breakaway by a faction of members of parliament and former ministers from Thaksin’s party in 2008, Bhumjaithai had for the first 17 years of its existence no popular politicians among its ranks, no clear economic policies, and no national following. Yet under the guidance of the shadowy Newin Chidchob, Bhumjaithai has gradually become a force in Thai politics and a crucial ally of the monarchy and its sympathizers. Known euphemistically by the party faithful as “the school principal,” Newin served as a junior minister under Thaksin and in other governments but stepped back from frontline politics two decades ago, ostensibly to concentrate on building up his Buriram United soccer team. He neither grants interviews nor appears in public but exercises tight control over Bhumjaithai’s strategy and personnel. Current Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, a U.S.-trained engineer and former deputy minister whose family owns the massive Sino-Thai Engineering and Construction company, has served as the party’s leader and public face since 2012. What Newin and Anutin lack in ideological vision, they have made up for in strategic cunning, accumulating power wherever possible and making themselves useful to the monarchical network. Correctly diagnosing the establishment’s desperate need for a reliable political party with which to collaborate, they set out to distinguish their party from other conservative contenders, which were typically packed with reliable but often underperforming former bureaucrats. To do so, Newin and Anutin transformed Bhumjaithai into a major vehicle for influential provincial business interests. Control of the key ministries was a crucial first step in the project to capture state power. As a precondition to joining coalition governments as a junior partner, Bhumjaithai demanded ministerial positions that would help it secure stronger local networks. In 2019, Anutin became minister of public health and subsequently boosted the pay of over one million health volunteers in villages across the country. Anutin’s support turned many of them into canvassers for Bhumjaithai—an electoral masterstroke, given that Thai elections are often won and lost in these provincial areas, where vote-canvasser networks are all-important. Then, in 2023, Bhumjaithai secured control of the powerful Ministry of Interior, which oversees local governance in Thailand, including more than 70,000 village headmen. In the right hands, the Interior Ministry can be a formidable patronage machine, exerting authority over everything from local budgets to Senate elections. The party then combined the health and headmen networks to penetrate every community in Thailand. Today, Anutin still holds the post of interior minister, in addition to his position as prime minister. Other behind-closed-doors moves solidified Bhumjaithai’s power. For most Thai citizens, the selection of 200 new senators in 2024 through an arcane and untested self-nomination system barely registered, creating ample opportunity for manipulation. Candidates linked to Bhumjaithai gamed the system and secured around two-thirds of the supposedly neutral upper chamber—a majority that has allowed conservative forces to quietly block independent-minded candidates for the Constitutional Court, the Election Commission, and the Anticorruption Commission and to exercise veto power over any future changes to the constitution. Missteps by the opposition also smoothed the path for the party’s ultimate takeover of the state. When the Bhumjaithai-controlled Constitutional Court removed Thaksin’s daughter, Paetongtarn Shinawatra, as prime minister in August 2025, the orange party—now known as the People’s Party—voted for Anutin, rather than another Pheu Thai member, to replace her. People’s Party leaders naively believed a Bhumjaithai government would be in office for only a brief period and that after winning an early election, progressive forces could push to amend the constitution and reduce the entrenched power of the elite. This was a disastrous miscalculation. In the February election, Bhumjaithai shocked most observers by decisively topping the polls, winning 192 seats to the People’s Party’s 120 seats. With Bhumjaithai in control of both the internal levers of power and parliament, the prospects for progressive constitutional reform evaporated. SAME AS IT EVER WAS? By neutralizing the Pheu Thai and the People’s Party, Bhumjaithai has made itself the most successful conservative party in modern Thai history. Far from transforming the country’s politics, however, this dominance has ground it to a halt. The incarnation of transactional conservatism, Bhumjaithai now controls every major mechanism of the state. But whereas in the past the various royalist and opposition factions jockeying for influence each stood for something tangible, the party is a cipher, favored by many conservatives, yet largely devoid of ideological or policy content or an organic base of support. Today, a country known for mobilizing millions of people around big ideas, both during hotly contested elections and through massive extraparliamentary movements, is led by a party with no apparent ideas at all. The political reform project that began in the 1990s has run its course. So, too, have Thaksin’s project to empower the disadvantaged, the military’s nationalist project to restore order and defend the monarchy, and the progressive project to transform Thailand into a more open and equal place. At the same time, Bhumjaithai’s vacuous opportunism reflects a new form of realpolitik that appears much more durable than previous iterations. Royalists have grudgingly rallied around the party because they have nowhere else to go. Thaksin, recently chastened by an eight-month prison term, has gone quiet. Progressives criticize and deconstruct what they decry as the “blue regime” (after the color of Bhumjaithai’s logo) but struggle to articulate a realistic strategy to challenge it. Despite the contradictions that underpin Anutin’s government, it has shown no sign of imminent collapse. This hollow dominance has yielded a strange impasse. For the last six months, Anutin’s administration has mostly treaded water, postponing major initiatives. That impasse may not hold as younger generations become a force in Thai politics. Indeed, conservatives’ grip on power remains deeply contested and contingent. A united opposition that puts aside the long-standing differences between pro-Thaksin and progressive forces could in theory topple Bhumjaithai at the ballot box. A return to Move Forward’s winning slogan in 2023—a Thailand that is “not the same as before,” code for the dismantling of gerontocracy and unearned privilege across the country’s creaking structures and institutions—could serve as the basis for an alternative administration. But even if an anti-Bhumjaithai coalition were to take back power, it would struggle to unwind the party’s control of Thailand’s political institutions. However long Bhumjaithai’s present tenure in Bangkok lasts, that takeover of the levers of state power will be its enduring legacy.
