item.title: Ditching Chinese Rare Earths Is Hard. Just Ask Japan.
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.76
Ditching Chinese Rare Earths Is Hard. Just Ask Japan. A cautionary tale for Washington’s diversification push. The clock is ticking before a tenuous U.S.-China trade truce expires this fall, and the countdown has left U.S. President Donald Trump increasingly desperate to ditch Chinese rare earths once and for all. Few world powers understand that feeling quite like Japan. After all, the country has been in Washington’s shoes before: China shocked the world in 2010 when it halted rare-earth shipments to Japan over a geopolitical spat, driving a supply chain reckoning in Tokyo. The clock is ticking before a tenuous U.S.-China trade truce expires this fall, and the countdown has left U.S. President Donald Trump increasingly desperate to ditch Chinese rare earths once and for all. Few world powers understand that feeling quite like Japan. After all, the country has been in Washington’s shoes before: China shocked the world in 2010 when it halted rare-earth shipments to Japan over a geopolitical spat, driving a supply chain reckoning in Tokyo. Sixteen years later, Japan is often hailed as the country that has most successfully diversified away from Chinese rare earths. Yet it is far from out of the woods. In apparent retaliation against Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks about Taiwan last year, Beijing has again unleashed its supply chain might against Japan. The pressure campaign is still going: Customs data released last month showed that Beijing continued to strangle its flows of key rare earths to Japan in June, and firms and manufacturers across the country are feeling the pain. As Washington follows in Tokyo’s footsteps, the latter offers a window into just how challenging it can be to break free of Beijing’s chokehold—with stark lessons for U.S. policymakers. “Japan is a cautionary tale,” said Gracelin Baskaran, a mining economist at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). One of the most formidable weapons in China’s trade arsenal has been its chokehold over global supply chains of rare earths, the elements that underpin powerful technologies ranging from fighter jets to wind turbines. China dominates around 85 percent of rare-earth processing and 92 percent of magnet production. Its command is particularly pronounced when it comes to the industrial separation of a subset of rare earths known as heavy rare earths—giving it immense leverage over other countries. That became clear in 2010, when China briefly halted rare-earth exports to Japan. Alarmed, Tokyo waged an all-out effort to plug its supply chain vulnerabilities, including by building stockpiles and inventories, pumping vast sums of money into the sector, and embracing public-private partnerships and off-take agreements. Tokyo’s efforts have spanned the globe. Japan has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Lynas, an Australian firm that recently became the first to successfully produce heavy rare earths outside of China. Japanese auto manufacturers have also turned abroad, with a raft of rare-earth agreements with countries ranging from Canada to Australia. “Japan sees this as a network strategy, that you cannot solve this puzzle on your own,” said Mireya Solís, an expert on Japanese foreign economic policy at the Brookings Institution. By 2018, Japan had cut its dependence on Chinese rare-earth imports to around 58 percent. Yet it remains the world’s biggest importer of rare-earth metals, according to a CSIS report that was co-authored by Baskaran. Even as Tokyo has cut its dependence on Beijing, it imports substantial quantities of rare-earth metals from countries whose industries are deeply intertwined with China, such as Vietnam, the report noted. The report’s verdict was blunt: “Claims that Japan has successfully de-risked its rare earth supply chains and reduced reliance on China are misguided.” Indeed, after China imposed broad curbs on certain rare-earth elements and magnets in 2025, some Japanese automakers were forced to suspend production. Rare-earth access remains “the big Achilles’ heel for Japan,” said Jane Nakano, an expert in energy security at CSIS. It has been difficult for Japan to secure supplies of heavy rare earths, which are particularly complicated to find and separate, according to Tom Moerenhout, who leads the Critical Materials Initiative at Columbia’s Center on Global Energy Policy. Since rare earths mineralize together in nature and are chemically similar, separation is required to isolate individual elements, although the process carries environmental risks. “In terms of the heavy rare earth ones—and then specifically dysprosium—they are still very much reliant on China,” Moerenhout, referring to a type of heavy rare earth. “For this particular rare earth, Japan has been doing every move correctly to diversify, but it just shows how long it takes to actually achieve the results on the ground.” Beijing has used that to its advantage. Tensions between both countries soared last November after Takaichi remarked that a potential blockade or seizure of Taiwan would constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan—and thereby authorize Japanese military action. Months later, China strangled its exports of rare earths and magnets to the country. For Japanese firms, the ongoing pressure campaign has been painful. While inventories and stockpiles have helped cushion the shock, months of disruption have taken their toll, so much so that the Trump administration reportedly went as far as to ask Beijing—unsuccessfully—to resume flows to Japan in June. Many companies are going into “absolute contingency mode,” Moerenhout said. Take Shin-Etsu, a major Japanese magnet maker, which reportedly stopped taking new orders for magnets with dysprosium and has announced plans to build a new refining facility. Japanese automaker Mitsubishi, which reportedly only has enough rare-earth stocks to last through mid-2026, recently partnered with the American firm ReElement Technologies to jointly advance a supply chain. And more businesses have been sounding the alarm. Of the 200 filings that mentioned rare earths to the Tokyo Stock Exchange in May and June, more than two-thirds warned that China’s export controls were having a negative impact or threatened to do so, Reuters reported. The Japanese government has also ramped up its efforts globally, with Takaichi recently spearheading a proposal among the G-7 to cooperate on critical mineral stockpiles to jointly counter China. Tokyo is also increasingly looking underwater, with big ambitions of partnering with the United States to exploit rare earths in the deep sea. But for all those efforts, the real test may be whether Japanese firms can withstand China’s continued squeeze. “It’s again the question of how long can they sustain this, and it’s not clear,” Solís said. Japan’s trials and tribulations may offer a warning for Washington as it embarks on its own journey to ditch Chinese rare earths. After the Trump administration unveiled steep tariffs on much of the world in 2025, China struck back in part by announcing its own rare earth curbs. After several rounds of other escalations and high-level trade talks, both sides agreed to a one-year trade truce that saw Beijing temporarily suspend its rare-earth export controls. That truce is set to expire in November, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping expected to meet in the United States in September. Ahead of both dates, rare earths have been top of mind for U.S. officials, who pressed the issue in a meeting with their Chinese counterparts in July. “In our discussion, I emphasized that we expect Beijing to fully meet its commitments on rare earths and U.S. agricultural products,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a post on X. Critical mineral security has been a top priority for the Trump administration, both domestically and abroad. Among other measures, Washington has ordered U.S. manufacturers to stop sourcing rare earths, magnets, and select other minerals from China by the end of this year, although it remains unclear whether they will be able to meet that deadline. Eager to secure new supply chains, the White House has embraced equity stakes in mining firms; turbocharged federal support for the sector; inked deals abroad, including with Tokyo; announced a $12 billion stockpile; pitched a global minerals trading bloc; and attempted to strongarm minerals from other places. The Trump administration’s campaign kicked into overdrive this month with $3 billion in new investments aimed at boosting domestic production and U.S. mining schools. “We’re reclaiming America’s rightful place as the minerals superpower of the world,” Trump declared earlier in August. Yet if Japan’s experience is any indication, that won’t happen anytime soon. That’s because with rare earths, self-sufficiency is a long and capital-intensive journey, Baskaran said. One reason is the amount of time that it takes to build a mine: It takes an average of 29 years in the United States, which is the world’s second-longest mine development timeline. There’s also the technological challenge. Rare-earths separation is highly complex, with upward of 50 stages of separation, Baskaran said. Much of the U.S. government’s current efforts revolve around supporting new rare-earth processing technologies, many of which are in the pilot stage, she added. “You’re developing new mines and developing new technology at the same time, and that’s not an overnight task,” Baskaran said. For both Tokyo and Washington, the race to diversify away from Beijing is in full swing. But it will take time to break free. “We don’t know how China will press its advantage, what concessions it may want to continue with the suspension,” Solís said. “But the fact is that the system has been established. We cannot unsee it.”

item.title: Who Reaps the Benefits of India’s Growth?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.36
Who Reaps the Benefits of India’s Growth? Early policy choices shaped the inequity and employment challenges facing the country today. India today has the fifth-largest economy in the world—and with an annual growth rate of roughly 7 percent, one of the fastest-growing. But for decades, the country was an economic laggard. The policies pursued by India’s founders, most notably its first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, produced neither growth nor equity. They granted a disproportionate role to the state, dramatically regulated industry, and limited India’s integration into the global economy. After fitful attempts to bring about reform in the 1980s, Indian policymakers were forced to grasp the nettle in the wake of an unprecedented fiscal crisis in 1991. Faced with few options, they sporadically embraced market-friendly reforms that ultimately set the country on a path of steady economic growth. That growth, in turn, played a critical role in reducing endemic poverty even as it contributed to deepening inequality. India today has the fifth-largest economy in the world—and with an annual growth rate of roughly 7 percent, one of the fastest-growing. But for decades, the country was an economic laggard. The policies pursued by India’s founders, most notably its first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, produced neither growth nor equity. They granted a disproportionate role to the state, dramatically regulated industry, and limited India’s integration into the global economy. After fitful attempts to bring about reform in the 1980s, Indian policymakers were forced to grasp the nettle in the wake of an unprecedented fiscal crisis in 1991. Faced with few options, they sporadically embraced market-friendly reforms that ultimately set the country on a path of steady economic growth. That growth, in turn, played a critical role in reducing endemic poverty even as it contributed to deepening inequality. India’s economic circumstances—despite the numbers—are decidedly mixed. Even amid the adverse effects of the Iran war and trade uncertainties in U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term, the country’s growth rate remains sound. However, India is confronting head on the problem of jobless economic expansion with soaring youth unemployment, as underscored by the Cockroach movement protests this summer. Both political scientists and economists of repute have sought to trace India’s development trajectory and offered various explanations for its successes and failures. These works have documented the ideational sources of the country’s policies, discussed critical historical junctures, and offered prescriptions to promote sustained growth and tackle persistent poverty. Few have taken on a task as monumental as Devesh Kapur and Arvind Subramanian’s new book, A Sixth of Humanity: Independent India’s Development Odyssey, which was republished this year as an academic title. Their work is significant because of its sheer scope. Owing to its careful discussion of the evolution of India’s economic policies, the book provides a clearer understanding of the country’s achievements as well as its persistent challenges. Kapur, a political scientist, and Subramanian, an economist, bring to bear their respective skills and training to produce a volume that is lucidly written, deftly argued, and intellectually sound. A Sixth of Humanity will no doubt be considered a milestone in the extant scholarship on India’s political economy in its assessment of policy choices made over the decades—but particularly in the country’s early years—and their lasting consequences. At the outset of A Sixth of Humanity, Kapur and Subramanian challenge a widely held proposition about India’s early developmental choices—and namely, its apparent embrace of the strategy of import-substitution industrialization (ISI). Proposed by Argentine economist Raúl Prebisch in 1950, ISI involved raising high tariff barriers that would limit imports and create a conducive milieu for so-called infant industries to thrive. Unless developing countries chose this option, Prebisch argued, they would remain “mere hewers of wood and drawers of water”—producing raw materials in exchange for industrial goods. Many countries in the global south adopted this pathway to economic development, including Brazil, Ghana, and Nigeria. Kapur and Subramanian argue that India, contrary to popular belief, didn’t implement ISI in a way that would have enabled the country to realize its full potential. Instead, its policies shut off foreign supplies, encouraged an unwieldy public sector, and choked off a potentially productive private sector. The public sector turned out to be loss-making, and private investment was limited, hampering both efficiency and innovation. This pushes against the conventional wisdom that India pursued a fulsome embrace of ISI. A Sixth of Humanity also argues that apologists for India’s growth strategy in its early years highlighted that the country’s economic performance was better than under British rule—but this was, of course, specious. Kapur and Subramanian show that between 1950 to 1980, close to 60 percent of India’s population remained trapped in poverty. This can be attributed in large part to a regulatory framework that limited entrepreneurship and innovation and stunted growth. Simultaneously, the Indian state pursued welfare measures that mostly benefited a small, privileged class within the organized sector of the economy. They largely contributed to the well-being of a small segment of the working class because those in the economy’s informal sector, such as daily-wage earners in agriculture and construction, did not enjoy protections. The workers outside the formal system’s ambit derived no advantages, while unionized labor often made big demands. In a strikingly counterintuitive fashion, India’s early democratization proved to be harmful for fiscal policy. In the late 1960s, as the dominant Indian National Congress lost ground and politics became more competitive, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi resorted to populist measures to bolster the party’s sagging electoral fortunes, including the nationalization of banks and the expansion of subsidies. Kapur and Subramanian argue that after the government embarked on this path, few politicians were willing to alienate their electoral constituencies—and India failed to return to fiscal prudence. These policies resulted in deficit spending with adverse consequences for growth and prosperity while coddling powerful interest groups. Large firms cornered segments of the market, which today has resulted in the growth of India’s crony capitalism. The Indian state’s ability to extract revenue also proved to be flawed, with only a small part of the population paying direct taxes. To compensate for this paucity of revenue, the government devised mechanisms for indirect taxation, from tariffs to consumption taxes. The result was a weak revenue base that often contributed to a deficit. Electoral considerations again played a role, and Kapur and Subramanian identify a handful of reasons for India’s anemic taxation system. Since a large segment of the population lived in rural areas and relied on agriculture in the 1950s and 1960s, the constitution exempted the sector from national taxation. India’s investment in inefficient public sector enterprises that were not subject to market discipline led to a drain on the treasury. Additionally, the country’s politically influential middle class has benefited from various tax exclusions. Choices made in the early years of the republic not to impose significant taxes on land transactions further harmed the treasury. Land values in India have soared since the liberalization of the 1990s, yet the state has still not undertaken commensurate measures to change the tax regime. Finally, during India’s initial flirtation with socialism, it taxed the very wealthy at extortionate rates, leading to widespread tax evasion. Other policy choices since the 1950s—most notably the neglect of critical infrastructure—have dogged India’s growth. Instead, the country focused on building large-scale, state-run factories designed to boost industrialization. In the past few decades, these shortcomings have been inadequately addressed with some showpiece developments, such as high-speed trains between major cities, but without tackling more basic needs, such as investing in quality public transport. Unfortunately, other approaches were also lopsided. For example, India’s leadership invested in education but not in public health. This was further skewed by privileging higher education over primary and secondary education, unlike in many East Asian states. The last issue did lasting damage to both growth and equity in India, with its burgeoning youth population. To that end, Kapur and Subramanian approvingly cite the conclusions of the late American political scientist Myron Weiner, who argued that India’s political elites failed to grasp the significance of mass primary and secondary education—and that this neglect could be attributed in part to the stranglehold of caste in Indian society, which contributed to a scant interest in the plight of the socially disadvantaged. Some of these trends came to the fore with the emergence of the Cockroach Janta Party movement this year. The online satire quickly evolved into nationwide youth-led protests that succeeded in forcing the resignation of India’s education minister over leaked exam papers. The movement didn’t stop there—it has kept pushing the government on the shortcomings in the education system, as it has spawned some copycats focused on other issues of inequity. If A Sixth of Humanity has one shortcoming, it is that unlike the work of the noted Indian economist Vijay Joshi, the authors offer few policy prescriptions. Joshi’s policy guidance in the 2010s included a need for greater privatization, increased labor market flexibility, improved governance, and boosting educational reforms. Unfortunately, New Delhi has made only sporadic attempts at implementing these or similar suggestions. The government is likely seeing the consequences, especially with growing youth unrest. Instead, Kapur and Subramanian conclude with a brief discussion of four forces that are likely to shape development policies in India and elsewhere in the world: geopolitical shifts, technological developments, climate change, and demographic changes. How India’s leadership responds to these imminent challenges will shape the future of one-sixth of humanity. Members of the younger generation are increasingly concerned about the likely effects of these shifts on their personal and professional fortunes. Unfortunately, the Modi government has yet to devise policy options that could address their very legitimate fears and offer them meaningful pathways to a more secure and prosperous future. Sumit Ganguly is a columnist at Foreign Policy and senior fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, where he directs the Huntington Program on Strengthening U.S.-India Relations. item.title: UAE Joins Global Efforts to Isolate Iran
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.16
UAE Joins Global Efforts to Isolate Iran Abu Dhabi is hoping that a trade embargo will force Tehran to surrender. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the United Arab Emirates’ economic embargo of Iran, renewed calls for a presidential election in Ukraine, and a potential breakthrough in U.S.-Canada trade talks. Severing Trade Ties The United Arab Emirates halted all trade and financial transactions with Iran on Wednesday until further notice. Having long held close economic ties with Tehran, Abu Dhabi’s decision marks a significant shift in Persian Gulf relations, and it places further global pressure on Tehran to surrender its war ambitions. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the United Arab Emirates’ economic embargo of Iran, renewed calls for a presidential election in Ukraine, and a potential breakthrough in U.S.-Canada trade talks. Severing Trade Ties The United Arab Emirates halted all trade and financial transactions with Iran on Wednesday until further notice. Having long held close economic ties with Tehran, Abu Dhabi’s decision marks a significant shift in Persian Gulf relations, and it places further global pressure on Tehran to surrender its war ambitions. According to an Emirati Foreign Ministry spokesperson, the embargo is in response to “regional escalations that undermine regional and international peace and security.” Last Saturday, Abu Dhabi accused Tehran of attacking an Emirati oil tanker traversing the Strait of Hormuz, and on Tuesday, the UAE’s Defense Ministry claimed that Iranian forces fired two ballistic missiles at “maritime traffic,” one of which fell into Emirati waters. Tehran denied the latter attack. In the early weeks of the Iran war, the UAE bore the brunt of Tehran’s retaliations against the United States, as the UAE hosts a major U.S. military base, Al Dhafra Air Base, as well as the U.S. Navy’s busiest and largest port of call in the Middle East. Emirati authorities have since reported more than 2,700 ballistic missile and drone attacks from Iran. The UAE has taken several measures to discourage Iran from continuing its assaults. In March, Abu Dhabi ordered the closure of a cultural club, several schools, and a historic Iranian hospital in the UAE’s largest city, Dubai, that were allegedly connected to the Iranian government. Later that month, the Emirati government began canceling visas of some Iranian expatriates. And in May, the New York Times, citing unnamed senior U.S. officials, reported that the UAE’s military had carried out secret strikes on Iranian territory. Still, the UAE had stopped short of imposing major economic penalties on Iran for its actions. According to the World Trade Organization, trade between the two countries in 2024—when the UAE was Iran’s largest source of imports—was around $28 billion. Dubai, specifically, has been accused of helping Tehran evade international sanctions by hosting companies that processed millions of dollars for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other Iran-linked groups. Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic advisor to Emirati President Mohammed bin Zayed, dismissed such allegations about Dubai on Wednesday as “untrue information and part of desperate media campaigns.” The UAE “remains firmly committed to safeguarding the integrity of the international financial system, in line with international law and the highest global standards,” the Emirati Foreign Ministry spokesperson added. It is unclear why Abu Dhabi chose now to impose an economic embargo on Tehran and to what extent the United States played a role in that decision. The Trump administration has repeatedly urged foreign allies to help isolate Iran on the global stage, hoping that such pressure will “force the Iranian government to make substantial concessions in negotiations—or even lead to an uprising that topples the regime,” FP columnist Anchal Vohra argued last month. Notably, Wednesday’s announcement came mere hours after U.S. President Donald Trump held a call with Mohammed bin Zayed. Today’s Most Read - The Top 10 Ways Trump Has Made America Weaker by Stephen M. Walt - Colby’s ‘Flexible Realism’ Won’t Work in the Indo-Pacific by Derek Grossman - Vance Pitches a New Objective for the Iran War by Keith Johnson What We’re Following Wartime vote. Ousted Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for wartime elections on Wednesday, marking the biggest internal challenge to President Volodymyr Zelensky’s rule since the Russia-Ukraine war began more than four years ago. “Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia,” Fedorov said, just hours after Zelensky asked lawmakers to confirm his new defense minister, Yevhenii Khmara. “We must find a legal, safe, and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to renew its full democratic process even in the conditions of a long war.” Fedorov’s six months in office were notable for his role in spearheading Ukraine’s drone development program, which has proved instrumental in effectively combatting Russia. However, he was fired last month over a dispute with then-commander of the Ukrainian armed forces, Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi—sparking rare anti-government protests. Fedorov appears to have capitalized on that momentum, warning that Kyiv faces a “systemic crisis of governance” that fears change. His call also comes as Zelensky is under increasing pressure due to a massive scandal related to alleged corruption, which has engulfed a significant number of the president’s top political allies. Ukraine is prohibited from holding elections when the country is under martial law, as it is now. And polling consistently shows that the majority of Ukrainians oppose wartime elections. However, Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly painted the lack of such a vote as evidence of Zelensky’s illegitimacy, and several foreign leaders, including Trump, have pressured the Ukrainian president to concede to Moscow’s demand. Three-day reprieve. Starting on Wednesday, Canada has a 72-hour window to negotiate terms to avoid sweeping U.S. tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. The 50 percent duties were slated to take effect on Wednesday, but Trump announced a three-day reprieve less than two hours before they were to go into force, citing a potential last-minute deal. According to a White House proclamation released on Tuesday, Canada has agreed to several trade concessions. That could include resurrecting talks over the Keystone XL oil pipeline, which the Biden administration scrapped in 2021 to fulfill a campaign promise to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and prioritize green energy. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed that “substantial progress has been made” in talks but that “there is important work still to be done.” Both sides would benefit from stepping back from the brink. Ottawa has threatened to impose retaliatory tariffs on Washington if it went through with these duties, likely reigniting a trade war. That could prove particularly damaging for the White House ahead of the United States’ upcoming midterm elections, which look to be an increasingly tight race for Republicans. Ending early. The U.S. and South Korean militaries confirmed on Wednesday that joint Ulchi Freedom Shield drills, originally scheduled to go through Aug. 27, will be cut short. Instead of an 11-day exercise, the annual event will end on Friday to comply with Trump’s recent demand that U.S. involvement be downsized in deference to his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Trump’s order, which came mere hours after the exercise kicked off, appeared to be a direct response to North Korean threats calling the drills a “rehearsal for an aggressive war.” Both Washington and Seoul have suggested that reducing Ulchi’s scale could help pave the way for reengagement with Pyongyang on denuclearization talks; on Tuesday, U.S. officials told the Wall Street Journal that Trump is pushing for a meeting with Kim as soon as this fall. However, North Korea remains unswayed by these actions. “The provocative, aggressive nature of the drills won’t change even though their duration and size were reduced,” said Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of Kim Jong Un. Meanwhile, many experts have argued that the scale-down undermines Seoul’s defense posture on the Korean Peninsula and damages a long-held alliance with one of Washington’s most powerful East Asian partners. Odds and Ends The Belgian city of Malmedy is known for its historic cathedral, sprawling moorlands, and really big breakfast. Last Saturday, the French-speaking city held its 30th annual Giant Omelet Festival, during which chefs cook a massive free meal for all who want to start their day with a little extra protein. This year’s omelet included 7,200 eggs (along with bacon and herbs) cooked in a specially designed 4-meter-wide pan. “It shows that we don’t need much to bring people together,” said Mathieu Kelleter, a member of the omelet group. item.title: A Land Without the Troubles?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.43
A Land Without the Troubles? Northern Ireland’s most outlandish plan comes to fruition in Jan Carson’s new novel. In 1998, the Irish Republican Army (IRA) killed 29 people in the Omagh bombing, only four months after the Good Friday Agreement purported to put an end to the three-decade-long sectarian conflict known as the Troubles. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in Northern Ireland’s history. During the Troubles, Protestant unionists and Catholic nationalists clashed over whether Northern Ireland should remain in the United Kingdom or become part of a united Ireland. The conflict still permeates social and political life in the country, where efforts to confront its legacy are ongoing. In 2024, Northern Ireland established an independent inquiry to determine whether British state authorities could have prevented the carnage of the Omagh bombing. Two years later, the inquiry drags on, impeded by the difficulty of collecting evidence that is over a quarter of a century old, and the pain of dredging up historical grievances. In 1998, the Irish Republican Army (IRA) killed 29 people in the Omagh bombing, only four months after the Good Friday Agreement purported to put an end to the three-decade-long sectarian conflict known as the Troubles. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in Northern Ireland’s history. During the Troubles, Protestant unionists and Catholic nationalists clashed over whether Northern Ireland should remain in the United Kingdom or become part of a united Ireland. The conflict still permeates social and political life in the country, where efforts to confront its legacy are ongoing. In 2024, Northern Ireland established an independent inquiry to determine whether British state authorities could have prevented the carnage of the Omagh bombing. Two years later, the inquiry drags on, impeded by the difficulty of collecting evidence that is over a quarter of a century old, and the pain of dredging up historical grievances. In Northern Irish author Jan Carson’s new novel, Few and Far Between, a young anthropologist named Alex sets out on another mission to examine a messy past when she visits the place where her mixed-religion parents raised her: a fictional island archipelago that once sheltered a utopian community from the Troubles. Through chapters from Alex’s ethnography and the narration of the book’s central characters, Carson explores the dynamics of memory, reconciliation, and accountability that continue to haunt Northern Ireland. As in her previous work, Carson laces the novel with dark humor and magical realism, wielding absurdity to broach the lingering repercussions of the Troubles alongside the existential threats of our time. Balancing cynicism with charming earnestness, the book grapples with the dangers of melancholy and nostalgia in both personal and political life, prompting readers to consider what we lose when we paper over the past—and what further damage is possible when we drag that past back up again. Few and Far Between imagines an alternate history in which an outlandish idea proposed in 1958 by Northern Irish leader Terence O’Neill to drain Lough Neagh, the largest lake in the British isles, came partly to fruition. (In reality, the scheme was quickly deemed unworkable.) “For those readers calling themselves Northern Irish, Neagh’s the hole in the doughnut of your country,” Alex writes. “For those readers who are Irish, living both north and south of the six-county line, Lough Neagh’s the cyclops eye peering out of your country’s head.” O’Neill had a vision of a new town springing up in the center of the former lake where Protestants and Catholics could work alongside one another—a proposal “more laughable than the concept of emptying out an enormous lake,” Alex writes. The scheme was only half-delivered, resulting in a receded waterline and the emergence of an archipelago known as the “Ark.” When the Troubles began in the late 1960s, the Ark offered “asylum,” quickly becoming populated by people in mixed Catholic/Protestant marriages or who otherwise faced discrimination on the mainland. A small utopian community sprang up, “[f]ueled by some kind of heady optimism,” and it actively integrated “without a thought for the traditional sectarian divide currently devastating the North.” Fascinated by the Ark as “both a victim of the ongoing conflict and an act of embodied protest,” famed anthropologist RJ Connolly brought his wife and three children to set up their home on one of the islands, where he began to study the community. The novel bounces between timelines: the 1970s, when RJ’s children—Marion, Robert-John, and Rosemary—are kids; and 2017, when Alex visits the islands to find Marion and Robert-John still living there as the Ark’s caretakers, even though both of their parents are dead, and the vast majority of the Ark’s inhabitants left after the Good Friday Agreement. Yet despite the peace process, Carson makes it clear that the North “remains traumatized.” No formal truth and reconciliation process followed the Troubles, and without a real outlet to address trauma, the state left society-wide wounds to fester with an almost willful blindness. Although Marion concedes that children, or “weans,” as she calls them, “deserve a future unsullied by the past,” liberation from that past is almost impossible to come by for those who lived through it. This culture of silence has shaped Northern Ireland’s political and social landscape, functioning as a deliberate strategy to facilitate the transition of suspected former IRA members from paramilitaries to legitimate political actors, and enable negotiations with the British government. It also had deadly consequences. IRA members often justified their violence by rationalizing it as a way to reach their end goal of a united Ireland. When IRA leadership abandoned that goal in exchange for peace, many of its members felt left behind. That resentment contributed to the continuation of extremist violence during peacetime, as exhibited by the Omagh bombing. In Carson’s timeline, just as in ours, jurisdictional and cultural frictions were resurfaced by the 2016 Brexit referendum, making peace “wobblier with each passing year.” Brexit threatened, among other things, the stability of the Irish border, where no physical checkpoints have existed since the Good Friday Agreement, and European Union market rules allowed the free flow of goods. Over 10 years after the referendum (in which a majority of Northern Irish voted to stay in the EU), British leaders still have not fully solved the messy task of regulating trade on the border without imposing security checks reminiscent of the Troubles. Carson symbolizes these tensions through the functions and magical properties of the Ark’s islands, which, over time, became “a repository for all the shite that was meant to get sorted but never did.” After the exodus of the Ark’s residents, the island called Eglish Flat becomes a dumping ground for illegal or unwanted items, including the weapons of ex-paramilitaries. The Good Friday Agreement required all paramilitary groups in Northern Ireland to fully disarm within two years; as a result, “you could’ve paved the road to Dublin with all the firearms that found their way to Eglish Flat.” But while “[a] buried gun’s not killing anybody,” as one ex-combatant claims in an interview cited by Alex, the state’s failure to address deeper, more systemic issues manifested in other ways. As of 2017, nearly 4,000 people had died by suicide in Northern Ireland since the Good Friday Agreement—more than were killed during the entire duration of the Troubles. Tom’s Hard, another island in the Ark, is a popular destination for those attempting suicide. Church Flat, meanwhile, is occupied by “Almost-Deads,” spirits of people in limbo between life and death. The Almost-Deads appeared on Church Flat in great numbers toward the end of the Troubles, an “apt metaphor for the liminal state in which the North currently finds itself,” Alex writes; an “island caught in a temporary stasis between the present and what is yet to come.” Finally, Middle Flat houses “traumatized comatose individuals” known as “Sleepers.” They are almost exclusively women, a fact that one fictional official finds unsurprising given that “women bore the brunt of the Troubles,” caring for and protecting their communities during the worst of the conflict. Nearly two decades after the first Sleeper arrived, the rehabilitation rate remains close to zero. Fewer people seemed to be afflicted by the phenomenon for a time, until “Brexit reared its ugly head, dredging up old hurts and fears.” The novel’s post-referendum plot is driven by an existential threat to the islands. A result of global warming, toxic algae “troubles the water,” blooming up throughout the lake and slowly destroying the Ark’s landscape. The government proposes a plan to flood the Ark. It’s a standard policy: Cover everything up and hope it goes away. But a flood would only postpone the environmental impacts of the algae bloom. It would also displace Marion and Robert-John and force them to relocate to the mainland. When Alex arrives, Marion and Robert-John see her as a potential savior. Hoping her future book will convince the devolved government in Stormont not to proceed with its plan to flood the islands, they attempt to paint the Ark in a positive light for Alex, concealing its uglier aspects and their own painful pasts—which include abuse from their otherwise-revered anthropologist father—to the best of their abilities. But in Few and Far Between, what goes down must come up. The islands seem to know what’s in store. They fight their destruction. The Sleepers get restless. Buried things start to reappear. When Marion discovers one particularly shocking truth, her version of reality is rent apart. But though this nearly destroys her at first, it eventually drags her out of a dangerous melancholy. Revelation can be painful, Carson suggests. It can also be liberatory. Although political violence between Catholics and Protestants is rare in Northern Ireland today, the country’s lingering divisions aren’t far from view. Belfast, for example, is still full of towering “peace walls” separating the two communities, street art staking claims to identity, and Palestinian and Israeli flags projecting local tensions onto global conflicts. “When they scratch the surface—which they frequently do, mostly with words but sometimes with fists—there is still a deep divide running through the heart of the place,” Marion notes of those living in Northern Ireland. That divide has also manifested in rising anti-immigrant sentiment today, especially among Protestant loyalists. Few and Far Between pushes readers to face these tensions head-on, and to consider how grievances might be addressed. Is it better to reopen old wounds, or let bygones be bygones? Though that question does not project neatly onto Northern Ireland’s fractured present, it’s clear that attempts to simply cover things up never turn out the way we’d like to imagine. In the novel’s epilogue, set in 2018, onlookers and news crews observe as lost items and souls bubble up from the depths of the lake, including ghosts of those who died by suicide on Tom’s Flat. “Sad-faced, cloudy-looking creatures … hung like mist on the water’s surface, eyeing the heavens jealously. They clapped their cold eyes on the camera and did not flinch or look away, as if to say, Do not ignore us. Don’t pretend we’re not here.” Maxine Davey is an editorial fellow at Foreign Policy. item.title: Southeast Asia Isn’t Buying Elbridge Colby’s Flexible Realism
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.19
Southeast Asia Isn’t Buying Elbridge Colby’s Flexible Realism Trump’s policies offer the region all the downsides of traditional U.S. policy with none of the benefits. U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby just wrapped up a weeklong tour of Southeast Asia. His aim was to reassure allies and partners in the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, and Cambodia that the United States will continue to prioritize the region. But the Trump administration’s actions continue to contradict top officials’ strategic messaging and fuel regional concerns of U.S. withdrawal. In the Philippines, Colby gave a speech to the Stratbase Institute, where he laid out the case for Washington’s tough-love approach to the region. Colby derided the liberal commentariat for painting a picture of U.S. disengagement from the region, insisting that the United States was “digging in.” U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby just wrapped up a weeklong tour of Southeast Asia. His aim was to reassure allies and partners in the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, and Cambodia that the United States will continue to prioritize the region. But the Trump administration’s actions continue to contradict top officials’ strategic messaging and fuel regional concerns of U.S. withdrawal. In the Philippines, Colby gave a speech to the Stratbase Institute, where he laid out the case for Washington’s tough-love approach to the region. Colby derided the liberal commentariat for painting a picture of U.S. disengagement from the region, insisting that the United States was “digging in.” At the same time, though, the administration redirected a U.S. aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, from the Pacific to the Middle East to support operations against Iran. Washington has also shifted THAAD missile defense systems from South Korea to the region, which is to defend U.S. bases in Gulf states that are now more vulnerable to Iranian strikes. The same week, Trump ordered the U.S. Defense Department to draw down U.S. military exercises with South Korea, which he said were “hostile” to North Korea, and cited his “very good relationship” with Kim Jong-un. The decision caused shock across the analytical community and will further undermine perceptions of the United States’ commitment to the Pacific—not least in Beijing, where the move will be seen as confirmation that the United States is pulling back from Asia. In his speech, Colby also characterized U.S. alliances as based on “mutual respect” and asserted that the United States wanted “partners, not protectorates.” But reality—and the pejoratives the U.S. President Donald Trump continues to direct toward U.S. partners such as Greenland—belies Colby’s more charitable characterization. In practice, Trump’s policies have been a mix of economic and political coercion alongside increasingly hollow claims that the United States is not abandoning the region. As such, they have offered regional leaders all the downsides of traditional U.S. policy with none of the benefits. The administration’s transactional approach is less new than it insists. In seeking to extract the maximum concessions from junior partners and allies while dismissing the notion that its actions are fueling widespread resentment, Trump has replicated the worst aspects of U.S. colonial-era and Cold War policies. During its global struggle against the Soviet Union, Washington often treated the autonomy of small states as a secondary concern. As a result, it ignored declarations of neutrality in Cambodia and Laos, and it supported rightwing dictators in Indonesia, the Philippines, and Thailand who supported their cause. In Jakarta, Colby met with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and other senior officials, including Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin, “to advance a defense relationship grounded in respect for Indonesia’s sovereignty, traditions, and history.” This created a nice public relations moment for social media, but Washington’s respect for Indonesian sovereignty was less apparent as it pressured Jakarta to grant it overflight access for military aircraft. The administration also proposed making Indonesia a hub for C-130 Hercules aircraft maintenance, potentially inviting further U.S. rotational presence. Colby also characterized the Trump administration’s foreign policy as “practical and pragmatic” and slammed “past administrations, which were hidebound by outdated convention or rigid adherence to liberal dogma.” But Colby’s frequent references to “pragmatism,” “realism,” and “common sense” are a rhetorical sleight of hand. Trump officials like to depict the administration’s policies as guided by some overarching strategic coherence, in contrast to past administrations’ values-based approach. However, Colby’s remarks obscure the fact that the Trump administration has blinders of its own. They are simply of a different type. Under Trump 2.0, Washington has imposed sweeping and unilateral tariffs. These harken back to a more protectionist and inward-looking period of history, namely the 19th and early 20th century before the creation of the World Trade Organization. The Trump administration’s emphasis on burden-sharing, which entails pressuring allies to spend more on their own defense, is another side of the protectionist coin. Like tariffs, this is intended to reduce the financial burden on the United States, giving the administration more revenue while allies and partners look after their own defense. But such a worldview is not value-free. It rests on several outdated assumptions about how the global economy functions, how deterrence works, and what keeps adversaries at bay in an anarchic world. In reality, a world in which countries are less economically interdependent, where there is less immigration, and in which states spend more on their own military power, trust breaks down and the chances of war increase. Colby and other senior Trump officials who espouse this false promise of “flexible realism” ignore the fact that trust and credibility do not rest on military might alone. They are forged by consistency and demonstrating strategic coherence between what you say and what you do. Colby can say all he wants that the United States is deepening engagement in the region and blame the liberal commentariat and its negative spin for misrepresenting the administration’s policies. But Washington only has itself to blame for growing regional anxieties. If regional leaders see a less reliable and increasingly distracted United States, it is because Washington has played a strong hand poorly in Southeast Asia while launching a costly and strategically misguided war in the Middle East. item.title: Sam Altman Admits It’s Going to Take a Long Time Before AI Goes Mainstream
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 6.15
If there’s one line the tech giants of the world have been incessantly trying to drill into our skulls for the past few years—in product release events, media appearances, and one terrible ad after another—it’s that AI is going to change pretty much everything about our lives, very, very quickly. But in the face of heated, widespread public backlash against the data centers powering the AI boom, steep costs for customers, and other hurdles, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been backtracking on that narrative. He admits that he and his fellow dyed-in-the-wool AI true believers may have been a tad too optimistic in their forecasts, and that it will likely take longer than they expected for AI to become as mainstream as, say, Google’s search engine or the iPhone. The vast majority of people, in Altman’s view, are far too deeply ingrained in their current technological habits to make a quick switch to AI-native platforms, such as OpenAI’s Codex, no matter how impressive their capabilities might look on paper (or how many marketing dollars companies spend). “I think I was wrong about a few things,” Altman told the podcaster David Senra in a video posted to the latter’s YouTube channel on Sunday. “One of them is just [the fact that] the economy just has so much inertia. People keep doing the same things…they’re buying from the same company, they keep wanting to use their tools in the same way. I think that’s actually a positive in many ways, and it’s going to make this big transition in front of us go smoother and slower, and I’m grateful for it. But I think it means we’ve all been too ambitious on timelines…” Changing people’s behavior, Altman said, “is much harder than the tech nerds realize.” He likened the adoption of AI to people still visiting Blockbuster in the early days after Netflix was founded (back when it was just mail-delivering DVDs, before it became a streaming service). But even this is a camouflaged sales pitch from Altman. In a blog post published last summer titled “The Gentle Singularity,” he argued that “superintelligence”—then a relatively fresh buzzword in Silicon Valley—would emerge slowly, such that humanity would be able to gradually acclimate to the changes it wrought upon our individual lives and society at large. That which seems scary and alien to many of us now will, in the fullness of time, come to seem mundane. People are creatures of habit, and most won’t abandon tools they’ve relied on for years in favor of an AI agent overnight. But force of habit and economic inertia are far from the only major barriers AI companies are facing. They’re also in the thick of a reputational crisis, as throngs of people actively protest (online and in public) against the spread and ecological impacts of data centers, AI-powered surveillance, and what some see as the beginning of a new wealth disparity even more pronounced than the one we currently live in. Then there are the very serious cybersecurity fears. A spate of frontier AI models, including two from OpenAI, have gone off the rails during internal tests and hacked into third-party organizations, sparking new public debate about the technology’s safety and the risks that could lie ahead should it fall into the wrong hands. OpenAI has said it’s slowing down the development of one of its new models, called Astra, to focus on building a more robust cybersecurity testing protocol and preventing similar hack-cidents from happening in the future. In his conversation with Senra, Altman acknowledged that the tech industry has not yet managed to capture the hearts and minds of the general public with its vision of the future, where we’re all assisted by superintelligent—and more importantly, safe—AI agents. “We have not as a field done a very good job of explaining to people what the benefits are and how the downsides can be mitigated,” Altman said in the interview.

item.title: Sunken WWI and WWII Ships and Subs Are Leaking TNT Pollution Into the Ocean
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.74
The German Type UC II minelaying submarine UC-30 was armed to do serious damage as it approached Denmark’s Wadden Sea Islands in 1917. The U-boat carried 18 mines, six torpedoes, and a crew of 27 Kaiserliche Marine seamen—all of whom sank to a watery grave when the German sub hit a British mine near the island of Rømø off Denmark’s southeastern coast. UC-30 remained undiscovered for almost a century. But now, thanks to Aarhus University geoscientist Katrine Juul Andresen and multi-institution team, the Kaiser’s attack sub has joined a catalogue of roughly 1,500 sunken World War I and World War II vessels, as well as thousands more wrecks, mapped off the nation’s coast. Andresen has been in a race against time to measure toxic leaks from these sunken artifacts to help remediation efforts to stop these wrecks from poisoning local marine food chains—including the many people who rely on North Sea commercial fishing for their sustenance. For the new study, published this month in the journal Marine Pollution Bulletin, Andresen and colleagues used blue mussels (Mytilus edulis) as aquatic canaries in the undersea coal mine and found that leaking munitions are now damaging the enzymatic pathways these species employ to naturally detoxify. “Pollution is definitely occurring,” Andresen explained in a statement. “We found traces of TNT in the wildlife, the seabed, and the water column.” “It is likely a relatively localized source of pollution, but it will worsen as the wreck continues to deteriorate and expose more of the explosive material inside the mines,” according to Andresen, who collaborated with marine ecologists at Germany’s Alfred Wegener Institute and elsewhere on the new research. Ticking time-bombs The most common categories of chemical explosives now resting in these decaying munitions under the North Sea are 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT), 1,3,5-trinitro-1,3,5-triazine (RDX), and 1,3-dinitrobenzene (DNB). None of them are safe, according to study coauthor Edmund Maser, a toxicologist at the University Medical Center Schleswig-Holstein in Kiel. “The problem with these ammunition compounds is that they are not only toxic but also carcinogenic,” as Maser told the American Geophysical Union’s Eos last year, after publishing a related study. Carcinogens bring a higher level of risk compared to lesser toxins that living things can more readily metabolize in small doses. “One single molecule could cause cancer,” Maser said. Andresen, Maser, and their colleagues found trace amounts of TNT in the seawater surrounding UC-30 at around 72.6 nanograms per liter (72.6 parts per trillion). But that minute amount belies its impact: The researchers’ test mussels displayed not only trouble detoxifying, but disrupted metabolisms, and reduced energy for reproduction (specifically glycogen in the bivalves’ digestive tissue). Some things should stay buried The study also conducted similar tests near two other wrecks, the WWI-era German light cruiser the SMS Mainz and the WWII-era transport KW 58 Hendricus, but Andresen noted that more work needs to be done both on the scope of these leaks and many still underexamined wrecks. “The question is how significant the effect is and how far from the wreck the pollution impacts the marine environment,” according to Andresen, who previously authored a 2024 study funded by the Danish government on the wider scope of this toxic shipwreck problem. “In the report, I found that there are 10,127 wrecks in Danish waters. Around 15 percent of them date back to the years around and during the two world wars,” she noted. “I am not aware of whether the agency has taken the work further since the report was published.” Germany, Andresen pointed out, has devoted considerable resources to retrieving similar sunken munitions in the Baltic Sea, but solutions are costly. Andresen has considered ideas as complex as robots and as comically simple as blowing the aging ordinance up. But, in some cases, she said the best approach may simply be doing nothing at all. “Some wrecks are fully or partially buried in the seabed. When covered by sand, the risk of polluting the surrounding sea is significantly lower,” Andresen pointed out. “It is a matter of identifying where the environmental threat is greatest—and then deciding whether the munitions on the wrecks should be removed.”

item.title: The HPV Vaccine Isn’t Just Preventing Cervical Cancer, New Research Reveals
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.71
A highly effective vaccine for the human papillomavirus is looking even better than we hoped, thanks to new research that suggest HPV vaccination can prevent a variety of cancers, not just cervical cancer. Researchers in Taiwan examined the medical records of over 1.4 million Americans, half of whom were vaccinated against HPV. Compared to unvaccinated people, HPV-vaccinated people were significantly less likely to develop cancers of the neck and head, they found. The findings provide “real-world evidence supporting the potential broader benefits of HPV vaccination,” the authors wrote in their paper, published this month in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases. The harms of HPV HPV is a ubiqutious passenger of humanity. Just about every person will catch the sexually transmitted virus at some point in their lives. However, there are actually around 200 types of HPV. Many HPV types will go unnoticed and never cause any illness. Others cause unsightly but ultimately harmless growths that we call warts (these include genital warts). And certain high-risk HPV types can linger in the body and raise the chances of cancer. HPV vaccines are intended to prevent the most common high-risk HPV types (the vaccine currently available in the U.S. also prevents some types that cause warts). These high-risk infections are responsible for the vast majority of cervical cancers in women, and studies have consistently shown that HPV vaccination programs are helping reduce the incidence of cervical cancer in conjunction with early screening. In some countries, these programs have been so successful that cervical cancer might already have been eradicated on a local level. However, HPV is also a major leading cause of several other cancers that affect men and women, including head and neck cancers. And the current study researchers wanted to study how vaccination is affecting the incidence of these cancers as well. Beyond cervical cancer The team analyzed medical records from a large database of U.S. patients across the country. They compared roughly 700,000 people vaccinated against HPV to a same-sized group of similar people who recieved other non-HPV vaccines, then tracked their outcomes for up to 13 years. By the end of the study period, 40 people in the vaccinated group had been diagnosed with a head or neck cancer, compared to 130 people in the unvaccinated group, the researchers found. Vaccinated people were especially less likely to develop oropharyngeal cancers (the oropharynx is the middle part of the throat, behind the mouth). Upon closer inspection, this associated risk reduction was only statistically significant among people who were first vaccinated between the ages of 9 to 26; vaccinated people in this age group were roughly 68% less likely to develop a head or neck cancer. This is probably because older people are more likely to have already caught high-risk HPV infections before they were vaccinated. The researchers did still observe a potential reduction in cancer risk even among older people, just not one that could be conclusively shown. These findings can ultimately only demonstrate an association between HPV vaccination and reduced cancers of the head and neck, not a clear cause-and-effect relationship. And because HPV-related cancers tend to take years, even decades, to emerge following exposure, it will take more time to know just how effective vaccination is at reducing risk. That said, other studies have found a similar link between taking these vaccines and a lower chance of these and other non-cervical cancers, including penile cancer in men. Unfortunately, though the HPV vaccine is now widely recommended for everyone starting as early as age 9, vaccination rates are lower in the U.S. than many similar high-income countries. As of 2024, only about 63% of U.S. teens were up-to-date with their HPV shots, whereas countries like Denmark and Spain are expected to reach 90% coverage by decade’s end.

item.title: Tesla Finally Sets a Launch Date for the Cybercab
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.73
Tesla’s purpose-built robotaxi finally appears to have a launch date. Elon Musk’s EV company posted a teaser on X over the weekend for an “Exclusive Access” Cybercab event taking place Sept. 3 in Austin. The Musk-focused news site Teslarati also posted an invitation to what Tesla is calling the “Cybercab Launch Event.” The invite says guests will get the opportunity to “experience the future of full autonomy.” Electrek reports that the event is invite-only but will be livestreamed. The outlet also reports that Cybercab rides will soon become available through Tesla’s existing Robotaxi app in Austin. The event comes as Tesla has been laying the groundwork to expand its year-old Robotaxi service. In February, the company posted a photo of what it said was the first production Cybercab to roll off the line at its Gigafactory in Texas. The Cybercab is a two-seat, “purpose-built fully autonomous vehicle.” Since it is meant to be fully driverless, it has no steering wheel or pedals. Amazon-owned Zoox also operates a purpose-built robotaxi that has no driving controls. The lack of traditional controls makes the Cybercab an unusually light EV. Recent regulatory filings with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), first reported by Car and Driver, revealed that the Cybercab has a curb weight of just 3,113 pounds. For context, that makes it roughly 700 pounds lighter than the lightest Model 3. The filings also show that it runs on a single front-mounted 219-horsepower permanent magnet motor and a 48 kWh battery pack for an unadjusted 418-mile range. The Verge reports that, after EPA testing adjustments, the Cybercab’s real-world range will likely be closer to 290 to 300 miles. The outlet also reports that its 165 watt-hours-per-mile(Wh/mi) rating would make it one of the most efficient EVs ever certified. When Tesla first launched its Robotaxi service in Austin in June 2025, Musk told investors the company planned to quickly expand into California, Nevada, Arizona, and Florida. “We’ll probably have autonomous ride-hailing in about half the population of the US by the end of the year,” Musk said in a July earnings call last year. More than a year later, Tesla says Robotaxi rides are currently available in Texas and Florida. Additionally, Electrek estimates that Tesla only has somewhere between 20 and 30 unsupervised vehicles operating at any given time. For comparison, Waymo operates at 3,000 autonomous vehicles across more than 11 cities and completes more than 500,000 paid rides a week. Still, there are signs Tesla is preparing to expand its operations. Last week, the Nevada Transportation Authority approved permits allowing Tesla, Waymo and Uber partner Aviari to operate commercial robotaxi services in Clark County, where Las Vegas is located. Tesla’s permit allows it to deploy up to 5,000 fully autonomous vehicles during its first 12 months. On top of that, Bloomberg reported in June that Tesla filed plans with the city of Austin to expand an existing service center with a “robocar” wash and charging stations. The company has also submitted plans for a Cybercab car wash in Las Vegas. Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: 8-Year-Old Girl in Louisiana Dies From ‘Brain-Eating’ Amoeba After Lake Swim
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.55
An 8-year-old’s recent summer lake swim has led to a heartbreaking tragedy. Last week, the Louisiana Department of Health reported that a resident, subsequently identified as Lillian Smart by her family, had contracted a rare infection of Naegleria fowleri, an amoeba that attacks the brains of those infected. Sadly, on Sunday, the family reported that Smart had succumbed to the highly fatal illness over the weekend. It’s only the fourth case of N. fowleri ever documented in the state, according to health officials. “The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from. Everyone did everything they could to keep her here,” her family wrote in a Facebook post to a group started to provide updates on her condition. The brain-eating amoeba N. fowleri is a shapeshifting amoeba that lives in soil and warm freshwater. It typically only eats bacteria and isn’t dangerous to people when it’s swallowed from drinking water containing the amoeba. However, when the amoeba enters the body through the nose, it can sometimes migrate to the brain. From there, it will attack and kill brain cells, triggering a massive bout of inflammation. This infection is formally called primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, or PAM. According to the Louisiana Department of Health, symptoms of PAM typically start with “severe headache, fever, nausea and vomiting and progress to stiff neck, seizures, and coma that can lead to death.” People usually feel sick about five days after exposure, but it can take up to 12 days. And though doctors can try to treat PAM with an aggressive cocktail of drugs and other interventions, the infection remains nearly always fatal. People often catch PAM from swimming in warm freshwater sources, such as lakes during the summertime, and that appears to be what happened to Smart in this case. Health officials say she likely acquired the infection while swimming in Lake Claiborne, located in northern Louisiana. A rare but rising threat Thankfully, N. fowleri infections are incredibly rare. There have been only around 180 cases recorded in the U.S. between 1937 through 2025, according to the Louisiana Department of Health, with three cases prior to Smart reported in the state itself. However, research has suggested that the global incidence of this infection is increasing in warmer parts of the world. And at least some scientists argue that climate change is and will continue to make N. fowleri a bigger problem over time. A study earlier this year revealed that the amoeba was commonly found in many recreational hot water springs across the western half of the country. Louisiana officials have issued an advisory to health care providers in the area about the case. And though the odds of catching N. fowleri are low, the department adds that people swimming in warm freshwater sources should always assume there is a risk and take steps to further lower it. Namely, you should try to limit any water that goes up the nose while swimming, such as by pinching your nose shut or wearing nose clips when jumping in. People should also always use distilled, sterilized, or boiled and cooled tap water for nasal irrigation, since that’s another potential route of infection.

item.title: OpenAI Has to Answer to Alabama on Hugging Face Hack
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.96
OpenAI’s general attitude towards the fact that one of its AI models went rogue and hacked into the systems of the open-source AI platform Hugging Face has been, “That’s our bad, but you gotta admit, it’s pretty cool, right?” The Attorney General of Alabama’s answer to that is a pretty resounding “No.” On Monday, Alabama AG Steve Marshall announced that he had launched an investigation into the incident and is demanding that OpenAI respond. To encourage that cooperation in the state’s investigation, Marshall issued a subpoena calling on the company to provide a slew of information around the incident. Among the details Alabama would like to see: all documents related to the Hugging Face hack and details on the model testing that resulted in it, details of every employee involved in the model’s training, names of anyone who raised concerns about the training before the incident, and all the details of OpenAI’s safety measures used in the training process. OpenAI will have until September 14, 2026 to comply with the state’s demands, so expect its lawyers to be quite busy for the next few weeks. Gizmodo reached out to OpenAI for comment regarding the subpoena, but did not receive a response at the time of publication. Alabama taking the lead on the issue comes after the state joined a coalition of concerned Attorneys General that recently sent a letter to OpenAI calling for increased transparency and safety measures from the company. Notably, the top prosecutors for states like Florida, Texas, and Utah demanded that OpenAI cease all tests that led to the Hugging Face hacking until “OpenAI shows that it can conduct such activities in a controlled and responsible way.” Last week, OpenAI did announce several changes to its safety protocols in response to the Hugging Face hack, which saw one of its unreleased models break containment and autonomously act to breach the other company’s systems, including stronger monitoring across its development processes—which might mean any monitoring, seeing as this incident somehow eluded OpenAI for about a week until it finally noticed. The company also called on California to strengthen its recently passed AI safety law, which requires transparency into the model training process. OpenAI reportedly wants the state to amend the law to include requirements that AI models be monitored during training for the possibility that the model could breach third-party systems. OpenAI is positioning the request as evidence that it’s serious about safety. But it’s also a bit of a cop out. It suggests that something like this wouldn’t have happened if someone had simply stopped them. Rather than, you know, just not doing it in the first place.

item.title: ‘Cars’ 20th Anniversary Screening Will Force You to Confront the Passage of Time
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.31
Stare into the abyss and soak in the realization that Cars, Disney and Pixar’s franchise-spawning and narratively confusing animated juggernaut, is celebrating its 20th anniversary this year. After its release in 2006, it was followed by two sequels as well as a spin-off, Planes, which got its own sequel. There have also been multiple TV series, video games, and a significant Cars presence at Disney’s theme parks. Somehow, the increasingly sequel-obsessed Pixar hasn’t announced a Cars 4 yet, but if you cast a glance at the success of Toy Story 5, you have to assume someone over there is talking about the possibility. In the meantime, the original Cars is making a victory lap back to theaters in honor of Lightning McQueen Day, which is September 5—9/5, the race car’s signature number. “Cars introduces Lightning McQueen (voiced by Owen Wilson), a hotshot rookie race car driven to succeed, who discovers that life is about the journey, not the finish line, when he finds himself unexpectedly detoured in the sleepy Route 66 town of Radiator Springs and meets the town’s offbeat characters, including Doc Hudson (voiced by Paul Newman), Mater (voiced by Larry the Cable Guy), and Sally (voiced by Bonnie Hunt),” reads the film’s official synopsis. Cars marked one of the final film roles for Hollywood legend and noted racing aficionado Newman, who passed away in 2008. It was the sixth-highest-grossing release of 2006, behind Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man’s Chest, The Da Vinci Code, Ice Age: Meltdown, Casino Royale, and Night at the Museum, some of which have perhaps not stood the test of time as well as Cars, despite who directed it. You can get advanced tickets for the Cars 20th anniversary screenings, which kick off September 4, at this link. Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, what’s next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: Long-Term Travel and the Accounts That Stop Recognizing You
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 7.10
Four months into a trip through South America, a long-term traveler can suddenly find their bank has flagged them as fraud. There may be no warning. The card is declined at the counter, the app refuses to open, and the only option is a phone number that does not accept calls from outside the account's country. Long-term travelers often encounter this problem, which is rarely triggered by the transaction alone. The connection also has a part. Banks and payment processors review factors like location, network reputation, and connection type when assessing a login. A ProxyWing ISP proxy provider uses IP addresses registered to internet service providers rather than data-center IPs, which helps explain why different connections may be classified differently. Why Unfamiliar Connections Can Trigger Account Lockouts What Actually Trips the Alarm It is seldom the amount you spent. It is the shape of the session. - Speed of movement matters. A login from Peru eleven hours after one from Colombia is fine, but eleven minutes is not. - The reputation of the network matters. Hundreds of people share hostel and cafe Wi-Fi, and if any have done something suspicious, the address carries that history. - Connection type. Traffic that looks like it comes from a data center rather than a home or a phone gets scored much more harshly, which is why certain VPNs make things worse rather than better. - Doing something unusual at the same time. Changing an address or adding a payee from an unfamiliar country is what turns a flag into a lock. The Two-Factor Problem Nobody Plans For Losing a phone at home is inconvenient. Losing it in month five of a trip can lock you out of everything at once because the phone is usually the second factor for the bank, the email that lets you reset the bank, and the authenticator app that protects the email. The chain matters. If your recovery codes are stored in the email account that needs the authenticator on the lost phone, you have a loop with no way in. This is the most common way travelers get genuinely stuck rather than merely inconvenienced, and it takes about fifteen minutes to prevent. - Print the recovery codes for your email plus primary bank on paper, carried separately from the phone. - Add a second authenticator device if any of your accounts allow it. An old phone without a SIM works fine and can be kept at the bottom of the bag. - Check whether your bank's two-factor works over SMS only. If it does, a local SIM will break it, so you need to know before you swap the card rather than after. What To Do Before You Leave The single most useful thing is boring. Set up a second account at a different bank, fund it, and carry the card separately. Everything else on this list is optional, but that one is not. - Register a travel notice if your bank still offers one. Many have quietly dropped them. - Make sure your phone number on the account is one you can actually receive calls on abroad, not just texts. - Download the offline recovery codes for anything that uses an authenticator app. - Take a photograph of the back of your cards, cropped so the number is not fully visible, and store it somewhere you can reach without your phone. - Tell one person at home which banks you use. If you end up needing someone to receive a letter or make a domestic call on your behalf, this saves a day. How Different Connections Get Treated | Connection you are using | How a bank tends to score it | Practical result | | Local SIM with mobile data | Low risk, looks like an ordinary phone | Usually fine | | HotelWi-Fii | Medium, shared but stable | Occasional extra verification | | Hostel or cafeWi-Fii | Higher, heavily shared | Verification, sometimes a lock | | Commercial VPN | High, recognized as a data center range | Frequently blocked outright | | Residential connection at home | Lowest | The baseline everything else is measured against | | AirportWi-Fii | High, transient and shared | Avoid logging into banking entirely | | Tethering from your own phone | Same as the phone itself | The best option on the road | The general pattern is similar across many banks: the closer a connection looks to an ordinary home line, the less friction a traveler is likely to encounter. The closer your connection looks to an ordinary home line, the less friction you get. This is also why the free VPN people install for privacy tends to be the thing that locks them out. Which Accounts Survive Travel Better Not all banks handle this equally; the difference is structural rather than customer service. Banks built around mobile apps cope better because their fraud models assume people move. Older institutions with branch-based verification cope worst because their recovery path assumes you can walk into a building. The pragmatic setup most long-term travelers use is one app-based account for daily spending, one traditional account holding most of the money and rarely touched, and a card from a third provider kept separate from the wallet. It sounds excessive until the first lockout. If You Are Already Locked Out Do not keep retrying. Repeated failed attempts push the account further into lockdown and make the eventual phone call longer. Find a dependable connection, ideally mobile data on a local SIM, and use the in-app message system if available. It is slower but works from anywhere. If you do have to call, use a voice-over-internet service that presents a number in your home country. Many bank fraud lines will not accept an international caller ID at all, and this is the difference between resolving it today and resolving it next week. FAQ Will telling my bank I am traveling prevent this? It helps for the first few weeks and then stops mattering. Most travel notices expire after thirty days, and many banks have removed them entirely in favor of automatic detection. Is a VPN a good idea for online banking abroad? Generally no. It protects the connection, but it makes you look less like yourself, and banks weigh that heavily. Use mobile data instead. Why does my card work in shops but the app will not open? Different systems score card payments and app logins. The card transaction has a physical terminal behind it, which is strong evidence you are there. The app login has only the connection. How long does a lock usually take to lift? If you can complete identity verification, minutes. If it needs a phone call to a domestic number, expect days. This is the main argument for the second card. Does using the same connection every day help? Yes, more than most people expect. Staying somewhere for a fortnight and using the same Wi-Fi builds a pattern the bank recognizes, which is why lockouts cluster in the weeks when you are moving fastest.
