item.title: Humanoid Robots Now Run Faster Than Usain Bolt, Can’t Stop Properly
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.16
Remember when Usain Bolt set the world record for the 100 meters in 2009? That time of 9.58 seconds still stands, but now humanoid robots are beating Bolt’s iconic time under test conditions. The second World Humanoid Robot Games (WHRG) began in Beijing this weekend, and one of the devices completed the 100-meter race in 9.39 seconds. However, at the end of the race, the humanoid robot collided with a crash mat and flailed its limbs until it hit the ground damaged. The race featured three humanoid devices, all of which finished similarly with no other way for them to stop without hitting the stands. One of the competing robots also caught fire on the ground, while others were stretchered off by the people involved in the games. You can see the 100-meter race in the video below. The race winner was a robot produced by Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, but Honor’s own Lightning Robot also reportedly beat Bolt's time in a trial run for the event, completing the dash in 9.47 seconds. The first WHRG took place last year, where the top robot completed a 100-meter race in 21.5 seconds. There has been a huge improvement in just 12 months, although the producers of these robots may now have more reason to focus on sprinting skills now that the WHRG is solidified as an annual event. If companies like Honor can prove their tech's prowess under these conditions, development teams are likely to focus on those capabilities to showcase what the tech can do. The WHRG features 51 events with more than 1,000 competitions across five days. Alongside robotic foot races, there are events for other sports, such as soccer and table tennis, with over 2,000 specialized robots competing from over 600 companies. It isn’t just the Olympics for robots, though. Outside of sporting events, the WHRG also sees robots perform other physical tasks, including household services, firefighting, and other forms of rescue. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Hackers Are Targeting Your Website. Here's How to Stop Them
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.58
The internet is a hostile place for an unprotected website. Although there are numerous complex cyber threats in the digital world, many website attacks boil down to brute-force attacks (hackers using scripts to guess your passwords) and malware injections (hackers sneaking malicious code into your files). The good news is that keeping your site safe needn't be complicated, with your hosting environment acting as the first line of defense. When choosing a web host, look for these simple, essential security features to protect your online business from malicious attacks. I'll start with the basics, then recommend additional ways to safeguard your website. The 6 Basic Hosting Security Features You Need There are six core security features you absolutely do not want to overlook—your website must have them. Web hosting services typically offer all of them, though some features may be available as a paid add-on. Other times, the web host may offer a rudimentary version of a given security feature with your plan, with the full-featured version locked behind a paywall. For example, HostGator's free malware protection is fairly skimpy; for full protection, you need to pony up for the Malware Protection or SiteLock plans. Here's what your web host should supply, at a bare minimum. The first two features I touch on operate at the server level, so your host must include them. - Automated server updates. Servers rely on foundational operating systems, databases, and control panels. So when web hosts update their operating systems and other server software, they fix background vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them. - Free SSL certificates. Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) technology encrypts plain-text data into unreadable code as it travels to and from your website. This prevents bad actors from eavesdropping on the transmitted data, potentially stealing customer data or admin passwords. While you can technically install and manage an SSL certificate yourself, it's such a fundamental and necessary feature in 2026 that a host that doesn't include one for free should be avoided. The following four features are also security necessities, but web hosts don't always include them for free; they're sometimes add-ons. - Automatic malware scanning and removal. Trustworthy web hosts scan your server directories daily for suspicious code patterns, backdoors, or unauthorized files. When threats are detected, the system isolates or deletes the infected script immediately to prevent data leaks. - Web application firewall (WAF). A WAF inspects incoming web requests in real time and matches them against known brute-force attack behavior. It blocks SQL injection attempts, malicious scripts, and cross-site scripting from hitting your live environment. - Brute-force attack protection. Bad guys use networks of compromised computers to test thousands of password combinations per minute. Brute-force attack protection detects high-frequency login failures from specific IP addresses and blocks those IP addresses from accessing your website. - Automated daily backups: Web hosts typically back up your site daily, so they can restore a clean version if anything goes wrong. If a malicious injection occurs, a single click can revert your entire system to its functional, pre-compromised state. Note, however, that while hosts frequently offer daily backups for free, some legacy hosts, like HostGator and Bluehost, charge extra to restore your website from said backup. If your web host charges extra for any of these latter four security layers (or lacks them entirely), you can enable them yourself using free third-party plug-ins or external services. For example, Cloudflare offers free, elite-tier firewalls and bot protection. Likewise, several free WordPress plug-ins, including UpdraftPlus and Wordfence, scan your site and automatically back it up to Dropbox, Google Drive, or other cloud storage. And ImunifyAV has free, server-level malware protection (a feature that must be supported by your host's control panel). In addition, you should run an external URL verification check using the free Sucuri SiteCheck once a week and consider manually backing up your website. Extra Security Tips for Beginner Businesses If you're an entrepreneur breaking into the web scene for the first time, your business is a prime target. Attackers assume you haven't set up advanced defenses yet, so prove them wrong by keeping these key tips in mind: - Limit admin access. Grant website editing permissions only to staff members who truly need them. - Use two-factor authentication (2FA). Require a code from your phone, in addition to your password, for anyone logging in to the site. - Collect minimal data. Only store the customer data you absolutely need, such as email addresses for account creation. Never save sensitive financial information, credit card details, or tax numbers directly on a basic web server database. Instead, set up external merchant accounts with secure gateways like PayPal, Square, or Stripe. These services handle transactions on their own hardened networks, keeping your servers clean and dramatically reducing your legal liability if a breach occurs. - Never use "admin" as your username. Change your default login name to something unique, so automated brute-force scripts have a hard time guessing your credentials. As you can imagine, "admin" is often the first name bad actors attempt to breach. - Remove inactive plug-ins and themes. Delete any extensions, themes, or plug-ins you no longer use. These old, forgotten tools and potentially out-of-date items are an easy way for a website to get injected with malware. - Protect your comments section. Turn on automated spam filters for website comments to stop bots from posting malicious links to your pages. What to Do If Your Site Gets Hacked Learning that your website has been compromised is stressful, but the faster you act, the more damage you can mitigate. Follow these steps posthaste to take back control. - Put your site in maintenance mode. Temporarily take the front end offline to prevent visitors from encountering malware or broken pages. - Restore from a clean backup. Use your web host's automated backup tool to roll your website back to a date before the hack. You can typically find the backup tool in your account control panel, such as cPanel, hPanel, or JetBackup. - Change all passwords. Reset the passwords for your hosting account, website dashboard, FTP, and database immediately. - Update the website's software. Visit your dashboard and update your site's core software, as well as the plug-ins and themes. It's also a good idea to enable auto-updates for plug-ins while you’re doing this, so they patch themselves in the future - Run a deep scan. Let your security tool or hosting scanner run a full check to ensure no hidden backdoors remain in your files. All these steps should safeguard your website from people of ill intent, so you can focus on what matters: running your business. About Our Expert In 2014, I began my career at PCMag as a freelancer. That blossomed into a full-time position in 2021, and I now review email marketing apps, mobile operating systems, web hosting services, streaming music platforms, and video games as a senior writer. I'm a graduate of Hunter College, a hard-core gamer, and an Apple enthusiast.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro Leaks Are Everywhere. Which Ones Can You Actually Trust?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.52
If you're not ready to try out a foldable, Apple's next iPhone event is also likely to include the launch of the iPhone 18 Pros. Customers usually hold off on iPhone purchases right before Apple’s fall event, but the RAM crisis and its associated price hikes may have you wondering whether it's best to buy now and avoid any more increases. Apple already raised prices across several major product lines in June, but the iPhone was not included, helping drive iPhone 17 sales during the last quarter. To make your decision easier, we’ve rounded up the biggest iPhone 18 Pro rumors we have heard so far. While these features and prices aren’t confirmed yet, they should help paint a picture of what to expect from Apple’s next big smartphones. iPhone 18 Pro: Revised Lineup The biggest rumor around the iPhone 18 lineup is its release timeline. Unlike previous years, where Apple released four phones in the same series in one go, Bloomberg reports Apple could take a two-pronged approach to ensure consistent revenue throughout the year. Flagship phones, such as the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and the first-ever foldable iPhone, could be unveiled in September, while the base iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2, and the iPhone 18e could be launched in spring 2027. We discuss the foldable iPhone in detail in a separate rumor round-up, so we’ll just stick to the Pro models here. iPhone 18 Pro: Design and Colors The iPhone 17 Pro models brought a major overhaul to Apple’s smartphone design language, with a new camera “plateau” and two-toned color scheme. This year, Apple isn’t expected to drastically change the device's appearance, but it could add a few bold colors and return to a more uniform color scheme on the back. Several leakers, including Sonny Dickson and Instant Digital, claim that Apple could go with a never-before-seen cherry red and a new light blue, alongside the regular dark gray. Dickson also shared pictures of potential dummies, including one in light gray. While the appearance of the rear is expected to remain the same, the in-hand feel could be a lot different. Ice Universe says the battery could get slightly larger on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, contributing to increased weight and bulk. More precisely, the leaker expects the device to be 0.25mm thicker and 7 grams heavier. iPhone 18 Pro Display On the front, we might see one significant change. The Dynamic Island, or the camera cutout, could be reduced by 35%, Ice Universe says. This won’t shrink the feature's overall functionality, but it could move the Face ID sensor’s illuminator to one corner below the screen. When it comes to display sizes, the consensus is that the iPhone 18 Pro will come in its usual 6.3-inch screen, while the Pro Max will have a 6.9-inch screen. Apple, however, has reportedly been pushing suppliers to provide much brighter displays and could use the more power-efficient LTPO+ display tech. iPhone 18 Pro Cameras The iPhone 17 Pro lineup bumped all three cameras to 48MP. For the iPhone 18 Pro, the biggest camera-related rumor we have heard is around variable aperture. While the iPhone 17 models had a fixed aperture, the iPhone 18 Pro may introduce a variable aperture. ETNews reports that the modified system has already entered production and would help the cameras deliver more light to the sensors in dark conditions and reduce light in bright conditions. Apple may also modify its relatively new Camera Control button. Introduced with the iPhone 16, the capacitive button at the bottom right of the phone lets you quickly launch the Camera app, take pictures, and adjust settings for zoom, exposure, depth, and other controls. Mastering the capacitive button, however, has proved difficult, with users noting that they have been accidentally launching the Camera app. Apple may finally fix the problem by removing the touch-sensitive components of the button and delivering a more user-friendly experience, 9to5Mac reports. iPhone 18 Pro Performance The iPhone 18 Pro is likely to receive a performance boost with the A20 chip. It will use TSMC’s 2nm technology, an upgrade from the previous generation’s 3nm tech. The transition will allow more transistors on each chip but also raise chip costs by 50%, MacRumors reports. The chip is also rumored to have TSMC’s Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module (WMCM) technology, which infuses RAM into the same wafer as the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. Overall, it is expected to be 18% faster and 30% more power-efficient than previous generations, according to leaker Fixed Focus Digital. Apple usually reserves the base variant of its chip series for the standard iPhone models, while the Pro models get the corresponding Pro chip. With the iPhone 18 series, Apple is reportedly considering offering just the high-end variant across the lineup. Another expected upgrade is for the modem. The iPhone 17 Pro models had an unspecified third-party modem, but the iPhone 18 Pro could get the company’s proprietary C2 modem. It will support 5G satellite connectivity and reduce the scope of location data retained by networks, according to MacRumors. iPhone 18 Pro Battery Apple never reveals its battery capacities, but multiple leakers have indicated a larger and more efficient battery for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. According to Digital Chat Station, the top variant will have a capacity of up to 5,200mAh, slightly better than the 5,088mAh capacity of its predecessor. With a more efficient modem and processor, the battery life could be significantly longer. The iPhone 18 Pro, on the other hand, could see a minimal bump from 4,252mAh to 4,288mAh. More recently, leaks posted on Korean and Chinese social media sites tip a US iPhone 18 Pro Max model with a 5,567mAh battery, a nearly 10% increase over the iPhone 17 Pro Max, MacRumors notes. iPhone 18 Pro: Pricing and Release This is what much of the decision-making hinges on. Apple has avoided raising prices for its biggest revenue generator, but rising RAM and storage costs are unavoidable, by outgoing CEO Tim Cook’s own admission. Common sense suggests a price hike for iPhones is inevitable in September. According to The Wall Street Journal's estimate, rising component costs would push the iPhone 18 Pro to start at $1,299. If you couple that with recent Apple trends, the iPhone 18 Pro Max could be priced $100 higher, taking its starting price to $1,399. In comparison, the iPhone 17 Pro starts at $1,099, while the 17 Pro Max starts at $1,199. When asked on a recent earnings call about potential price hikes for the iPhone, Cook said it's "too early to come to a definitive conclusion of what happens there. Because it takes a little while for the channels to adjust since there's channel inventory, it takes a while for the consumer to respond. We'll understand that more in the weeks ahead." The iPhone 18 Pro’s release date hasn’t been finalized yet. Going by previous event dates, Sept. 9, 2026, probably makes the most sense for the announcement, with a ship date the following week, but we'll have to wait for those invitations to hit our inboxes to know for sure. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: LG's 1,000Hz Monitor Launches for $999. Is It Overkill?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.51
It might be unnecessary, but US customers can now buy a 1000Hz gaming monitor from LG. The company today kicked off sales of the LG UltraGear 25G590B, which was originally announced in May. The vendor has dubbed it the world’s first full HD gaming monitor that can run the ultra-high refresh rate natively at 1080p resolution. LG is stressing the “native 1000Hz” aspect, even though other monitors from Samsung, TCL, and Acer also offer the same refresh rate, but only as an optional mode capped at the lower 720p resolution. Thus, buyers won’t need to compromise to unleash the peak rate with LG's monitor, which the company also says can be overclocked to 1,100Hz. LG is marketing the product to esports players, claiming the monitor can give them a slight edge in first-person shooters by letting them “see faster. Aim sharper.” Theoretically, the 1,000Hz should make the motion more fluid. In a video, LG says 1,000Hz can result in “sharper visuals” and less motion blur. But it's unclear whether it’ll make a meaningful difference for actual gamers. Owners will also need a powerful GPU capable of hitting high frames per second in their games. The monitor itself uses an IPS display with a 1-millisecond response time. The 24.5-inch size was picked since it's compact enough to keep the entire screen within the player’s field of view, making it preferable for competitive gaming. To ensure you’re getting the most out of the monitor, LG says the product includes a built-in “FPS counter.” The monitor is now for sale on the company’s website for $999. It’s currently listed as a preorder, but shipments are slated to arrive as soon as Thursday, Sept. 3. “To celebrate its launch, customers who preorder by August 31, 2026, can receive two years of LG Premium Care for $1 and earn 5% back in MyLG Rewards,” the company added. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: RingCentral RingEX Review: A Powerful and Extensive VoIP Platform
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.34
RingCentral RingEX is an advanced and reliable VoIP system that caters to both large and small businesses. Far beyond just a platform for taking calls, the feature-rich RingEX lets you compose text messages to employees and clients, host video meetings, and even send faxes internally. The platform's exceptional AI abilities (including automated call summaries, an AI receptionist, and AI sentiment analysis) and comprehensive integration options are also highlights. Its interface could be clearer in some places, but RingEX is easily an Editors’ Choice winner. It shares that distinction with Intermedia Unite, which has better international calling features, and Zoom Phone, which offers compelling AI tools at a lower monthly cost. All RingCentral plans can accommodate up to 100 users; if you exceed that limit, you need to contact the company for custom pricing. A 14-day trial is available for all plans; it supports up to 20 lines. RingEx's starter Core plan ($20 per user per month, billed annually) supports unlimited calling to Canada and the US, a 100-call toll-free limit, video chats for up to 200 people, and 25 SMS messages per person per month. You also get breakout rooms and whiteboards for meetings, on-demand call recording, a multi-level interactive voice response (IVR) system, and call log reports. At this tier, you also get some AI features such as real-time notes for calls via the desktop or mobile apps, call transcriptions, and summaries of video meetings. However, you miss out on advanced call monitoring features, basic analytics, hot desking, and select integrations with CRMs and other vertical business apps. The Advanced plan ($25 per user per month, billed annually) unlocks advanced call handling features (barging, monitoring, and whispering), automatic call recording, basic analytics, hot desking, custom user roles and permissions, unlimited internal faxing, and the aforementioned CRM and business app integrations. The per-person SMS limit increases to 100 sends, the monthly toll-free call allocation goes up to 1,000 minutes, and advanced call routing rules become available. At this level, you also get AI tools for drafting and translating SMS and internal team messages. All of these perks add quite a bit of value over the base tier. Finally, the Ultra plan ($35 per user per month, billed annually) introduces 200 SMS sends per person per month, 10,000 monthly toll-free call minutes, device analytics and alerts, real-time notes for calls via desk phones, and unlimited storage for team messages, files, and recordings. The two major add-ons for RingEX are the AI Receptionist ($39 per user per month) and the Conversational Intelligence ($60 per user per month). The AI Receptionist can answer calls autonomously, provide answers to callers from an automatically generated knowledge base, and route calls (among other features). The AI Conversation Expert allows you to gauge caller sentiment, populate a CRM with call info, and even provide coaching to your employees. For comparison, Intermedia Unite charges $27.99 and $32.99 per user per month for its Pro and Enterprise plans, respectively. Those tiers include unlimited international calling to select countries (RingEX charges extra for this) and similar AI features (though AI Receptionist and Interaction Insights features are listed as coming soon). Generally, you get more SMS sends per person with Intermedia, though the core features and experience are roughly comparable. Zoom Phone, meanwhile, charges less ($16 per user per month, billed annually) for unlimited calling to Canada and the US, while still providing competitive AI and video conferencing tools. Like most communications platforms, RingEX is easy to set up. You simply log in with an email and a password. Just note that it might take you some time to digest the myriad features. You should start by setting up your company's phone numbers. Then, set aside about an hour to configure personal greetings and the IVR menu system. Using the admin portal, you can type in a phrase you want to use when someone calls the main business phone line. I added, “Welcome to the Brandon Media Empire, your call is important to us...” and laughed when I called and heard a virtual receptionist give me that greeting. I only wish the IVR settings were easier to find. In the admin portal, look for the AI tab, then the AI Receptionist option. Otherwise, setting up call monitoring and call routing takes just a few clicks. Routing worked well on all of my test calls. I appreciate that RingCentral doesn't require you to go through many of its configuration wizards. You can simply navigate directly to the setup interfaces you want. Guidance is still available if you need it. RingEX makes it easy to set up deep connections with various CRM, including HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics, and Salesforce. A new App Connect browser extension allows you to log communications directly in about 20 different CRMs. Should your business needs change, RingCentral also offers a smooth upgrade path to its RingCX call center product; it uses the same interface and accepts the same login credentials. RingEX’s user experience is attractive and intuitive; its interface looks remarkably similar to that of a standard business messaging app, such as Slack or Microsoft Teams. A row of icons on the left lets you quickly access fax, phone, texting, and video call functions, and a large search box lives at the top of the screen. In seconds, you can ring up a new client, hold a video chat with your boss, or even fax a contract. I appreciate the app's use of a bright orange color to highlight important sections and settings. I feel more productive using RingEX versus a service such as Zoho Voice, which uses a bland, mostly white color scheme. I mostly tested RingEX on the web and via its Android and iOS apps, but it also offers desktop apps for macOS and Windows. All iterations are straightforward and feel snappy to navigate. The mobile apps retain many of the features from the desktop and web versions. For example, I was able to access a task list, pull up faxes, and view analytics from the mobile app. If you have issues with setup or administrative tasks, RingEX offers 24/7 chat and phone support. Email support is also available; in my experience, a support tech tends to respond within about an hour. In testing, I emailed support about setting up the voicemail system for employees and how to set a company greeting. A representative responded with helpful instructions and tips. Not many competitors offer 24/7 support across all plans, but Zoho Voice plans include 24/5 chat, email, and phone support for comparison. Importing contacts is a bit confusing at first. I initially expected to be able to do this in the app's Contacts section, but you must go to the admin portal instead. A link to the latter in the Contacts section would help clarify things. I also had to rearrange the columns of data (such as email and phone number) in my test spreadsheet for the import process to work, though that's not a big deal. You can import contacts individually or in bulk. RingEX provides a novel option for the latter: you can customize the template first (say, by adding a fax number field or removing the middle name) and then download and use the resulting CSV file. You can also sync contacts via your Google or Microsoft account, which works fine. As mentioned, the mobile apps function effectively as softphones. RingEX also supports several dozen brands of traditional desktop phones. It offers to sell you phones, or you can bring in existing devices. Supported brands include Alcatel, Cisco, and Poly. As for headsets, RingEX works with models from Poly, Jabra, and Yealink. Intermedia Unite compares favorably here. It sells branded phones and supports models from Poly and Yealink. Both RingEX and Intermedia also let you integrate existing phone hardware. As for third-party software integrations, RingEX's App Gallery is second to none. Aside from supporting all the standard Google and Microsoft services, dozens of options are available. As mentioned, plenty of CRMs are available to connect via App Connect. Intermedia Unite supports the core business apps you will likely need, but you need to rely on its Extend API to connect other services, including many CRMs. Making calls with RingEX couldn't be easier. Every test call sounded pristine regardless of the platform and who was on the other end of the line. I enjoyed seeing both a call summary and real-time transcription of conversations, courtesy of the AI assistant. The real-time transcription is especially impressive. I read a page from a book aloud to test it, and RingEX captured what I said almost perfectly, missing just a few phrases and names. As mentioned, the AI Assistant can also help you compose SMS text messages with a click (if you subscribe to at least the Advanced tier). RingEX also handles video meetings without a problem. It supports screen sharing and recordings, while the AI Assistant lets you review portions of a meeting where specific people were speaking and determine who spoke the most. You can now track call sentiment (such as the overall tone or if anyone became angry or upset), but only by adding the aforementioned Conversational Intelligence add-on (also called AI Conversation Expert, or ACE). This feature works only with calls of at least two minutes and requires some time to analyze the conversation. In a test call, the bot accurately generated action items and gauged the sentiment as neutral (and not requiring immediate action). The system generally works as advertised to evaluate whether an issue is resolved, rather than simply identifying the customer's tone. However, in another test call, ACE stopped working and didn’t save the recording correctly. I expect RingCentral to address the stability issues. Meanwhile, the AI Receptionist add-on is quite powerful. When someone calls in or texts, the AI assistant can handle everything on its own, whether that means scheduling an appointment, resolving a complex issue, or routing a call to a specific person. In testing, I set up an AI receptionist for the PCMag site. Like magic, the AI created a knowledge base and configured the voice and persona (called Natalie). During test calls and a text message exchange, I asked about PCMag's coverage areas and got accurate answers. The add-on seems worth its $39-per-month cost if you are looking to reduce human workloads. Analytics runs in a separate tab rather than in the main RingEX interface, which can be a little confusing at first. I would prefer if the reporting tools were part of the main interface. Nonetheless, the features on offer are extensive and allow you to get a quick snapshot of call quality for every agent, check call volume against established service-level agreements, and see the number of text messages processed. All the reports are colorful, easily accessible, and quick to digest. If you pay for the AI Receptionist add-on, you can also view extensive analytics about its activity, including how many calls it resolved without human involvement. Although you can't build custom reports in the traditional sense, you can adjust the filters and time frames for any report and save it for reuse. I also like that you can suggest an idea for a new report. This level of customization matches what's available in Intermedia Unite; it also doesn’t let you build reports from scratch (unless you upgrade to the full Contact Center product). RingEX supports multi-factor authentication, and its privacy policy is both reasonably up to date and easy to understand. You can optionally encrypt all calls and SMS messages. You can read about recent security notices here, the latest of which involved a sophisticated social engineering campaign. Final Thoughts RingCentral RingEX - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. RingEX is a powerful AI-enabled communications service that helps businesses connect internally and externally via calls, text messages, and video meetings. I especially like its comprehensive support for third-party apps, modern user experience, and overall reliability in testing. The new AI Receptionist add-on also stands out for its ability to bolster productivity. Some parts of the app feel a bit complex due to the sheer number of available features, but that doesn't prevent RingEX from earning our Editors' Choice award. Intermedia Unite, which offers better international calling support, and Zoom Phone, which costs less, are also Editors' Choice winners. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert I'm a technologist, business writer, and book author. I first started writing in 2001, after I was downsized from a corporate job. In the early days of my writing career, I wrote features about biometrics and reviews of Wi-Fi routers and laptops for Laptop Magazine. My first feature stories and reviews for PCMag appeared in print circa 2004. Since 2001, I have published more than 15,000 articles, including business columns for Inc. and Forbes.

item.title: Don’t Buy an iMac Right Now: Apple May Be Readying a New M6 Version
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.31
A refreshed iMac joins the long list of rumored upcoming Apple products, according to a report by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. The new rumor included in Gurman’s latest Power On newsletter says a new model is imminent and may be on sale before the end of the year. Gurman says the iMac will remain similar to what we’ve seen before, keeping the same overall design and focusing on new internals. Gurman says to expect new color options as the main aesthetic change, though he doesn’t specify which ones. Apple’s current iMac comes in blue, green, orange, pink, purple, silver, and yellow. The latest iMac model launched in October 2024 with an M4 processor doing the heavy lifting, so it would make sense for Apple to overhaul its internals. Apple has kept this overall look and design for its iMac since it brought the desktop back with an M1 chip in 2021. We then saw a refresh that included the M3, before the latest version with an M4. If you wait for an M6 iMac, you’ll have the choice of the latest model, or you may be able to find the M4 version for less from other retailers as they clear out stock. However, Apple may not be ready to drop its prices, given that it raised the iMac from $1,299 to $1,499 in late June. It's unclear how much a new M6 iMac will cost. Other rumored Apple announcements, alongside its first foldable phone and the iPhone 18 Pro series, include smart home gadgets such as new Siri speakers, with one expected to include a screen to compete with devices like the Amazon Echo Show and Google Home Hub. Gurman’s latest report also references sources who have tried Apple’s first attempt at a foldable phone, saying many testers couldn’t be more excited after trialing the device. They cite the form factor, the durability of the hinge, and the iPad-like layout from using the inner display as highlights of the experience. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: ChatGPT vs. Gemini: Don't Pick a Chatbot Until You Read This
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.97
Table of Contents If you’re interested in trying out an AI chatbot, ChatGPT and Gemini are two of the biggest names in the space. However, they’re very different services. For example, whereas ChatGPT focuses on providing the most powerful models possible, Gemini prioritizes deep integrations across Google apps and a broader feature set. And that's just one important distinction. I've spent years testing both chatbots and am here to compare them across several key categories, from context windows to image generation to platform support, to help you pick between them. Full Specs | ChatGPT | Google Gemini | | |---|---|---| | Free Version | | | | Free Version | | | | AI Model | | | | AI Model | GPT-5.6 | 3.7 Flash and 3.1 Pro | | Cites Sources | | | | Cites Sources | | | | Ability to Browse Web | | | | Ability to Browse Web | | | | Can Resume Prior Conversations | | | | Can Resume Prior Conversations | | | | Image Generator | | | | Image Generator | | | Price: Gemini Is a Far Better Value Both ChatGPT and Gemini have free versions that limit your access to features and models. Premium plans start at $8 per month for ChatGPT Go and $4.99 per month for Google AI Plus. The chatbots generally support similar features, such as deep research, image generation, web search, and more. However, Gemini plans also include Google Drive cloud storage (starting at 15GB for free), a robust suite of integrations across Google apps, and video generation, making it a much stronger value. The more expensive tiers of ChatGPT and Gemini unlock higher usage limits, more advanced models, and unique features, such as complex reasoning models with ChatGPT Plus ($20 per month) or Google’s Antigravity coding app with Google AI Pro ($20 per month). Which plan is right for you depends on what you plan to use an AI chatbot to do and how often. As such, I can't pick out any of the plans as obviously the best for most people. Winner: Gemini Platform and Ease of Use: Both Are Available Everywhere You can access ChatGPT and Gemini on the web or through mobile apps (Android and iOS). ChatGPT also has desktop apps (macOS and Windows) and an official extension for Google Chrome. Gemini has a macOS app, and you can also access some of Gemini’s features in the Google app on Windows. Gemini integrates directly into Chrome, of course. Whereas ChatGPT's Codex interface for coding is a part of the main app, Google maintains the separate Antigravity app for coding. ChatGPT is available elsewhere, too, such as through Siri. As mentioned, you can access Gemini across Google apps, such as Calendar, Docs, Drive, Gmail, Maps, Notebook, Keep, Photos, Sheets, and YouTube Music. Both ChatGPT’s and Gemini’s models also appear on sites like Perplexity. However, you get the most features out of these chatbots via their dedicated apps and web portals. OpenAI doesn’t make much hardware, but Google integrates Gemini across its Chromebook Plus line of laptops and has plans for Google Books. The interfaces of both chatbots are largely consistent across platforms. They are easy to use and don't overwhelm you with options and toggles. However, ChatGPT offers more settings to tweak than Gemini, including options to customize its models' personalities during chat. Winner: Tie AI Models: Dedicated Options for Complex Reasoning and Speed ChatGPT’s current lineup of models, the 5.6 series, has three major versions: Luna, Terra, and Sol. Luna is efficient and quick, Terra is balanced with midrange intelligence, and Sol is OpenAI’s most capable model. After selecting a model, you can also adjust its intelligence to achieve your ideal blend of efficiency and power for your prompt. Gemini offers Flash and Pro variants of its models. Whereas Flash is suitable for simpler tasks and speed, Pro is a complex reasoning model better suited to tougher tasks. You can’t adjust the intelligence levels of the models in Gemini’s chatbot interface, something you can do in the Antigravity app. However, you can enable extended thinking for both the Flash and Pro models to tackle tougher prompts. At the time of writing, GPT-5.6 is ChatGPT’s latest model series, while Gemini’s newest model is 3.7 Flash. Below, you can see how these models handle different prompts. Winner: Tie Web Search: ChatGPT Goes Deeper With Queries ChatGPT and Gemini can easily search for up-to-date information on the web and source it well. However, if you engage ChatGPT’s most intelligent models, you get deeper, more accurate responses to prompts than with Gemini’s Pro model. For example, when I asked Gemini 3.1 Pro (with extended thinking enabled) to tell me what the current meta is on The Finals, it gave me incorrect information, unlike ChatGPT. As part of their web search experiences, ChatGPT and Gemini can also help you shop. If you ask for buying advice, both present clickable tiles with links to retailers. Neither is a great resource for deciding what to buy, but Gemini uniquely lets you upload a photo of yourself to virtually try on clothes. However, this feature helps you only with the look, not the fit, so it's of limited usefulness. Winner: ChatGPT Deep Research: Both Are Effective Research Tools ChatGPT and Gemini can both generate reports that are dozens of pages long and include tons of sources on just about any topic. For example, when I was deciding on a microwave to buy, neither had trouble generating in-depth reports comparing potential options across a variety of different categories. Gemini’s report interface is easier to navigate. It has some quality-of-life features ChatGPT lacks, such as a one-click way to export reports to Google Docs. The quality of reports is usually a match, with both ChatGPT and Gemini sometimes doing a better job. Gemini can complete research more quickly, but not always. In general, I prefer ChatGPT’s reports, but my colleague Lance Whitney prefers Gemini’s, so which is more useful is a matter of personal preference. Winner: Tie Image Editing and Generation: Gemini Excels at Editing Both ChatGPT’s and Gemini’s image generation tech is among the best available, whether you're making complex diagrams with lots of text, narrative-driven comics, or simple images. Errors and distortions are minimal. However, with AI image editing, Gemini tends to better preserve the original image's color and introduce fewer artifacts, albeit at the cost of increased blur. Above, you can see how ChatGPT (first slide) and Gemini (second slide) fared with the following prompt: "Generate me an image of a cozy suburban home with an open floor plan. I want to see a nice living space with a dining room, kitchen, and living room. Nothing too fancy.” Above, you can see how ChatGPT (first slide) and Gemini (second slide) removed a distracting hand from an image (third slide). ChatGPT significantly pumps up the contrast and saturation of the edited image and tessellates the leaves on the trees. Winner: Gemini Video Generation: No Support From ChatGPT ChatGPT used to generate videos through its Sora model, which was highly competitive. However, OpenAI has since shut it down. Gemini’s Omni and Veo models continue to work exceptionally well, generating realistic videos with audio. You can even use Veo's Flow tool to extend generated clips and create more cohesive scenes. Gemini’s video generation isn’t perfect, though, so you will need to tweak your prompt across multiple generations to get something you're happy with. Winner: Gemini File Processing: ChatGPT’s Image Recognition Impresses Both ChatGPT and Gemini can process a wide variety of files. Whether you want them to answer questions about a manual, edit a resume, or tell you something about an image, neither disappoints. However, image recognition is a particular strength of ChatGPT, and it can understand complex images more effectively. For example, when I provided both bots with a picture of my computer's internals, ChatGPT correctly identified more components with greater specificity than Gemini. Both chatbots still sometimes fabricate quotes from the provided documents or misinterpret images, so make sure to double-check their results. Winner: ChatGPT Creative Writing: Handle Any Writing Task Easily ChatGPT (first slide) and Gemini (second slide) can both generate generally competent poems, plays, stories, and more. Just keep in mind that chatbot writing tends to feel generic, due to repetitive phrasing, topic selection, and word choice. For example, I asked both ChatGPT and Gemini to write me a free-verse poem, and both chose to write about the interior of a house, mentioning rain and streetlights in the first few stanzas. Winner: Tie Complex Reasoning: ChatGPT Is the Star Gemini can handle most computer science, math, and physics questions with ease and competently show its work. However, Gemini’s complex reasoning models can’t quite match the intelligence of ChatGPT’s, which routinely think more deeply and give higher-quality answers. Of course, whether this is an issue depends on the specific prompt. Both chatbots can and will also give you incorrect answers, so double-checking their work is vital if you’re doing anything important. Winner: ChatGPT Coding: Gemini Can’t Compete With ChatGPT Gemini impresses with its speed when coding, but otherwise, it just can’t keep up with ChatGPT. ChatGPT’s models, such as GPT-5.6 Sol at the highest intelligence setting, are vastly more intelligent than Gemini’s models and can complete more complex coding tasks with fewer issues. Beyond simple tasks, I don’t recommend relying on Gemini’s models for coding, unless you’re an experienced programmer who can properly oversee its work. Winner: ChatGPT Integrations: Impressive AI Connections Across the Google Suite ChatGPT integrates with plenty of consumer apps, such as Google Drive and Slack, and professional tools, such as GitHub or Monday. Essentially, you can prompt GPT about your information and data within these apps. Meanwhile, Gemini is built directly into Google’s apps, making it more convenient. Whether you want to ask a question about a shared Chrome tab, get help with editing an essay in Google Docs, hear ideas for a new curated YouTube Music playlist, unlock personal insights in Gmail, or upgrade your YouTube watching experience, Gemini can do all that and much more. It’s difficult to understate the power and comprehensiveness of Gemini’s integrations. Winner: Gemini Agents: Gemini Spark Is Tough to Beat Gemini Spark isn’t perfect, but it’s my favorite AI agent to date, thanks to its impressive performance and speed. Since Spark can also leverage Gemini’s Personal Intelligence and whatever information it needs across your connected Google apps, it can be an invaluable way to automate tasks. Meanwhile, ChatGPT recently discontinued its AI agent. Winner: Gemini Context Windows and Usage Caps: More Context With Gemini ChatGPT’s context window goes up to 400,000 tokens on its highest-tier plan, and the more expensive the plan, the higher your weekly usage limit. However, text chat with ChatGPT is technically unlimited, so long as it remains “reasonable.” Gemini has a similar weekly usage cap but a context window of up to 1,000,000 tokens. In general, if you aren’t coding, you likely won’t need an expensive plan for either chatbot to use it as much as you want. However, it’s much easier to run into usage caps on either chatbot's free plan. Winner: Gemini Privacy: Everybody Wants Your Data for Training Privacy on ChatGPT and Gemini is a mixed bag. Both collect significant amounts of data, including all your chats, and use that data to train their AI models by default. However, both options let you turn training off. Google, at least, doesn’t collect and use Gemini data for training purposes in Workspace apps by default. Google and OpenAI both have sordid histories of hacks, leaks, and other digital wrongdoings, so I strongly caution against sharing anything too sensitive with either. Here's how they rank on privacy, and what ChatGPT knows about you. Winner: Tie Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. And The Winner Is... ChatGPT Although ChatGPT and Gemini are both quality chatbots with impressive specialties, the former wins this comparison. Between ChatGPT's peerless response quality, excellent file recognition capabilities, and unbeatable vibe coding tools, it's decidedly the most technically advanced AI service I've tested. Other aspects, such as its competitive image generation features and robust third-party app integrations, also solidify its status as the chatbot to beat. Still, Gemini is objectively a much better value, with deep connections across Google's ecosystem and class-leading video generation abilities. If you spend significant amounts of time in the Google apps, Gemini could well be the better chatbot for you.

item.title: Thousands Are Calling, Chatting With Starlink's AI To Place Orders
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.97
While Starlink.com has long been the official storefront for SpaceX’s satellite internet service, a large number of customers are also talking with Starlink’s chatbot to place orders, including through phone calls. On Monday, SpaceX shed some light on the company’s efforts to use the company’s Grok AI for Starlink’s customer support. The same chatbot has also been answering calls over the company’s hotline at 1-888-GO-STARLINK (888-467-8275), which SpaceX has been advertising over its website and through video commercials. The company’s AI business reports the voice-based version of Grok has not only been handling customer issues, but also driving new sales. “At Starlink, we’re using Grok Voice to resolve over 15,000 inbound customer support and sales calls a day,” SpaceXAI wrote in a tweet. (Back in February, the company officially absorbed Elon Musk’s startup xAI.) In the same tweet, the company added: “Grok diagnoses hardware issues, ships replacements, and fulfills over 3,000 orders a week across voice calls and chat.” Although the company didn’t give a detailed breakdown on the orders, the tweet does give a glimpse at the customer support volume. The chat function has also been available on Starlink.com, giving interested customers a way to start a conversation with the AI chatbot. Last year, SpaceX introduced the Grok-powered AI support into the Starlink app before expanding it to the Starlink.com site. In April, we then spotted Starlink’s customer support using Grok to handle calls over the 888-GO-STARLINK number. The same chatbot can also arrange for a human Starlink representative to call you back. The Grok integration might help Starlink address its customer support, which has been infamous for being slow or even non-responsive. In the past, some users have reported quick response times and free hardware replacements, but others have complained about needing to wait for days to resolve their issue. On top of this, Starlink had long pushed users to file a customer support ticket online, and only began trialing a dedicated customer support hotline in the US and Canada back in 2024. That said, the Grok integration isn’t perfect. Last month, one customer complained to PCMag about Starlink customer support, alleging the AI chatbot failed to honor the free Mini dish perk for their Residential Max plan. That's possibly because Starlink had briefly discontinued the perk, but not before the customer had already subscribed to the the Max plan, a nuance the AI may have failed to understand. The same chatbot can also struggle to offer the correct solution to replace older Starlink Gen 2 routers that brick, and overlook a key compatibility issue, according to the YouTube channel DISHYtech. Hence, reaching out to a human Starlink representative might still be needed for more complex issues. In the meantime, SpaceX is touting Grok Voice to pitch it as a customer support tool for interested businesses. The latest version, “Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0,” is being priced at $0.08 per minute of audio. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Too Many Texts? 'Pigeon Messaging' Apps Aim to Slow Things Down
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.88
Modern technology has made our lives easier, but it also brings a barrage of notifications and the pressure to be available 24-7. If you're digitally detoxing or you find it difficult to cope with the quick back-and-forth of messaging services like iMessage or WhatsApp, a new, somewhat gimmicky trick might work for you. As USA Today reports, two recently released apps, Carrier Pidge and Roost Social, aim to slow the rate at which you talk to friends and family, emulating a return to the days of carrier pigeons. Carrier Pidge sends your message at a rate of 110 miles per hour using GPS tech on your phone and the location of whoever you're messaging. “A text across town? A few seconds. A message across the country? Hours," the tagline reads. It’s also designed with what the developers call a “whimsical pigeon fate system,” which means that 0.2% of messages won’t be sent at all. It’s designed to emulate a pigeon getting lost mid-flight, so neither you nor the sender will know it didn't arrive. Roost Social is a similar idea with a real-time messaging mechanic and a way to watch your messages travel across the globe. There’s no pigeon fate system, but it comes with more breeds of birds, allowing you to change the speed of messages and even level up your flock. These minigames help you boost your bird's speed, as if you were training it yourself. In the US, Carrier Pidge ranks 76 among Social Networking apps on the App Store, while Roost Social ranks 95. Neither will take on the might of WhatsApp, Telegram, or iMessage anytime soon, but they’re both exciting for anyone looking to take their foot off the gas a little. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Apple's Foldable iPhone Reportedly Impressed Early Testers
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.71
We’re weeks away from the potential launch of Apple’s first foldable, and a new report based on early impressions suggests the device is one of Apple’s most exciting products in recent years. The rumored iPhone Ultra is expected to feature a passport-style form factor similar to Samsung’s recently launched Galaxy Z Fold 8, along with a nearly crease-free 7.8-inch internal display, a 5.5-inch cover display, and a dual-camera system on the rear. People who have already tried the device are impressed with how it fits in their pockets, the durability of the hinge, and the iPad-like layout of the internal display, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. Some testers also noted that the Ultra excels as a camera viewfinder, while performing decently across gaming, productivity, and entertainment. Gurman expects the iPhone Ultra to popularize the foldables segment and convince some users to purchase one. They may, however, face two major drawbacks. First, since the Ultra only offers a dual-camera setup, some users may miss the telephoto lens for optical zoom. Second, those accustomed to Face ID may not enjoy going back to the Touch ID fingerprint sensor, he says. As always, there’s a lot of buzz around Apple’s entry into a new segment. The company is expected to unveil the foldable at its annual fall event, rumored for Sept. 8, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro models. According to multiple leakers, the iPhone Ultra will be available in limited supply at launch and could be priced above $2,000. Gurman also noted that Apple may increase the price of other iPhones due to rising memory costs. It raised prices of its Macs, iPads, and Vision Pro for the same reason in June. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Is Claude Down? Anthropic Says It Fixed the Latest AI Outage
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.61
UPDATE 6:15 a.m. ET: Anthropic says the issues that caused an hours-long outage have been resolved, claiming all of its systems are now operational. The AI company has yet to explain what caused the outage, and it's unclear whether it plans to do so. Original Story: Having problems connecting with Claude AI this morning? You’re not alone with many struggling to connect to Anthropic’s tools during an hours-long outage. Reports of issues on Downdetector began at 12:30 a.m. ET on Aug. 24 and continued for an hour before Anthropic officially acknowledged an issue. An update at 1:27 a.m. ET saw Anthropic say the issue caused "elevated errors on requests to Claude Mythos 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, and other Claude models." At 3:47 a.m. ET, Anthropic said, "At this time, we have seen errors stabilize on Opus 5 and Fable 5, and are working to fully resolve success rates on all affected models. We will provide an update as soon as possible." That's the latest we've heard from Anthropic, but failure rates reported through Downdetector are dropping, suggesting more people are able to connect to the correct tools. If you continue to see issues, you will have to await further news from Anthropic. We've yet to find out exactly what caused this issue, but we expect to hear from the artificial intelligence tool's creator later to learn the cause of this latest outage. Anthropic also uses its status page to boast about its outage stats, claiming 99.29% uptime for claude.ai tools over the last 60 days. A large percentage of its included downtime comes from the last few hours, although it routinely sees small pockets of issues that cause minor outages that don't usually last this long.
