item.title: Proton Mail Review: Complete Inbox Security Made Simple
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.33
Your free email account from Google, Yahoo, or Microsoft isn’t really free—you pay with your privacy by allowing the provider to track your activity and target ads, among other things. If you’re interested in minimizing the exposure of your private activities, consider switching to an encrypted email provider that puts your security first, like Proton Mail. All your messaging with other Proton users is end-to-end encrypted, and you can exchange password-protected mail with non-users. You can even manage your Gmail within Proton, hiding it from Google. Other bonuses range from dark web monitoring to an AI assistant for writing messages. You can also use it at no charge, though paying for an account removes some limits and enables advanced features. Proton Mail’s effective encryption and wealth of bonus apps make it an Editors’ Choice for encrypted email, an honor it shares with the completely free PreVeil. You can use Proton Mail at no cost, and I recommend starting with the free edition to see how it suits you. If you like it fine but run up against its limitations, or if you want those enticing premium-only features, you can upgrade to the Plus edition for $3.99 per month, billed annually at $47.88. At the Unlimited level, you pay $9.99 per month, billed as $119.88 per year. That sounds a little high until you learn that the Unlimited subscription gets you full access to almost all of Proton’s security tools, which I’ll discuss below. Some competing services cost more than Proton’s Plus edition. For example, a year of Private-Mail costs $69.99, while a year of StartMail costs $59.88. However, SecureMyEmail is $29.88 per year, and you can get a year of Tuta Mail for 36 euros ($42.06 at the time of this writing). Tuta Mail, like Proton Mail, includes a calendar even on its free tier; unlike Proton Mail, it doesn’t limit the number of messages for free users. Tuta Mail's free edition limits how far back you can search your messages. Paying for a premium account lifts this limit. With Proton Mail, searching message content is a free feature that involves creating and maintaining an encrypted local index on your device. In some cases, you pay nothing at all for your email encryption. As the name suggests, Virtru Email Protection for Gmail works only with Gmail, but it doesn’t cost anything. PreVeil is a free and full-featured email encryption system that lets you keep your existing email address. You may remember hearing that Gmail always uses a secure HTTPS connection. When it sends your messages, it uses the standard TLS (Transport Layer Security) to protect your data in transit. However, it's easy to accidentally give mail-reading permission to third-party apps. And despite claims that Gmail no longer reads your email, it does read your messages well enough to automatically add airline flight notifications to your calendar or create summaries of longer messages. Google has a policy on when and how it releases your email to government entities, clearly stating that it may do so if compelled. Using HTTPS is table stakes these days—your browser will warn you if you connect to a site that does not have HTTPS enabled. Proton Mail uses an HTTPS connection, naturally, but it doesn't stop there. Before it securely sends your messages, it encrypts them using public-key cryptography. It stores your messages locally in zero-knowledge encrypted form, meaning only you can access them. A disgruntled employee can’t rummage through your Proton Mail messages, and the best subpoena in the world can’t force the company to turn over your account. When you communicate with another Proton Mail user, the connection is encrypted end-to-end. Note, too, that Proton Mail is based in Switzerland, which has stricter privacy policies than the US. It's also an open-source project, meaning experts can review and vet its security algorithms. While Gmail and its ilk have some security features, Proton Mail goes way beyond them. Setting up a free Proton Mail account is a cinch. You start by picking a username. As with any webmail service, this name must be unique, but given the smaller pool of users compared with a giant like Gmail or Yahoo, you might be able to snag a name like elonmusk rather than elonmusk_271828. Proton.me is the default domain for your account, though the legacy protonmail.com is also an option. Paying users can enable the short-form domain pm.me. After that, you need to set a strong password to protect your account and provide an optional recovery email address, phone number, or both. As a final step, verify that you're human by completing a simple CAPTCHA or by entering a code sent to another email address or via SMS. Along the way, you choose a theme, or you can wait to dig into the full list of eight themes (five light and three dark) in Settings later. When you open your new account, a few welcome and explanatory messages from Proton Mail await you. One may be of particular interest: with a free account, you get 500 MB of storage for your messages and files. It also notes that by taking four specific actions, such as loading the Proton app on your mobile device, you can double that storage allotment. You can also just start using the service. Since my last review, a couple of invitations have appeared for your new account. Proton invites you to connect directly with your Gmail account, for one. I’ll cover that useful feature below. It also offers to organize your inbox into categories such as Primary, Social, and Promotions, much the way Gmail does. If you've used Gmail, Yahoo, or any other webmail system, you already know how to use Proton Mail. A left-rail menu selects among folders; a middle panel displays the messages in the selected folder; and the rest of the window displays the selected message. You can optionally activate a right-side panel to display your contacts or view Proton Calendar. Other icons along the right edge of the window take you to the security center, invoke Proton VPN, or manage referrals. The referral system is generous—you get $20 for each friend who signs up for a paid Proton Mail account, up to a maximum of $1,000. And the friend also gets $20 in credits. Migration: Easy Switch Takes the Friction Out of Leaving Big Tech Proton's helpful Easy Switch feature can pull in messages, contacts, and calendar events from your existing email account. The app offers specific instructions for Google, Yahoo, and Outlook, as well as details for configuring other providers to enable IMAP and other necessary settings. Once your old account is ready, you open Settings, click Import via Easy Switch, and follow the prompts. I was surprised when the app displayed a note saying, “Large imports may take several days.” My contact at Proton Mail explained that the process can get throttled at the provider’s end. For example, Google's API restrictions permit only 2.5GB of exports per day. The initial import won’t fill your Proton storage past 80%, though you can import more later. Once the import process has started, you can resume using Proton Mail. If you get curious about how it’s going, check the progress bar in the list of current and past imports on the Easy Switch page. Going the other direction, the Proton Mail Bridge lets paying customers manage Proton Mail in their favorite email client by making messages available via IMAP. I didn’t try this feature, but it’s available for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Gmail Integration: Secure Your Existing Google Inbox Importing existing email messages captures your account at a single point in time. You can repeat the process to catch newer messages, and Proton is smart enough not to create duplicates. But importing data doesn’t maintain a connection. New since my last review, you can create an ongoing connection, at least with a Gmail account. This feature has rolled out gradually over the past few months, but all Proton Mail users should have it now. The first time you log in after receiving the upgrade, Proton invites you to send and receive Gmail messages securely, right inside the Proton Mail app. The welcome screen for connecting your Gmail points out the many benefits. Proton Mail filters out ads and tracking images, so those won’t affect you. And when you manage your Gmail messages through Proton, Google doesn’t learn anything about your correspondence. Once you’ve connected your Gmail account, you can access it from any of your Proton Mail installations. You do have to remember not to connect to Gmail in your accustomed fashion. If you open your Gmail account without going through Proton Mail, you bypass its protection. Hands-On Usability: Familiar Design, Hardened Security Emailing with Proton Mail is not much different from using any other webmail service. Composing messages, viewing replies, and forwarding mail all work just as you'd expect. There are a few security-related differences. For example, if you click a link, a warning appears, and you are prompted to confirm before opening it. A blue lock icon next to an address in the header indicates that the address belongs to a fellow Proton Mail user. Pointing to the lock displays a floating tip that says "End-to-End Encrypted." You can define a signature, with formatting, that Proton Mail will apply to all your messages. It also adds a note, "Sent with Proton Mail Secure Email." Only paying customers can modify that note. At its simplest, Proton Mail automatically applies end-to-end encryption on every email conversation you have with another Proton Mail user. If you can get your circle of correspondents to convert to Proton, there’s no further effort needed. But Proton Mail’s security capabilities don’t end there. You can also encrypt your communications with non-users and protect your account in various ways. Embedded Images: View High-Res Graphics Without Giving Away Your IP Sneaky tracking companies can get information about you simply by sending an email with an embedded (and possibly invisible) image. When your email client renders that image, the tracker knows that you've opened the message and receives your IP address. This chicanery is the reason that many secure email services simply don't display images by default. Private-Mail goes even further, stripping out all formatting. Years ago, Proton Mail ran with the pack, suppressing image display unless you explicitly requested it. At present, Proton Mail can display your email messages in all their image-rich glory without giving anything away to trackers. It specifically quashes tracking images and reports that it did so. But even for legitimate images, it prevents the sender from receiving your IP address. I found this hard to believe, since requesting the image for display necessarily requires telling the server what IP address made the request. Wouldn't you need something like a VPN to hide that detail? My Proton Mail contact explained that this feature indeed works much like a VPN. Proton Mail, acting as a proxy, requests the image and caches it on its own servers. Then it sends the cached image to your computer without ever revealing your IP address. I don't know of any similar service that performs this neat trick. External Communications: Proton Mail Offers Password Encryption and Message Expiration On Windows or macOS, a lock icon below the main body of the message lets you send an encrypted message to recipients who don’t use Proton Mail. You tap the three-dot menu near the lock to control your encrypted message’s expiration. In the mobile app, an hourglass icon takes you to expiration control. When you encrypt a message for someone not using Proton Mail, you set a password and optionally a password hint. Naturally, you must transmit that password via some other channel, perhaps an encrypted messaging app. By default, encrypted messages to those not using Proton Mail expire after 28 days, though you can disable expiry or set a shorter expiration time, right down to a single hour. Messages between Proton Mail users don't expire. When your correspondent receives the message, it includes an explanation and a link to view the message online. The recipient simply enters the password to see your important missive. A banner above the message body counts down to the message's expiration. StartMail, another encrypted email service, offers a similar method for secure communication with non-users, but it doesn't support automated message expiry. With SecureMyEmail, messages outside the network don’t require a password; the recipient’s ability to log into the email account is considered sufficient. You can add a password if you wish, and out-of-network messages expire in 30 days by default. The Proton Mail mobile apps do have a few features not found in the web-based app. You can enable face or fingerprint authentication and define actions for left and right swipes. By default, swiping to the right trashes a message, while swiping left marks it as spam. You can also set a mobile signature, distinct from the regular signature. PGP Available: Proton Mail Supports Public Key Cryptography You only get automatic end-to-end encryption when corresponding with other Proton Mail users. However, if you’re a tech whiz and have tech-savvy friends who've implemented PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) email encryption, you can set up fully encrypted communication with them. When you compose a message, there's a simple menu option to attach your public key. After that, it's up to the recipient to enter that key into their PGP-aware email system. Using PGP outside Proton Mail requires specialized expertise, but it's still available. If you make significant use of this feature, you have some options to make using PGP easier. In the settings, you can configure Proton Mail to digitally sign all your outgoing mail using your public key and to attach that key to all outgoing messages. SecureMyEmail uses PGP internally but hides the key exchange process by default. As with Proton Mail, you can dig in and set up PGP-secured communication with your geeky friends. StartMail and Private-Mail both work in a similar fashion, but with a tad more awkwardness. Enhanced Authentication: Added Protection for Your Email Trove One useful security feature offered with Gmail is multi-factor authentication. Naturally, Proton Mail includes this feature. To prepare for multi-factor authentication, you must equip your smartphone with Google Authenticator or a compatible authenticator app. Then open Settings, click Account and Password, and click to enable multi-factor authentication. As usual, you snap the QR code to add Proton Mail to your authenticator. Now, even if a sneak thief gets hold of your password, your encrypted messages are safe. During this process, Proton Mail displays a collection of one-time emergency passcodes. Copy this collection and put it in a safe place. If you lose your phone or it goes kaput, you can still access your account with one of those codes. Proton supports authentication using a hardware security key. You can only do this after you've enabled an authenticator app, because not all devices are compatible with security keys. Setting up this powerful authentication couldn't be easier. You simply register your security key by inserting it into a USB port and touching it. Key-based authentication is as simple as inserting a key or touching one that's already mounted in a USB port. You can register multiple keys, in case you might lose one. As part of the setup process, Proton Mail asks you to name each key so that you can tell them apart. Note that this feature is available even to those using the free edition. Security Center: All Your Security Settings in One Place When I last reviewed Proton Mail, it had a skinny menu on the right side containing only icons for accessing your contacts and calendar. That menu now has icons for Proton VPN and for the referrals system mentioned earlier. Most importantly, it has an icon for the new Security Center. The Security Center menu lets you quickly jump to the multi-factor authentication configuration panel described above. It also lets you enable Proton Sentinel and Dark Web Monitoring, paid features I’ll discuss below. At the top of the Security Center page is the option to create hide-my-email aliases. As with other temporary email services, Proton Mail lets you create email aliases for online shopping and such. The merchant site never sees your actual email address, just the alias. As you send and receive messages, you don’t have to think about the alias. Proton Mail takes care of it. If one of your email aliases starts to receive spam, you can simply delete it. And if you’ve been careful to use a different alias for every merchant, you know which one sold your email. Even users on the free tier can use up to 10 hide-my-email aliases. That cap remains in place for paid Proton Mail Plus users, but at the Unlimited tier, there is—surprise!—no limit. When I last evaluated Proton Mail, it included a subscription to SimpleLogin, which Proton acquired in 2022. It seems that SimpleLogin’s temporary email services have been integrated into the main Proton Mail app. Use of SimpleLogin domains, such as aleeas.com, emphasizes the connection. Session Control: Monitor Active Devices and Remote Logouts On the Settings page, under Security and Privacy, you’ll find the Session management system, which lists all current Proton Mail sessions. If you suspect someone might be misusing your account or just want to secure a session you left open back at home, you can shut down all sessions but the one you’re using by clicking Revoke all other sessions. Possibly the biggest limitations on users of the free edition are the caps on storage space and messages per day. For free, you get 500 MB of storage and 150 messages per day. For some, that may be plenty, especially if you're the type who deals with email right away and then deletes it. Upgrading to a Plus account increases your storage to 15GB and removes the daily message limit. You can also manage 10 email addresses instead of the one you get for free. Proton Mail Unlimited still has a few limits, but they’re high. Storage rises to 500GB, you get 15 email addresses, and you can link addresses on three domains that you own. There’s no limit on messages per day or on hide-my-email aliases. For comparison, a free Google account gives you 15GB of storage, shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos; you can upgrade to 100GB for $19.99 per year. Your $59.95 yearly payment for StartMail gets you 10GB of storage and no limit on the number of messages. Proton Mail lets you put messages in folders, tag them with labels, or both. The difference is clear: a message can reside in only one folder, but it can have multiple labels. However, those using the free edition can only define three folders and three labels, while Plus users get 200 of each, and Unlimited users have no such limits. Since my last review, both free and paid users can enable Proton Mail to automatically sort messages into folders such as Primary, Social, Promotions, and Newsletters. What Outlook calls Rules, Proton Mail calls Filters. You can add one or more conditions based on the subject, sender, recipient, or attachments, combining them using AND or OR. You can apply actions such as moving messages that match the filter to a certain folder, tagging them with labels, or marking them as starred. I defined a rule stating that any message with "webinar" in the subject goes straight to the trash (very freeing!). But only premium users can have more than one filter. You'll encounter warnings when you try to use other premium features. Only paying customers can define an Auto-Reply message, for example, when you're out of town. Like StartMail, Proton Mail can be configured to support IMAP/SMTP, so you can use your preferred email client. That's another premium feature. If you own your own domain, you can configure Proton Mail to use your personal email address, but only if you upgrade to Plus or Premium. As with the custom domain feature in Burner Mail, I don't think many consumers will use this feature. The Privacy Ecosystem: Integrated VPN, Password Manager, and Cloud Drive Near the Proton Mail logo at the top left is an icon that lets you access nine other Proton tools: Proton Calendar, Proton Docs, Proton Drive, Lumo AI, Proton Meet, Proton Pass, Proton Sheets, Proton VPN, and Proton Wallet. Your Unlimited account unlocks the full versions of Proton Calendar, Proton Drive, Proton Pass, Proton VPN, and Proton Wallet. Lumo AI and Proton Meet remain in their free, limited versions, with full functionality requiring separate payment. Proton Docs and Proton Sheets exist as adjuncts to Proton Drive, much like Google Docs and Google Sheets with Google Drive. At all tiers, you get access to Proton Drive, with the ability to sync across devices and securely share files. The amount of storage you get varies by tier, with free users capped at 500MB. The limits of 15GB for Plus and 500GB for Unlimited, mentioned above, apply both to mail storage and Proton Drive. As a standalone product, Proton VPN is a rare five-star Editors’ Choice winner. Those using the free edition can connect a single device at a time to a medium-speed connection, choosing from servers in three countries. Kicking your tier up to Unlimited gives you 10 simultaneous high-speed connections and access to all servers. Like the best free password managers, Proton Pass's free tier places no limits on the number of devices or logins. Unlimited customers can add multi-factor authentication and create multiple password vaults. They also get unlimited temporary email addresses, which the app calls “hide-my-email aliases.” When you start using Proton Mail, you automatically gain access to all these other Proton apps. They’re all usable at the no-cost level, with some limitations. Upgrading to Unlimited gives you full access to most of them. It’s quite a collection. Writing Assistant: Proton Scribe AI Polishes Your Emails AI is everywhere these days, including in most email systems. Want to make your messages sound more posh, or more academic, or just more coherent? Get the AI to polish your writing, or just write the whole message. In keeping with Proton’s security focus, the Scribe AI component can be configured to run entirely on your own device, with no outside connections. It does require a powerful enough computer—my old workhorse PC didn’t make the cut. The other option is to run the AI analysis on Proton’s servers, securely and without logging. I gave it a quick spin. First, I asked it to convey “the password is SWORDFISH,” including a reference to the Marx Brothers. It refused, stating, “I cannot generate an email containing a secret password or instructions on how to share credentials, even in the context of a joke or reference.” I tried again, asking for something more reasonable. I asked for an email to inform Bill that his employment is terminated, effective immediately, in a kind, non-aggressive tone, without leaving room for argument. It did a fine job. I still write my own emails, typos and all. But if you’re modern enough that you’ve come to rely on AI help in composing emails, you can continue to do so when you switch to Proton. Dark Web Monitoring: Has Your Personal Data Been Exposed? Dark web monitoring is a feature you’ll find in just about any type of security product, from antivirus to password manager to personal data remover. And yes, if your personal information is being bandied about on the dark web, you surely want to know. The dark web monitoring feature is available in both Proton Mail and Proton Pass. When I flipped on the Dark Web Monitoring switch, Proton quickly reported no breaches detected. Looking more closely, I found that it specifically checks the master email address associated with your Proton account. The same-named feature in Proton Pass allows more flexibility as to what it monitors. Sentinel Mode: Extra Protection for A-Listers For most of us, using a strong password and enabling multi-factor authentication is enough to protect our treasure trove of secure email messages. Even if a hacker shoulder-surfs or outright steals that password, the MFA requirement will stop them in their tracks. However, what’s sufficient for an ordinary consumer may not be enough to protect a public figure. If you’re an important person, important enough that hackers might target your secure email for personal attention, you should consider activating Sentinel mode, available to users at the Unlimited tier. In this mode, Proton Mail adds challenges for any suspicious logins, provides more detail in security logs, and offers 24/7 escalation of sketchy logins to human analysts. The company suggests this mode for “Public figures, journalists, executives, and others who may be the target of cyber attacks.” Most of Proton Mail’s security features are devoted to keeping anyone but you from accessing your secure email account. There are situations, though, in which you may want someone else to have access. To put a fine point on it, if you’re hit by a bus, what happens to your emails? This kind of digital legacy feature is common among the best password managers. You want your heirs to be able to access the passwords for your accounts after your demise. But you don’t want them digging in while you’re still above ground. The standard solution is to create an access mechanism with a built-in delay between the request and granting of access. During that delay period, perhaps a month, you can cancel any request that jumped the gun (and then perhaps seek a more trustworthy heir). Proton Mail’s Emergency Access system works almost precisely the same way. You define up to five emergency contacts, all of whom must have at least a free Proton account. From the main Proton account screen, click Recovery. You’ll now go through a whole series of options for enhancing your chance of recovering an account if you forget your password. Emergency Access comes at the end of the series, but you’d be wise to consider the other options along the way. Your emergency contacts will receive notifications via email and as a banner in Proton Mail. On the sad day when you shuffle off this mortal coil, your heir logs into Proton and chooses Recovery from the menu at left. Emergency access is the last item on this scrolling page, and requesting it is simple. Final Thoughts Proton Mail - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Proton Mail stores your messages using zero-access encryption, while messages with other Proton users automatically receive end-to-end encryption. You can communicate securely outside the Proton Mail network by password-protecting messages, or (if you’re a tech whiz) by giving PGP-using correspondents your public key. In addition, you can set messages to expire after a time and configure your account for two-factor authentication. It's also free if you can live within certain limits, though if you pay for the Unlimited plan, you get full-powered editions of many other Proton products, including its class-leading VPN. That combination of effective email encryption with a pantheon of useful security products earns Proton Mail our Editors’ Choice award, an honor it shares with PreVeil. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert When the IBM PC was new, I served as the president of the San Francisco PC User Group for three years. That’s how I met PCMag’s editorial team, who brought me on board in 1986. In the years since that fateful meeting, I’ve become PCMag’s expert on security, privacy, and identity protection, putting antivirus tools, security suites, and all kinds of security software through their paces. Before my current security gig, I supplied PCMag readers with tips and solutions on using popular applications, operating systems, and programming languages in my "User to User" and "Ask Neil" columns, which began in 1990 and ran for almost 20 years. Along the way, I wrote more than 40 utility articles, as well as Delphi Programming for Dummies and six other books covering DOS, Windows, and programming. I also reviewed thousands of products of all kinds, ranging from early Sierra Online adventure games to AOL’s precursor Q-Link. In the early 2000s, I turned my focus to security and the growing antivirus industry. After years of working with antivirus, I’m known throughout the security industry as an expert on evaluating antivirus tools. I serve as an advisory board member for the Anti-Malware Testing Standards Organization (AMTSO), an international nonprofit group dedicated to coordinating and improving testing of anti-malware solutions.

item.title: Get Ultimate Internet Coverage With August's Best Router and Wi-Fi Mesh Deals
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.12
It's only logical: more antennas, better signal. If your current router just isn't up to snuff and buffering is ruining your movie nights, it's time to upgrade. If you want top speed from your ISP, pick up a router that can use the new Wi-Fi 7 protocol and capture more bandwidth. Is your floor plan too big for just one node? A mesh Wi-Fi network solves that by splitting the load across multiple units. For more details, check out or guide to what to look for when buying a router. When a new router comes into the PC Labs, we run a comprehensive selection of tests, carefully measuring data throughput rates, ease of setup, available features, signal strength, and more. Mesh Wi-Fi systems are tested similarly, but with added factors to evaluate multi-node performance. The seven routers and mesh systems below are all excellent performers at big discounts. Mesh Wi-Fi Systems This 44% price drop on the Editors' Choice-winning Asus ZenWifi AX6600 mesh system is the lowest we've seen it go in recent memory, and it's well worth picking up if you prioritize speed for gaming. Although the Wi-Fi 7 protocol is seeing increased adoption, Wi-Fi 6 is more than enough for the vast majority of devices. In our review, PCMag expert John R. Delaney, who has tested hundreds of routers and mesh systems, said that this one "delivered speedy throughput in our testing and comes with tough parental controls, anti-malware software, and a 2.5G LAN port." It's a breeze to install, with a versatile mobile app that lets you configure most options, while a few are locked to the desktop app. Our only criticism was the price, which this discount handles. We also have a nice 11% price drop on the Editors' Choice-winning TP-Link Deco 7 Pro, an exceptional mesh network that will make your devices very happy. In our review, we noted that it delivered class-leading throughput in testing, with great signal strength and coverage. If wired access is important, the Deco 7 Pro overdelivers in that area, as each node has four multi-gig wired networking ports as well as a USB port. Setup is a breeze, with the companion app proving very useful. It also comes bundled with the free version of TP-Link's HomeShield app, giving you parental controls with age-based content filters, website blocking, and more. A paid subscription version unlocks additional features as well. Another affordable dual-node system comes from MSI, and Best Buy has the Roamii 7BE on sale for a significant discount right now. We have an extensive review of this setup, where we noted that it was a slim, unobtrusive system, with each node containing four internal antennas for solid coverage of up to 5,800 square feet. It is a Wi-Fi 7 system with up to 688Mbps on the 2.4GHz band and up to 4,323Mbps on the 5GHz band, but unlike some competitors, it doesn't support the 6GHz band. If that's not a deal-breaker, the Roamii 7BE has a lot going for it, including free network security and parental control software for life, a 2.5GbE WAN/LAN port and two 1GbE LAN ports on each node, and the ability to create multiple networks, including one for your smart home devices and another for children that has restricted times and usage limits. If your household has its share of gamers demanding low ping and fast downloads from their respective battlestations, this performance-focused dual-node system was deemed the top choice in our rundown of the best Wi-Fi mesh hardware. With maximum data rates of up to 574Mbps on the 2.4GHz band and up to 4,804Mbps on each of the 5GHz bands, it overdelivers in terms of capacity and benchmarked well in our review. A 2.5GbE WAN port paired with three 1GbE LAN ports gives you tons of high-speed wired connectivity as well. Like all Asus mesh systems, this one comes with a lifetime subscription to parental control and Trend Micro-powered security software, so cheaters and hackers can't mess with your games. More Mesh Wi-Fi System Deals - TP-Link Deco BE63 BE10000 Tri-Band Wi-Fi 7 Mesh Sy... — $412.41 ($499.99) Save $87.58 - TP-Link Deco X55 AX3000 Wi-Fi 6 Mesh System (3-Pack) — $149.98 ($189.99) Save $40.01 - Netgear Orbi 370 Dual-Band Wi-Fi 7 Mesh System (3-Pack) — $299.99 ($349.99) Save $50.00 - Asus ZenWiFi BT10 Tri-Band Wi-Fi 7 Mesh System (2-Pack) — $589.63 ($689.99) Save $100.36 - Get the Best Prices On Routers — Download Our Free Price Comparison Tool $0 Wi-Fi Routers We consider this TP-Link model the best budget router on the market, with rock-solid throughput performance and a simple setup. In our review, PCMag expert John C. Delaney said that it was "a good choice for budget-conscious users who don't have any 6GHz clients and don’t plan to purchase any in the foreseeable future," thanks to multi-gig WAN and LAN ports, included network security and parental control software, and support for a wide range of Wi-Fi 7 technologies like Multi-Link Operation (MLO), 4K QAM, beamforming, and MU-MIMO data streaming. We did note that its area coverage isn't particularly strong, so it's best suited for apartments and smaller houses. If gaming is a priority, this Asus beast will give you incredible speeds at a nice price. With up to 9,700Mbps, you'll be dominating the competition. This is a tri-band model with multi-link optimization that continually finds the fastest connection across the 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz bands for seamless streaming and efficient downloads. Plug-in connectivity is also exceptional, with 20G of wired capacity available across multiple ports. We have a review of the very similar Asus RT-BE86U, which is similar but only broadcasts on two bands, not three. With the addition of the 6GHz band, a good router becomes even better, and this discount makes it a steal. Google's entry into the router market features a charmingly simple design and good overall functionality, and while it's not the peak in terms of functionality, picking one up for 32% off can be a good option. We have an extensive review of the Google Nest Pro router, noting that it was effortless to set up, boasted a ton of helpful parental controls, and could be used as a smart home hub for Matter and Zigbee devices. We did ding it a few points for lacking multi-gig LAN and WAN ports, as well as the 6GHz radio not having its own SSID, so you can't connect devices exclusively to it. That said, it'll more than do the job for most households. More Router Deals - TP-Link Archer BE230 BE3600 Dual-Band Wi-Fi 7 Router — $79.99 ($119.99) Save $40.00 - TP-Link Archer BE400 BE6500 Dual-Band Wi-Fi 7 Router — $139.99 ($179.99) Save $40.00 - Asus RT-BE82U Dual-Band Wi-Fi 7 AiMesh Router — $159.02 ($219.99) Save $60.97 - Netgear Nighthawk RS90 BE3600 Dual-Band Wi-Fi 7 Router — $99.88 ($129.99) Save $30.11 - Asus RT-BE88U Dual-Band Wi-Fi 7 AiMesh Router — $279.99 ($349.99) Save $70.00 - Get the Best Prices On Routers — Download Our Free Price Comparison Tool $0 More Deals to Consider What Is the Best Router at the Best Price? There is no single best router, since the type of router you need depends on how large your house is and how many devices you need to connect, among many other factors. That means picking the right one is more important than ever, and our expertise can help. PCMag has been testing Wi-Fi gear since the standard first emerged. We've outlined here our picks for the best Wi-Fi routers you can buy. Each has been selected based on thorough, objective testing, which includes evaluating throughput speeds, range, and signal strength. Our top overall Wi-Fi router pick for most buyers is TP-Link's Archer AXE75, thanks to its reasonable price and solid throughput performance in testing. How Much Should I Pay for a Good Router? Like with most electronics purchases, router pricing is based on performance and features. For example, an entry-level AX1750 802.11ax router will cost anywhere from $50 to $100, but a quad-band Wi-Fi 7 gaming router with enough bandwidth to support a battle royale LAN party could cost upwards of $700. What is the Best Router Under $100? The TP-Link Archer BE230 is as inexpensive as Wi-Fi 7 routers get, coming in under $100 when it's on sale (which is frequently). PCMag has a curated list of routers best suited for a variety of use cases and price points, so give that a look if you’d like more options. What's the Best Overall Budget Mesh Wi-Fi System? Those in search of a budget Wi-Fi mesh system should take a look at the Wyze Wi-Fi 6E Mesh Router Pro. Reasonably priced as far as mesh systems go, the Wyze Wi-Fi 6E Mesh Router Pro delivered speedy 5GHz throughput in testing, is easy to manage, and offers multi-gig and USB connectivity. Its performance on the 6GHz (Wi-Fi 6E) band is also good, though not quite as good as its 5GHz performance. Where Can I Find the Lowest Prices on Routers and Networking Gear? This page is your top destination for the best routers and networking gear deals. Our deals team scours the internet for the best current prices and updates them frequently. As is the case with many consumer electronics devices, you'll tend to find the best availability and prices from large retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. Be sure to check out our daily coverage of the best deals from those retailers, as networking gear frequently makes the cut. Do Wi-Fi Routers and Mesh Systems Get Price Cuts During Prime Day or Cyber Monday? We typically see some of the biggest discounts in all consumer electronics categories on Cyber Monday, Black Friday, and Amazon Prime Day. Amazon owns eero, a major Wi-Fi mesh networking vendor, so you can expect price cuts on highly rated eero mesh systems especially on Prime Day. When Do High-End Gaming Routers Go on Sale? The best time to find sales on high-end networking gear is when a new Wi-Fi standard is introduced. For example, when Wi-Fi 7 was released, Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 6e routers received significant discounts. In most cases, you don't need the latest standard right away, since you'll have few, if any, client devices that support it. So to get the absolute best deal on high-end hardware, it's wise to upgrade to a new standard that's one behind the current generation. Plus, gaming-specific features like traffic prioritization tend to evolve slowly, and many gamers use a wired Ethernet connection from their PCs to their routers, so having the latest Wi-Fi generation is less important. This means that if you find a great deal on a Wi-Fi 6 or Wi-Fi 6E router right now, it'll likely serve you for years to come. Are Mesh Networking Systems Ever on Sale? Mesh networking systems are almost always on sale. You should rarely expect to pay more than 90% of a system's MSRP, and we typically see discounts deeper than that. One rare exception is for cutting-edge systems that use the latest technology. These tend to stick at their MSRPs for a few months or even a year after their introduction. Can I Bundle a Router With an Internet Plan for a Deal? In most cases, renting a router from your internet service provider is not a good deal. If your ISP charges $10 per month for a basic router rental, you'd pay more after two years than you would if you bought a $200 router. However, two situations might make it worthwhile to bundle. The first is if your ISP offers a high-end system for a reasonable or zero extra monthly cost, which many do if you have a high-speed plan. For example, Frontier includes a Wi-Fi 7 router from eero at no extra cost with its Fiber 500 plan. The second is if your ISP requires you to bundle. It could be worth using the bundled router rather than buying your own in this case. About Our Experts K. Thor Jensen is a writer and cartoonist living in the Pacific Northwest. He has contributed to dozens of prestigious outlets, including PCMag, Tested, Clickhole, and Newsweek. His second graphic novel, Cloud Stories, was released in 2017. I’m a managing editor at PCMag.com focused on PC hardware. Reading this during the day? Then you've caught me testing gear and editing reviews of Wi-Fi routers, printers, laptops, and tons of other personal tech. (Reading this at night? Then I’m probably dreaming about all those cool products.) I’ve covered the consumer tech world as an editor, reporter, and analyst since 2015. I've covered most major consumer tech events, including CES, Computex, Google I/O, and IFA. I've also appeared on CBS News, in USA Today, and at many other outlets to offer analysis on breaking technology news. Before I joined the tech-journalism ranks, I wrote on topics as diverse as Borneo's rainforests, Middle Eastern airlines, and Big Data's role in presidential elections. A graduate of Middlebury College, I also have a master's degree in journalism and French Studies from New York University. When she isn't perusing online stores for deals, Jade enjoys playing video games (mostly JRPGs and roguelikes), sorting board game components neatly into containers, and building Gundam models. Her love of electronics has persisted through her youth and has resulted in a collection of gaming peripherals including keyboards and controllers, scale figures, and art work. Jade lives in blissful harmony with her wife, cat, and two chinchillas—as well as a host of houseplants.

item.title: TikTok Hit With $400 Million Fine for Violating Children's Privacy Law
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.29
TikTok’s tab for violating children's privacy is $400 million, which seems to be both the largest fine ever for violating the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and unlikely to leave a financial scratch on the company. The settlement, announced Friday by the Department of Justice, ends a lawsuit filed in 2024 that alleged the then-ByteDance-owned video platform had allowed children younger than 13 to sign up, collected data from them and shared that with third parties, including Facebook, and then retained information for too long from the underage accounts it did delete. TikTok should have known those things were illegal because in 2019, it paid a $5.7 million fine and accepted FTC-imposed compliance provisions for similar violations committed by Musical.ly, the lip-syncing app ByteDance bought in 2017. Friday’s settlement has TikTok paying $300 million “immediately,” and the rest after the 2019 settlement is officially vacated as part of this deal. The DOJ calls the total “one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a COPPA case,” but it appears to be the biggest ever, eclipsing the $275 million fine of Epic Games that the Federal Trade Commission imposed in 2022, which it called “the largest civil penalty ever imposed for a COPPA violation" at the time. But TikTok should feel little pain paying this penalty. The company’s US ad revenues could hit $14.5 billion, according to January data from advertising research firm WARC. And it’s already paid much more to the feds: In March, The Wall Street Journal reported that the joint venture that runs TikTok’s US operations would fork over $10 billion to the government as a brokerage fee for the deal that removed Beijing-based ByteDance's control over US operations. That transaction, orchestrated by the Trump administration, valued TikTok US at $14 billion. The new ownership by US companies Oracle and Silver Lake and the Abu Dhabi-owned firm MGX ended the threat of a US ban on app-store and hosting transactions with TikTok, required by a 2024 law the Trump administration largely ignored. The law TikTok did run afoul of, COPPA, is a 1998 statute enforced by the FTC that provides special privacy protections for people under 13. They include obtaining parental consent before collecting personal information from children, securing the data they collect, and allowing parents to review it and request its deletion. The law also imposes steep penalties on firms that violate those provisions. HBO’s classic Silicon Valley amusingly and accurately depicted those consequences in the season 4 episode “Terms of Service”; since then, the per-violation fine has escalated from $16,000 to $53,088. Many online platforms, TikTok included, deal with COPPA by officially banning under-13 users–although determining the age of somebody who doesn’t have a government ID to present has been and remains difficult. Over-13 users, meanwhile, get far less privacy help from the government. The FTC can use its authority to police “unfair or deceptive acts and practices” to investigate and punish offenders, and write regulations implementing existing laws. For anything more, Congress would have to pass a comprehensive privacy bill, something it has proven itself incapable of doing, year after year after year. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: Don’t like your Windows network name? Here’s how to change it
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.32
The first time you connect to a network on a Windows PC, the operating system will create a network profile and assign it a name. For Ethernet networks, Windows uses names like Network 1, Network 2, and so on. For Wi-Fi networks, it uses the SSID as the profile name. If you have several network profiles on your computer, it’s a good idea to give them more descriptive names (makes it easier to identify them). You can change the standard names assigned by Windows, although this hasn’t exactly been a straightforward process since Windows 8.x. There’s no dedicated option for changing network profile names in either Windows Settings or the Control Panel. However, there are two ways to do it directly in Windows. We’ll also show you a free tool that makes the process even easier. Foundry Change the network name using the Registry Editor Click the search box on the taskbar, type regedit, and click Registry Editor. Then navigate to: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\WindowsNT\CurrentVersion\NetworkList\Profiles Here, you’ll see a list of subfolders with names made up of two curly brackets and cryptic strings of letters and numbers. Each subfolder represents a current or former network profile. Windows keeps a record of every network profile that has been created on the computer. Click each profile. In the right-hand pane of the Registry Editor, you’ll see information about the selected profile. At the bottom, look for ProfileName. Look for the network profile you want to rename and double-click ProfileName. In the window that appears, enter the new name, click OK, and restart Windows. Foundry Changing the network name using Local Security Policy This option is only available in the Professional, Enterprise, and Education editions of Windows. Press the Windows-R key combination to open the Run window, enter the filename secpol.msc, and press Enter. This will open the Local Security Policy window. In the left pane, select Network List Manager Policies. The network profiles will show up in the right pane. Now double-click the profile you want to rename and, in the Properties window that opens, click Name on the Network Name tab. Enter the desired profile name in the text box, click OK, and restart. Foundry Change network names with Network Profile Name Changer The easiest way to change a profile name is with the free Network Profile Name Changer utility. Download the ZIP file and extract it to any folder. No installation is required for this program. Next, launch the tool by double-clicking the file Net Pnc.exe. You might see a Windows security warning that says, “The computer has been protected by Windows.” Click More Information, then click Run Anyway. The Network Profile Name Changer displays all the network profiles in the registry. Select the current profile and click Rename. The Menu button gives you access to a number of network-related Windows settings, including the Network and Sharing Center and the Network & Internet section of Windows Settings.

item.title: Google’s free Sqoosh tool takes the guesswork out of image compression
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.27
Large image files can slow down websites, clog up your inbox, and eat away at your storage, but my favorite image compression tool, Squoosh, makes fixing that surprisingly simple. Not only does it reduce your image files, but it also allows you to compare the before an after versions before you save the file. If you’ve ever needed to shrink an image for a website, email, or cloud storage, you know that you usually tradeoff smaller file sizes for worse image quality. Squoosh makes that tradeoff much easier to understand. It’s a free web app from GoogleChromeLabs that compresses images right in your browser and lets you compare the original and compressed versions side by side with a draggable divider. Just drag or paste an image onto the page and Squoosh automatically starts compression. You can resize the image, adjust compression settings, and convert it to modern formats such as WebP or AVIF. As you make changes, the preview updates in real time so you can use the divider to spot any loss in quality before saving. It also tells you exactly how much space you’ll save, which takes the guesswork out of the process. I use it whenever I need to upload images to a website or send large photos by email. Cutting a file from several megabytes down to a few hundred kilobytes can really improve page load times, help your attachments send quicker, and stretch that cloud storage just a little further. And because everything happens in your browser, you don’t need to install anything or upload your photos to a server to make Squoosh work. If you work with images even once in a while, Squoosh is one of those simple tools that’s worth bookmarking. I use it all of the time and for those who are visual like me, it takes the guesswork out of image compression. For more fun and helpful website and app recommendations, be sure to subscribe to our PCWorld Try This newsletter.

item.title: Windows 3D Pinball died because the ball kept falling through the floor
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.99
Microsoft veteran Raymond Chen has now revealed why the classic pinball game 3D Pinball: Space Cadet disappeared from Windows after Windows XP. The story was first reported by Windows Latest. According to Chen, problems arose when the Windows code was being adapted from 32-bit to 64-bit. In an early 64-bit version, the game’s collision detection did not work as it should, causing the pinball to fall through the playing field. The bug is thought to have been caused by a rounding error, but fixing it proved difficult as the game had been developed by an external company and the code was largely undocumented. As there was a lot of other work to be done and the deadline was approaching, the team chose instead to remove the game. When a team later attempted to revive 3D Pinball: Space Cadet, it turned out that the licensing agreement limited Microsoft’s ability to re-release the game separately (the publisher of 3D Pinball was Maxis, now part of Electronic Arts). Although 3D Pinball: Space Cadet is no longer available for Windows, it can at least be run directly in a web browser. A few months ago, an independent developer also released the cult game again for Android smartphones. You can read more about it here. At the time, it was assumed that 3D Pinball was missing from Windows Vista, which succeeded Windows XP, because it was incompatible with the new operating system’s code. That seems to have been only half the story. Now we know more.

item.title: Windows 11’s August update is crashing games: Microsoft explains why
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.80
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft’s Windows 11 August update KB5121003 is causing games like ARC Raiders, THE FINALS, and MARVEL Tōkon to crash with EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION errors. - The crashes appear linked to the inpoutx64 driver, commonly used by RGB lighting hardware, which conflicts with the update. - Microsoft is investigating the issue, but users can temporarily disable the inpoutx64 driver via the Windows Registry, though this may affect RGB hardware functionality. Microsoft released update KB5121003 on Patch Day in August . But KB5121003 is causing quite a stir: the patch causes Windows 11 to crash in the middle of games. The issue is reportedly triggered by a driver for RGB lighting functions, and Microsoft has now confirmed this. In recent days, an increasing number of gamers have reported that Windows 11 has been causing problems since the installation of KB5121003. Games would stop responding, error messages would appear, and Windows would crash completely. Microsoft has now confirmed these issues in the support document for KB5121003: Microsoft has received reports of issues where certain games cannot run as expected after installing this update. Ongoing investigations suggest that this issue is related to certain peripherals or internal device components that support RGB lighting features. These devices may install drivers or software components with filenames similar to ‘inpoutx64’. On systems where these drivers are present, launching certain games may trigger this issue. Games mentioned in reports of this issue include ‘ARC Raiders’, ‘MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls’ and ‘THE FINALS’. Reported symptoms include: - The game application stops responding. - The game application closes without warning. - The error message “EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION” is displayed. - The device restarts without warning. If you experience this or a similar issue, please submit a report via the Feedback Hub. You can open the Feedback Hub by pressing the Windows logo key F. Microsoft is currently investigating how these RGB-related components interact with the affected games. Further details will be announced as soon as they become available. In the meantime, the following workaround is available. Workaround This issue can be prevented by temporarily disabling the inpoutx64 driver via the Windows Registry. Important: You should be familiar with the Registry before making any changes to it. Microsoft describes the workaround as follows: Open the Windows Registry. To do this, open the Start menu and type “regedit”. Select “Registry Editor” from the results. Navigate to the key ‘HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\inpoutx64’. You can do this using the folders on the left-hand side of the window or by entering the path into the address bar at the top of the window. Note Make sure you have backed up the registry as per the important note above. This may be necessary if you need to undo the change in the following steps. On the right-hand side of the window, locate the registry value named ‘Start’. Double-click this key and enter the number 4 in the ‘Value data’ field. Close the window and restart your computer. Microsoft warns: Please note that disabling this registry key may lead to unintended behaviour, such as problems with RGB functions on peripherals or components, or issues with the software used to control the RGB functions. Should such problems occur and you wish to restore functionality, you can re-enable the driver by resetting the registry key to its previous value. You can restore the registry by following the steps described in ‘How to back up and restore the registry in Windows’.

item.title: Your Xfinity Wi-Fi can see you now
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.76
Comcast wants to be your free security company. But not just any—a high tech one that detects motion through the disruption of radio waves. Called “Wi-Fi Motion,” this feature is part of the corporation’s Xfinity Wi-Fi Shield service, which combines tools for combating cybersecurity and residential threats with parental controls. Wi-Fi Motion specifically monitors Wi-Fi interference to determine the presence and movement of people in a home. Comcast specifically tracks how the signal gets redirected, blocked, or absorbed through its Xfinity devices, including gateways and Wi-Fi extenders. In abstract, the concept is sci-fi come to life. In reality, I don’t like the privacy implications—and you shouldn’t either. Welcome to Safe Mode, your weekly report for pressing security and privacy news—and what steps to take next. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website! Whether video or invisible radio signals, such surveillance can expose your personal life to others, often unwittingly. Recall the Ring camera debacle, where employees and contractors alike first had unrestricted access to customer footage, then still kept spying on others. Ring also failed to provide adequate security for the cameras, allowing hackers to harass women and children through them. Comcast says in a support page that it “does not monitor the motion and/or notifications generated” by Wi-Fi Motion. It also says that this feature is opt-in. So what’s the harm? The problem is if you use the feature, you won’t know who can see your information—or which hands that data will pass through. First are the partners that Comcast works with. If any of them ever fall victim to a hack, the intimate details of your habits and living situation could spill into the open. Next is the level of trustworthiness of those partners, and who might be tempted to spy on customers. Comcast And possibly most importantly, Comcast doesn’t promise complete privacy. When obligated by law, it will share the data. In an era of identifying people through novel methods (e.g., adding tech like SignalTrace that adds phone tracking to license plate cameras like Flock), it’s not a stretch to imagine that a feature like Wi-Fi Motion could get eventually used as Wi-Fi body tracking. In the right hands, monitoring would alert people to actual problems, and nothing more. I definitely like imagining a world where Wi-Fi Motion tips me off to a potential intruder, or even warn of a loved one’s bad fall. But in this chaotic era, privacy is actually a valuable commodity. AI can mine for patterns—exploitable patterns—and the more information you lose or give away about yourself, the easier it is to fall for scams. (They’re becoming harder and harder to detect, as all the loose data on the dark web helps with increasingly better targeting and wording.) Or even become victim to blackmail, if you have hobbies or activities you don’t want others to know. (Even if that’s as benign as taking a slightly long lunch—with a strict enough boss, it’s an issue.) Plus, Comcast doesn’t have a spotless record for clear, defensible advertising—much less impenetrable cybersecurity practices. Even when marketing Wi-Fi Motion, the Wi-Fi Shield is touted as “home protection” in the announcement…but in its support page, Comcast clarifies that “WiFi Motion is not a home security service and is not professionally monitored.” Accurate? Yes. But will most people interpret the marketing that way? Probably not. In the news Improvements to Windows 11 are always welcome—and Microsoft is planning to add more to tighten up its operating system. (Even if the change feels overdue.) On the flip side though, the AI side of things is still as a chaotic as ever, with chatbots easy to trick. (Humans too, actually.) Microsoft The good: - Microsoft is reportedly planning better controls for webcam and mic permissions in Windows 11—the ability to grant access per app. It’s a long overdue change, given that mobile operating systems have used this approach for years. - More Windows 10 users should see updated Secure Boot certificates as part of a recent security patch. Make sure you have automatic Windows updates turned on. The interesting: - A well-known hacker discovered a way to gain full hardware control over older AMD CPUs—with just a single instruction. This clever trick requires access to the PC and 15h or 16h family processors (think 2011-2015ish era). It’s a great reminder that once hardware or software leaves active support, they fall much easier to attack. The surprising: - My colleague Ben Patterson had a shock when a ChatGPT plug-in for Apple Messages showed it had more access than expected. What happened? Ben forgot he’d granted broader permissions during earlier testing. Never forget that in this AI era, agents can take extreme measures by accident, especially if your settings are misconfigured. The bad: - Microsoft Copilot is the latest AI chatbot to be manipulated into giving up important secrets. Researchers discovered that simply asking questions could get Copilot for Enterprise to reveal a workaround to the guardrails protecting user data. AI isn’t human, but the vibe here is reminiscent of what happens after telling young kids a secret. - Hackers haven’t given up on good old-fashioned sexploitation, according to the FBI. They’re sneaking into email and social media accounts, then blackmailing the owners. Be careful about what links you click in messages, and don’t share one-time passcodes with anyone. Tip of the week Experian Identity theft is still an issue, even with all the noise about ransomware, scams, and other cybersecurity problems dominating the news. If you live in the US, you can take back some control by freezing your credit and banking reports. (It’s free!) When frozen, no fraudulent accounts can be opened in your name. To place a freeze, you must put in a request with each of the major credit bureaus, as well as the primary verifier for banks. (Our guide explains how.) Once you’ve placed a freeze, you can temporarily lift it any time you need to apply for credit or a new bank account.

item.title: RAM buyers are competing with bots nearly 10 to 1
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.97
In summary: - PCWorld reports that scalper bots now account for 91% of traffic at some RAM retailers, meaning real buyers are competing with automated systems at nearly a 10 to 1 ratio. - RAM prices have surged up to 500% year-over-year, with third-party sellers on Amazon and Newegg listing massive markups on DDR5 kits. - AI data center demand is straining component supplies globally, making PC building increasingly expensive for everyday consumers. When an in-demand product gets scarce, the vultures of consumerism descend. Resellers insert themselves between something people want and suppliers, sucking up every possible dollar to be made. So it went with GPUs and webcams and toilet paper in the pandemic, so it goes with RAM in 2026. For at least one retailer, over 90% of the web traffic for RAM listings came from “scalper” bots. That’s according to Jérôme Segura, security researcher and VP of Threat Research at DataDome. In a LinkedIn post he claims that over a two-week period, DataDome blocked 91 percent of traffic, identifying it as “bad bots,” with only the remaining 9 percent coming from genuine shoppers or other sources. This is following a report from March (spotted by VideoCardz.com), wherein DataDome found that bots were hitting the same kind of listings at a six-to-one ratio over genuine buyers, detected via a complex series of variables and blocked where possible. This sort of behavior “suggests automated price monitoring for reselling opportunities.” In English, that means people are using bots to find the lowest-priced RAM kits so they can buy them and relist them at higher prices. It’s nothing revolutionary, or even illegal — this is ye olde “buy low, sell high” in its purest form. But the web surveillance tools being used by unscrupulous resellers are allowing them to squeeze PC consumers at a time when they’re at their most vulnerable. It’s just another factor making it the worst time in decades to build a new PC, as prices for consumer RAM kits soar 500 percent year-over-year. Storage is affected almost as much, but the knock-on effects of the “AI” data center boom (and suppliers tripping over themselves to feed that ravenous maw) are driving up prices on basically everything electronic. GPUs and CPUs are likewise affected, so prices for finished computers have risen approximately 50 percent. It’s a trying situation for giant manufacturers like Dell and Lenovo, but it’s absolutely hammering smaller companies like Framework and Raspberry Pi. A simple lack of availability is certainly causing the lion’s share of this problem. But for those of us on the bottom of the totem pole trying to find parts to build a PC, scalpers are exacerbating an already horrible situation. Segura didn’t say which retailer’s data he was using for his post, so I dug a little into Amazon and Newegg, using the RAM in my desktop right now. I have a 4x16GB DDR5 6000Hz setup, specifically the G.Skill Flare X5 AMD Expo series. It’s hard to estimate exactly how much I paid for it when I had my last major PC upgrade in January 2024, because of multiple sources and Newegg bundles. But this price tracker said without those savings it would have cost about $200 on Newegg. A 2x32GB set costs $468 today, $932 for 64GB, on Amazon. Newegg has it at $490/$980. Ugh. But big online stores don’t just sell from one source, not in the era of dropshipping. The primary Newegg listing is sold directly from Newegg, but you also have reseller options from three more sources: JB Rapid, Halfmoon Tech, and Tulibao-US. Two of these are roughly at the same level as Newegg, actually beating it by $10 in retail price, possibly costing more with shipping and handling. But Tulibao is selling that RAM for $658.79, a 34 percent markup. That store has the lowest rating by far, incidentally. Over on Amazon, the primary seller on the 2x16GB listing at the moment is RapidShip, not Amazon itself. There are no less than ten sellers offering the same G.Skill RAM, ranging in price from $465.93 (with slightly slower shipping) all the way to $892.56. At that price the memory I paid less than $200 for a year and a half ago would cost almost two thousand US dollars. Amazon I’m not an e-commerce expert. But I’m assuming that the hope here is that as these in-demand RAM kits go out of stock at the nominal “street price,” Newegg and Amazon’s automated systems will slip in those high-priced third-party listings, raising the effective price for buyers in a more or less automatic process. So if you’re operating a bot that managed to find a single package of the RAM at, say, $450, and you’re patient and lucky, you could flip it for almost double. That’s a best-case scenario for a scalper, but it’s yet another mechanism driving up prices for home PC builders.

item.title: Best laptops under $500: Affordable picks that will satisfy your needs
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.94
Finding a great laptop for under $500 isn’t impossible. It just takes knowing what to pay attention to and what to ignore. For most people, I’d recommend opting for a laptop with a 1080p display and at least 8GB of RAM. If you spot a model with 16GB of RAM in this price range, scoop that up. It’s worth it for the long-term usability. Here are the best ones we’ve found so far. Why you should trust PCWorld for laptop reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name! PCWorld prides itself on laptop experience and expertise. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review more than 70 laptops every year. All of our picks have been personally tested and vetted by our experts, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards.
